lessons.title: Associated Types

answers: Never, associated types are always better
When one type should implement the trait several times
Only for iterators
writing.exampleCaption: One implementation per type, so the output never has to be annotated.
writing.explanation:
A trait parameter can distinguish multiple implementations for the same implementing type. An associated type is chosen by each particular implementation; a trait may have both parameters and associated types. For a non-generic trait such as `Iterator`, one implementation fixes that type’s `Item`. `Iterator` uses `Item` this way, which is why you write `Iterator<Item = u32>` rather than passing the element type at every call site.

An associated type is a type chosen by a particular implementation of a trait. `Iterator::Item` is the classic example: once a type implements `Iterator`, its `Item` is fixed for that implementation. A caller can write a bound such as `I: Iterator<Item = u32>` to say exactly which stream it accepts. This is different from giving the trait a type parameter that might allow the same implementer to implement several versions.

In the `Container` example, `Bag` chooses `String` for `Item`. The `get` method then returns `Option<&String>`, borrowing an element from the bag rather than copying it. Read `Option<&Self::Item>` from the inside out: there may be no element, and when there is one, it is a reference to the implementer's chosen item type. Try changing the bag to hold `u32`; the associated type declaration and implementation return type must change together.

Associated types make caller signatures shorter and communicate that there is one natural output type for a given implementation. They do not make a value dynamic at runtime. Compare a trait with `type Item` to a generic trait parameter in a toy design and ask whether a single implementer should reasonably have multiple item types. Choose the form that matches the relationship in your model. The compiler will enforce the choice wherever the trait is used.

An associated type also helps documentation: the implementation can name its element once, and every method uses that same choice. This is useful for parsers, streams, and containers where one implementer has a natural output. If an API really needs several output types for the same implementer, a generic trait parameter may describe the contract better.
writing.feedback: `From<T>` is generic precisely because a type converts from many others.
writing.question: When should you prefer a generic parameter instead?
writing.rule: An associated type is fixed per trait implementation; trait parameters can distinguish implementations for the same type.
writing.success: `parse` returns that type, and callers never have to name it.
writing.summary: An associated type fixes one output type per implementation.
writing.task: Implement `Parser` once by choosing its `Output` type.

recall.answer: `v.iter()` has `Item = &u32`, not `u32`, so the associated-type bound fails (E0271). Pass `v.iter().copied()` to yield `u32` values, or `v.into_iter()` if you no longer need `v`.

recall.question: If `Iterator` used a type parameter (`Iterator<T>`) instead of `type Item`, what would become worse for code that uses iterators?
recall.answer: One type could implement `Iterator<u32>` and `Iterator<String>` at once, so the item type of `it.next()` would be ambiguous and callers would have to name it. With `type Item`, each iterator type has exactly one item type, fixed by its implementation.

lessons.title: Operator Traits

answers: Into is derived alongside From automatically
A blanket impl gives Into to everything that implements From
The compiler special-cases .into() for every type
writing.exampleCaption: `Add` powers `+` and `Display` powers `{}`, so `Money` reads like a built-in.
writing.explanation:
`a + b` calls `Add::add`, `{}` calls `Display::fmt`, and `.into()` calls `Into`, which you get for free by implementing `From`. Because they are normal traits, your own types participate in the same syntax as the built-in ones, and the compiler checks the result type at every use.

Operator syntax in Rust is backed by trait implementations. `a + b` invokes `Add::add`, and the implementation selects an associated `Output` type. In the `Money` example, adding two money values yields another `Money`; the newtype prevents an ordinary integer from being treated as money without an explicit conversion. This is useful because a small wrapper can make invalid operations harder to write while keeping familiar arithmetic syntax.

Do not overload an operator merely because you can. Readers expect `+` to combine values predictably; surprising side effects or hidden I/O make code harder to trust. Decide whether addition consumes operands, borrows them, or needs multiple implementations. The sample's `Money` is `Copy`, so by-value addition is cheap. A large owned type may benefit from reference-based implementations to avoid unnecessary moves. Use checked arithmetic or a wider representation if overflow matters for the domain.

`Display` and `Debug` serve different readers: `Display` is an intentional user-facing representation, while `Debug` helps inspect a value during development. `From<T> for U` expresses an infallible conversion and provides `Into<U>` automatically; a fallible conversion belongs in `TryFrom`. Implement a formatter for `Money`, add two values, and compare the result with your expected units. Keep the trait's semantic promise as clear as its syntax.

For a domain type, specify units and error behavior before implementing arithmetic. Money measured in cents should not add to a temperature, and a conversion from floating-point input may be lossy or fallible. A `From` implementation must not hide a failure; use `TryFrom` when invalid input is possible. Write tests for zero, negative values if allowed, and overflow boundaries. Operator syntax makes code compact, but the type system and tests must keep its meaning precise.
writing.feedback: The standard library has `impl<T, U: From<T>> Into<U> for T`.
writing.question: Why does `.into()` work without writing an `Into` impl?
writing.rule: Implement From, and Into is generated for you — never implement both.
writing.success: `500_u32.into()` produces a `Money`, and you can say where its `Into` came from.
writing.summary: Operators and conversions are ordinary traits you can implement.
writing.task: Give `Money` a `From<u32>` implementation and convert with `.into()`.

recall.question: With the lesson's `Money` type, what does `println!("{}", Money(100) + Money(250))` print, and what does that reveal about its `Display`?
recall.answer: `+` calls `Add::add`, giving `Money(350)`, and `{}` calls `Display::fmt`, which prints `3.5`, not `3.50`. Formatting cents through `f64` drops the trailing zero, so a money formatter should print whole units and two-digit cents explicitly.

recall.question: Why should converting user-entered text into `Money` be `TryFrom<&str>` rather than `From<&str>`?
recall.answer: `From` promises an infallible conversion, so it could only panic or invent a value on bad text. `TryFrom` returns a `Result` and makes failure part of the contract; like `From` gives `Into`, it gives you `try_into()` for free.

answers: String is Copy
inspect only borrowed it
println! restores it
writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A parameter of type `String` takes ownership, while `&str` only borrows text. Read the signature before deciding whether the caller should keep using its value.

A function signature is an ownership map. `fn inspect(text: &str)` asks for temporary read access and lets the caller keep its `String`. `fn store(text: String)` takes ownership, so the caller cannot use that binding after the call unless the function returns it or the caller cloned it beforehand. A parameter like `i32` is passed by value too, but `i32` is `Copy`, which leaves the original usable. The syntax is the same; the type determines the effect.

Walk through the example: `name` owns its bytes, `&name` creates a borrowed view for `inspect`, and the borrow ends after its final use in the call. The last `println!` can therefore read `name`. Change `inspect` to accept `String` and pass `name` without `&`; the final print now triggers a move error. Returning a `String` is a legitimate design if the function transforms ownership, but a printing helper has no reason to consume its input.

When designing an API, use `&str` if any UTF-8 text view will do, `&String` only when the `String` container itself matters, and `String` when ownership or mutation independent of the caller is required. For mutable access without transfer, use `&mut String`. Try calling one borrowed helper with both a string literal and an owned string. The more flexible signature often makes the surrounding code simpler and avoids clones inserted only to satisfy an unnecessarily consuming function.

lessons.title: Mutable Borrows

answers: Shared read access
Exclusive write access
A copied value
writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
An `&mut` reference permits mutation without transferring ownership. Exclusivity lasts through its final use, preventing another reader or writer from observing a half-finished update.

An `&mut T` gives one caller exclusive temporary access to a value. The owner still exists, but it cannot read or write through another path while the mutable borrow is active. This is more than a rule about syntax: it prevents a reader from seeing a partially updated structure and prevents two writers from racing to change the same state. After the last use of the borrow, the owner can be used again.

In `add_one`, the star in `*value += 1` follows the mutable reference to the integer it points at. `score` must be declared `mut` so it can be borrowed mutably. The call lends access; it does not move `score` into the function. The final print shows the updated owned value. Try storing `let edit = &mut score;`, then attempt to print `score` before `edit` is last used. The compiler flags the overlapping access. Move the print after that last use and the program becomes valid.

The same pattern applies to methods on vectors and structs. A mutable borrow lets a helper change an object in place without returning a replacement object. Keep the exclusive region short and meaningful. If a large function needs many unrelated mutable borrows, split it into operations with clear boundaries. This can make borrow errors easier to diagnose and can reveal which fields should be separate. Reach for interior mutability only when ordinary exclusive borrowing cannot express the actual access pattern.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
Passing `&mut *value` creates a shorter reborrow instead of moving the original mutable reference. This lets a helper work briefly and returns control to the outer borrower afterward.

A mutable reference can temporarily lend its access to another function. In `twice`, each `bump(&mut *value)` creates a shorter reborrow from the outer `&mut i32`. The first helper finishes before the second begins. The original reference is not consumed, so it can be used again after the helper calls. The important property is the timeline: there is one active writer at a time.

The `*` dereferences the outer reference to the value, and `&mut` forms a new mutable borrow of it. Rust often performs this reborrow implicitly at a call site, but writing it out makes the mechanism visible. If the first helper kept the reference beyond its call, the second exclusive borrow could not start. A return value tied to that borrow may also keep it active. Read compiler errors as a sequence of active loans rather than as a demand to clone a mutable reference; mutable references are not freely duplicable.

Try adding a print through `value` between the two `bump` calls, then after both calls. Both are fine if each reborrow has ended. Next, return the first reborrow from a helper and try to call `bump` again before its last use; the conflict shows why the short duration matters. Reborrowing is common in methods that coordinate several mutating helpers, and understanding it keeps such code simple without resorting to shared runtime mutation.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
Destructuring can move an owned field and copy or borrow the rest. After a partial move the whole struct is unavailable, but fields that were not moved may still be used directly.

A struct can be partly moved when one field owns data and another field is still independently usable. In the example, `user.name` is a `String`, so assigning it to `name` transfers that field's ownership. `user.level` is a `u8`, so it can still be read and copied. The whole `user` value can no longer be used as a complete `User` because one of its fields is missing. The compiler tracks that state precisely.

This is useful when consuming one payload but retaining metadata. Destructure a value and decide for each field whether to move, copy, or borrow it. A pattern such as `let User { name, ref level } = user;` moves `name` and borrows `level`. If you need the original struct intact, borrow the name instead of moving it, or clone only that field when an independent owned copy is truly needed. Cloning the entire struct is often wasteful and hides the intended ownership transfer.

Try printing `name` and `user.level`, then attempt `println!("{user:?}")` after the move and inspect the error. Rebuild a new `User` from the moved name and copied level to see how ownership can be reassembled. Types implementing `Drop` cannot have individual fields moved out this way, because their destructor expects a complete value. In those cases, consider replacing a field through an `Option` or using an API that consumes the whole object deliberately.

With larger structs, destructuring at the boundary of a function can make the intended field-level ownership transfer clearer than scattered accesses throughout the body.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
`Cell` and `RefCell` allow mutation behind an immutable outer binding. `RefCell` enforces the same shared-or-exclusive rule at runtime and panics if code violates it.

Normal Rust borrowing checks shared readers and exclusive writers at compile time. `RefCell<T>` moves that particular check to runtime for single-threaded code. An immutable binding can contain a `RefCell<Vec<_>>`, and calling `borrow_mut()` can still modify the vector inside. The outer reference is immutable; the cell enforces the inner access rule with a runtime borrow counter. It does not turn conflicting access into something safe to ignore.

In the sample, the temporary mutable guard from `borrow_mut()` ends after `push`, so a later `borrow()` is allowed. Keep a `RefMut` guard in a variable and try calling `borrow()` before dropping that guard: the program panics because a writer and reader would overlap. The fallible `try_borrow()` and `try_borrow_mut()` variants return an error instead of panicking, which can be useful when a conflict is a normal possibility. Hold guards for as short a period as practical.

`RefCell<T>` is not the tool for sharing mutable data across threads; types such as `Mutex<T>` address synchronization there. Use interior mutability when the surrounding API legitimately needs a shared outer reference while an inner value changes, such as a test spy or a local cache. Do not use it to escape a confusing borrow error before understanding the original ownership model. Runtime checks trade earlier compiler feedback for a more flexible access pattern, so that trade should be intentional.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
Rust omits obvious lifetime annotations using a small set of rules. One borrowed input can usually determine the returned borrow, keeping signatures readable without weakening the proof.

Elision means the compiler fills in common lifetime relationships you did not write. In `fn first(text: &str) -> &str`, the only borrowed input is `text`, so the returned slice must be tied to it. The function cannot create a reference that outlives the caller's text. Writing the equivalent named lifetime can be educational, but it does not make the result live longer or change runtime behavior.

The simple rules become less obvious with two borrowed inputs. A function `fn choose(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str` leaves the compiler unable to know which input the result borrows from. If the body can return either, name a shared relationship in the signature. If the result always comes from `a`, make that explicit. Methods have a useful convention: when `&self` is an input, an elided output borrow is tied to `self` unless you specify otherwise. These are rules of signature interpretation, not guesses based on the function body.

Practice by writing the explicit version of `first` and checking that it compiles exactly as before. Then add a second borrowed parameter used only as a search needle; if the return still comes from `text`, annotate that relationship accurately. Draw arrows from the output reference back to the input that owns its data. This skill makes API signatures easier to read and avoids over-annotating code where elision already communicates the contract clearly.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
Return a borrow when the result is a view into an input; return an owned value when new data is created or must escape independently. The choice affects allocation and API flexibility.

The lifetime of the data behind a return value should determine its type. `trimmed(input: &str) -> &str` returns a view into existing bytes, so it can avoid allocation, but the caller cannot keep the result after the input is gone. `label(input: &str) -> String` creates uppercase text in a new owned buffer. The caller may keep that buffer independently of the input. Neither choice is universally better; each promises a different relationship.

Follow the example with a `String` created in an inner block. A borrowed trimmed view must be used before the source leaves the block. An owned uppercase result can be moved out and printed afterward. If a function sometimes borrows and sometimes must allocate, `std::borrow::Cow<'a, str>` can express either case, but it adds complexity that a beginner API may not need. First choose a clear owned or borrowed contract, then optimize if measurements justify it.

Do not return a reference to a local `String` assembled inside a function; the value would be dropped when the function returns. Return that `String` by value instead, relying on move semantics. Conversely, do not allocate just to return a substring that the caller will use briefly while the input remains alive. Test both signatures with a string literal and with an owned string. Ask who owns the bytes after the call and how long the result must remain valid; those answers should make the return type feel inevitable.

A borrowed return can still be ergonomic: callers can call `.to_owned()` only when they need independence. That lets the common short-lived path avoid allocation while preserving an explicit escape hatch.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A trait object stores a pointer to data and a table of methods. It enables mixed concrete types in one collection at the cost of dynamic dispatch and some optimization opportunities.

A trait object lets code work with a value whose concrete type is chosen at runtime. `Box<dyn Draw>` owns a value on the heap while exposing only the `Draw` behavior. A vector of these boxes can contain buttons, charts, and labels as long as each implements `Draw`. A generic `Vec<T>` normally has one concrete `T` for all entries, so it cannot directly hold several unrelated structs. The trait object is the bridge when a heterogeneous collection is genuinely needed.

At a call to `item.draw()`, the program follows a method table associated with that value's concrete type. This adds an indirection and can limit some optimizations, but it also means new implementers can join the collection without rewriting the renderer. The object still obeys ownership rules: the vector owns the boxes, and borrowing the slice for `render` does not consume them. `&dyn Draw` would borrow a single drawable instead of owning it.

The trait must be usable as an object; not every trait method fits. A method that returns bare `Self` or is generic over another type may need a `where Self: Sized` restriction or a different design. Start with a small behavior contract such as `draw(&self)`. Implement it for two types, store both in one vector, and count the calls. Use static generic dispatch when all values have one concrete type known at compile time. Choose dynamic dispatch for the runtime mixture, not as a default for every trait.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A generic `impl` can grant a trait to all types satisfying a bound. Blanket implementations are powerful because they shape which future implementations remain legal under coherence rules.

A blanket implementation defines one rule for every type satisfying a bound. In the example, any sized `T` that implements `Display` also receives `Named`, whose `name()` delegates to `to_string()`. This avoids writing essentially the same implementation for each printable type. The benefit is broad, but so is the commitment: every current and future `Display` type covered by the rule gets that behavior.

Trace a call on an integer and one on a custom struct with `Display`. Both resolve to the same generic implementation, specialized for their concrete type. A type without `Display` has no `Named` implementation from this blanket rule, so a caller demanding `Named` cannot use it. The implicit `Sized` bound on `T` also leaves out `str` itself, unless the `impl` adds `?Sized`. This is a compile-time capability relationship, not a runtime registry. The code does not inspect the type's name or perform a dynamic check.

Blanket implementations interact with coherence. If your crate already grants `Named` to all `Display` types, a more specific `Named` implementation for one overlapping `Display` type conflicts on stable Rust. Also, the orphan rules limit which trait/type combinations your crate may implement. Before publishing a broad blanket `impl`, ask whether future special cases should behave differently. Try adding an overlapping implementation and read the compiler error. Sometimes a newtype wrapper or a narrower bound gives users more room to customize behavior later.

As a design exercise, imagine a type whose `Display` format changes over time. Would the generated name remain appropriate? A blanket rule is strongest when the mapping from the bound to the new behavior is stable for all covered types.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A trait may provide a method body that implementations inherit. Defaults reduce repetition, while required methods still define the minimum contract each type must supply.

A default method supplies behavior that implementers may inherit. In `Summary`, each type must provide `title()`, while `summary()` can be built from that required method. A new type gets a useful summary immediately after implementing the minimal contract. It may override the default when its presentation needs more context, but callers can still rely on the trait method existing.

This is a way to centralize a policy that is genuinely shared. If the default silently makes assumptions that are false for some types, it can produce misleading output. Keep required methods small and explicit, and make the default's dependency on them visible. For example, `summary()` calls `self.title()` so the implementation's title is always reflected. If the trait grows a new required method, every implementer must update; if it grows a default method, existing implementers usually continue to compile.

Create two structs implementing `Summary`: one inherits `summary()`, and the other overrides it. Call both through a generic function constrained by `Summary` and compare output. Then imagine a third type with no meaningful title. That is a sign the trait may be the wrong abstraction for that type, even if a placeholder string would make it compile. Good defaults reduce repetition while preserving an honest contract for every implementation.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A function may be generic over both a data type and a lifetime. Keep each parameter only when the body needs it; extra bounds make an API less reusable without adding safety.

The `choose` signature has two independent kinds of abstraction. `T: PartialOrd` says what operation the body may perform on the values: comparison. `'a` says how long the borrowed inputs and returned reference are related. These parameters solve different problems. Replacing the lifetime with a broader trait bound cannot make a dangling reference safe, and adding a lifetime cannot make an incomparable type satisfy `PartialOrd`.

The result borrows one of the two inputs. Because the body may choose either, the caller must use it only while both candidate sources are valid. Suppose the left value lives throughout a function and the right value lives in an inner block. Calling `choose` and using the result inside the block is fine. Keeping the result for use after that block is not, because it might point to the right value. The generic type does not change this rule; it applies whether `T` is an integer, a string wrapper, or a custom ordered type.

Try calling `choose` with two `i32` values, then with a custom type that implements `PartialOrd`. Next, create one input in a smaller scope and observe the lifetime error when the result escapes it. Fix the use site, not the annotation label. Keep trait bounds as narrow as the implementation needs, and keep lifetime relationships as specific as the returned data requires. A clear signature explains both the operation and the ownership story.

The letter chosen for a lifetime has no special power. Rename it consistently and the contract is the same. The useful information is which references share the label and which output is tied to them.

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
Adapters such as map and filter describe work but do nothing until a consumer asks for values. A clear pipeline separates selection, transformation, and collection without temporary vectors.

An iterator pipeline can read like a data-processing sentence: choose items, transform each chosen item, then consume the result. The sample starts with borrowed values from an array, filters for even numbers, squares them, and sums the squares. The final answer is 20 for `[1, 2, 3, 4]`. The adapters are lazy; `sum()` repeatedly pulls the next item through the chain. No intermediate vector is required.

Look closely at references. `values.iter()` yields `&i32`, while `filter` passes a reference to each item into its predicate, so the closure sees an extra reference layer and the example uses `**v`. The following `map` receives each item as a plain `&i32`, and `v * v` needs no star because multiplication is also implemented for references. Writing types beside the closures for one exercise can demystify those stars. If you use `into_iter()` on an owned vector instead, values are moved into the pipeline, changing what remains available afterward.

Use `inspect` temporarily to see when each element reaches a stage. Then insert `.take(1)` before `sum()` and predict which elements are evaluated. Be careful where you place it: taking one input before a filter is different from taking one matched output after a filter. A pipeline becomes hard to read when it hides side effects in `map` or uses many conversions without names. Split it into intermediate bindings when the operations need explanation. The goal is a clear ownership and evaluation story, not the fewest lines.

Try replacing the array with a vector and selecting `.iter()` versus `.into_iter()`. With `.into_iter()` the filter closure sees `&i32`, so `**v` must become `*v`. The numeric answer stays the same, but the ownership of the source changes. That is part of the API contract.
writing.feedback: Correct: When sum consumes it.
writing.question: When does the pipeline perform work?
writing.rule: Adapters such as map and filter describe work but do nothing until a consumer asks for values.
writing.success: You can say why nothing runs until `sum`, and why the filter needs `**v`.

recall.question: What are `a` and `b`?

lessons.title: Closure Capture Modes

answers: Capture ownership
Return type
Call syntax
writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A closure borrows, mutably borrows, or moves each captured value according to its body. The move keyword transfers captures even when the body would otherwise only borrow them.

The callable traits describe how a closure uses its captured environment. A closure that only reads captures can be called through `Fn`. One that mutates a captured variable needs `FnMut`, so the closure value must be mutable when invoked. One that consumes a captured value may be callable only once and satisfies `FnOnce`. `Fn` is the most reusable capability; `FnOnce` is the least demanding bound for a caller that invokes a callback exactly once.

In the sample, `move` transfers `name` into `announce`, allowing the closure to own the string independently of the original binding. But the body merely prints by borrowing its captured string, so the closure can still be called more than once. Add `drop(name)` inside the body and it consumes the capture; a second call then fails. This is why `move` and `FnOnce` should not be treated as synonyms. Capturing by value answers who owns the data; the body determines what kind of calls remain possible.

Experiment with three closures: read a counter, increment it, and consume a string. Try passing each to functions bounded by `Fn`, `FnMut`, and `FnOnce`, then read the errors. A callback API should ask for no more capability than it needs. If it calls the callback once, an `FnOnce` bound accepts the widest set of closures. If it may call repeatedly without mutable access to the closure, `Fn` is the right promise.
writing.feedback: Correct: Capture ownership.
writing.question: What does move change about the captures?
writing.rule: A closure borrows, mutably borrows, or moves each captured value according to its body.
writing.success: You can explain why `move` alone does not make a closure `FnOnce`.

writing.task: Say who owns `name` after `move`, and how many times `announce` can be called.

recall.question: A function calls its callback exactly once. Why is `F: FnOnce()` a better bound than `F: Fn()`?
recall.answer: Every closure implements `FnOnce`, so that bound accepts the widest set, including closures that consume a capture such as `move || drop(name)`. Under `Fn`, that closure is rejected (E0507, cannot move out of a captured variable in an `Fn` closure).

recall.question: `announce` can be called twice here. Why is the final line rejected?
recall.answer: `move` transferred ownership of `name` into the closure, so the outer binding is gone: E0382 borrow of moved value. The body only reads its capture, so the closure itself stays `Fn` and repeatable.

lessons.title: Phantom Types

answers: Size zero and alignment one for every T
One pointer, regardless of T
The same size and alignment as T
writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
PhantomData tells the type system that a zero-sized marker matters to ownership or state. It enables APIs where illegal transitions have no callable method, without adding runtime storage.

`PhantomData<T>` is a zero-sized marker that tells the compiler a type is logically related to `T` even when it stores no `T` value. In `Job<State>`, the state appears only at the type level. `Job<Ready>` and `Job<Running>` can have the same runtime fields but expose different methods. A transition can consume one state and return another, so calling a `finish` method on a job that was never started becomes a compile-time error.

`PhantomData<T>` itself has guaranteed size zero and alignment one for every `T`. The containing structure still follows its own layout rules. The marker has no runtime payload, but it is not decorative. It affects how the compiler reasons about ownership, variance, drop checking, and automatic traits in more advanced code. That is why the choice of marker type matters in low-level APIs. In a beginner typestate design, the central idea is simpler: the state is represented by a type rather than a boolean field that every method must check at runtime.

Sketch a `start(self) -> Job<Running>` method defined only for `Job<Ready>`, then a `finish(self) -> Job<Done>` defined only for `Job<Running>`. Try calling `finish` on the original ready job and inspect the method-not-found error. Notice that each transition consumes its old state, preventing two parallel versions of the same logical job from being used accidentally. Use this pattern when invalid transitions are costly enough to justify the extra types; a small ordinary enum may be clearer for a simple runtime choice.
writing.feedback: `PhantomData<T>` is guaranteed to have size 0 and alignment 1 for every `T`. Its ownership, variance and auto-trait effects still matter; the containing structure has its own layout.
writing.question: What layout is guaranteed for `PhantomData<T>` itself?
writing.rule: PhantomData tells the type system that a zero-sized marker matters to ownership or state.
writing.success: You can explain why `PhantomData<State>` is needed, and what it costs at runtime.
writing.summary: Track a compile-time state with no stored value.
writing.task: Say what `Job<Ready>` stores at runtime, and what the `state` field is for.

recall.question: What happens when this compiles, and why is it caught at that stage?
recall.answer: It fails with E0599: no method named `finish` for `Job<Ready>`. The state is part of the type, and `finish` is only defined in `impl Job<Running>`, so the illegal transition is not a callable method. No runtime flag needs checking.

recall.question: Why should a typestate transition like `start` take `self` rather than `&self`?
recall.answer: Taking `self` consumes the `Job<Ready>`, so after `let running = job.start();` any further use of `job` is E0382. Only one version of the logical job exists, and the old state cannot be used alongside the new one.

lessons.concept: A validated constructor behind a parsing trait

writing.summary: Convert raw text into a value that cannot represent an invalid port.
writing.rule: A conversion is useful when its output establishes an invariant, not just a new spelling.
writing.explanation:
A network port number fits in a u16, but this application's user-selectable port must also be nonzero. A private field and a checked constructor prevent callers from manufacturing an invalid value through ordinary safe code. `FromStr` then makes the text boundary idiomatic: callers write `text.parse::<Port>()` and handle the declared error. The conversion is fallible because not every string belongs to the domain.

Keep syntax and domain failures distinct when the caller can act on that difference. In the lab, malformed text and numeric overflow produce `invalid`; the valid integer zero produces `zero`. The parser trims surrounding whitespace, but it does not invent a default when the input is absent. Decide separately whether a command-line flag, a configuration file, or a form field is allowed to omit the value.

A `From<T>` implementation promises an infallible conversion, so do not implement it by panicking for an ordinary invalid input. Use `TryFrom` for a fallible typed conversion and `FromStr` for parsing borrowed text. These traits can delegate to the same checked constructor, avoiding divergent rules between your JSON adapter and your command-line adapter. A constructor should not secretly open a socket merely because it validates a port number.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. The typed lab checks zero, whitespace, the largest valid u16, negative text, and overflow. The reading demonstrates the trait implementation; the lab focuses on the checked parsing boundary so its observable contract is straightforward. As an extension, wrap the result in a private-field Port and make every public creation path use the same invariant.

recall.question: Why keep `Port`'s field private and make `FromStr`, `TryFrom` and any constructor all call one checked function?
recall.answer: A private field means safe code outside the module cannot write `Port(0)`, so every `Port` that exists is valid. Routing all creation paths through one check stops, say, the JSON and command-line adapters from drifting to different rules.

lessons.title: Compose Optional Fallible Input
lessons.concept: map, transpose, and explicit defaults

writing.summary: Keep missing configuration distinct from a configuration that is present but invalid.
writing.rule: Apply defaults to absence, not to every failure.
writing.explanation:
An optional configuration value can have three outcomes: no value was supplied, a valid value was supplied, or an invalid value was supplied. `Result<Option<T>, E>` preserves those outcomes. Converting an error into None with `ok()` loses the distinction, and adding `unwrap_or` too early can make a typo look like a deliberate default.

Map a parser over `Option<&str>` and the intermediate type becomes `Option<Result<T, E>>`. `transpose()` changes that nesting into `Result<Option<T>, E>`. It does not run the parser for None, hide an error, or pick a default. A match expression can implement the same behavior and may be easier while learning; combinators are useful when they keep the boundary readable.

The exercise accepts an optional nonzero u16 port. None stays Ok(None). Some text is trimmed, parsed, and validated using the same policy as the previous lesson. Some empty text is an invalid supplied value, not absence. That distinction matters for environment variables, web forms, and configuration merging, where an explicit invalid override should not silently fall back to an older value.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. Verify absent input, valid text, blank text, zero, and overflow separately. After the conversion succeeds, the application can deliberately choose `port.unwrap_or(default_port)`. Keep that policy outside the parser so another caller can require a value instead. Error-preserving composition is more important than making a chain of adapters as short as possible.
writing.exampleCaption: map, transpose, and explicit defaults
writing.task: Preserve None as Ok(None). For supplied text use the preceding port policy: zero is a zero error, bad syntax/overflow is invalid, and nonzero u16 becomes Ok(Some(n)). In the Crabrix app, open the compiler lab and complete the supplied function in solution.rs. The reading question is a separate exercise.

writing.question: What is the type after transposing Option<Result<u16, E>>?
answers: Result<Option<u16>, E>
Option<u16>, with every error removed
Result<u16, Option<E>>
writing.feedback: Transpose preserves absence and errors while moving Result to the outside.

recall.question: What does this print, and why is it not `Ok(None)`?
recall.answer: `Err(ParseIntError { kind: Empty })`. The value was supplied, just empty, so the parser runs and fails. `transpose` only produces `Ok(None)` when the option itself is `None`; it never turns a failed parse into absence.

writing.summary: Accept several string-like types when the operation only needs a borrowed view.
writing.rule: Ask for ownership only when the operation needs to keep or consume the value.
writing.explanation:
A function that only inspects text does not need a String allocation from every caller. A borrowed `&str` is often the simplest signature. `AsRef<str>` is useful when an API intentionally accepts several owned or borrowed string-like types and immediately obtains a string slice from them. It is a cheap reference conversion, not a general parsing or validation mechanism.

The example accepts a generic input, calls `as_ref()`, trims surrounding whitespace, and returns the number of Unicode scalar values. It never stores a reference after the call returns. Taking T by value still moves an owned String passed directly; callers that want to keep it can pass a reference. Generic syntax does not repeal ownership rules.

Choose the narrowest useful contract. A public function taking `&str` is easy to read and accepts `&String` through coercion. An `AsRef<Path>` parameter can be convenient for a file adapter, but path conversion does not grant filesystem permission. Similarly, `AsRef<str>` does not prove a string is a valid URL, port, or record. Keep the validated domain constructor from the earlier lesson as a separate operation.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. The lab calls the same function with a string literal, a String, and a borrowed String. It includes accented text and an emoji so byte length cannot accidentally pass as character count. Rust chars are Unicode scalar values; they are not the same as user-perceived grapheme clusters, so describe the result precisely rather than calling it a universal display width.
writing.exampleCaption: AsRef without unnecessary ownership
writing.task: Trim surrounding whitespace and count Unicode scalar values for any AsRef<str> input. This is not byte length or grapheme count. In the Crabrix app, open the compiler lab and complete the supplied function in solution.rs. The reading question is a separate exercise.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness finishes all normal and boundary cases. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.question: If an owned String is passed by value to fn f<T: AsRef<str>>(value: T), is the original still available?
answers: Always, because AsRef implies Copy
No, unless it was borrowed or cloned before the call
Only when the text is ASCII
writing.feedback: AsRef supplies a borrowed view inside the function. Passing the owned argument by value still moves it.

recall.question: What does this print, and why do the two numbers differ?
recall.answer: `2 8`: after trimming, `É` and the crab are two Unicode scalar values. `len()` counts UTF-8 bytes of the untrimmed string: two spaces, two bytes for `É`, and four for the crab. Passing `&owned` leaves the `String` usable.

recall.question: Why doesn't accepting `impl AsRef<str>` remove the need for a validating constructor such as `Port::from_str`?
recall.answer: `AsRef<str>` is only a cheap reference conversion that gives you a `&str` view; it says nothing about the text's contents. Whether the string is a valid port, URL or record still has to be checked by a separate, fallible operation.

lessons.title: Modules

answers: It lives in a different file from main
Items are private by default, so it needs pub
A module function has to return a Result
writing.exampleCaption: `mod` declares it; `pub` decides what leaves it.
writing.explanation:
mod declares a module and use brings a path into scope, while pub decides what actually escapes. `Cargo.toml` describes the package around them — the same file the package manager reads to resolve your dependencies.

A module gives names and boundaries to related code. In the example, `mod greeter;` tells Rust to compile the module from `src/greeter.rs`; `greeter::message()` follows a path to an item inside it. The `use` keyword can shorten a path in the current scope, but it does not change whether an item is visible. Visibility starts private. `pub` opens an item to callers permitted by the module hierarchy, and a public function exposed from a library crate becomes part of the interface other crates may rely on.

Start a tiny project with `src/main.rs` and `src/greeter.rs`. First call the function by its full path. Then import it with `use` and compare the call site. Remove `pub` and read the compiler diagnostic. This sequence separates three ideas that are easy to blur: file layout determines where code is found, module paths determine how it is named, and visibility determines who may call it. A file is a convenient module boundary, not a permission switch by itself.

As a project grows, prefer modules named for responsibilities rather than for arbitrary technical layers. Keep small helpers private and expose the minimum stable API. If callers need to write a long, surprising path, consider a deliberate `pub use` re-export at the crate root. That keeps internal files free to move without forcing every caller to change. `Cargo.toml` describes the package and dependencies; it is related to the project but does not replace Rust's module tree.
writing.feedback: Privacy is the default; `pub fn helper` makes it reachable.
writing.question: Why can't main call helper?
writing.rule: Items are private by default; `pub` is what exposes them.
writing.success: It compiles from `src/main.rs` and prints the edited output.
writing.summary: Modules split a crate into files, and privacy shapes the surface.
writing.task: Open the multi-file project, trace mod greeter, and change its public function.

recall.question: `greeter::message` is not marked `pub`. What happens if `main` writes `use greeter::message;` and calls `message()`?
recall.answer: It fails with E0603, function `message` is private. `use` only shortens a path in the current scope; it never changes visibility. Only `pub` exposes the item.

recall.question: Why might a library add a `pub use` re-export at its crate root?
recall.answer: It gives callers a short, deliberate path to an item that lives deep in the module tree. Internal files can then be moved or renamed without forcing every caller to change their paths.

answers: A return type so the harness can read the result
An assertion — the test passes no matter what compute returns
The #[cfg(test)] attribute above the module
writing.exampleCaption: Tests live beside the code and can see its private parts.
writing.explanation:
`#[test]` registers functions with the test harness. A `#[cfg(test)]` module is excluded from ordinary builds, including `cargo build --release`, but included by `cargo test --release`. Test mode and optimization profile are separate choices. Unit tests sit beside the code and can reach its private details; integration tests live in `tests/` and see only the public API, which is a useful check on your own interface.

A test records an observable promise. `#[test]` marks a function that the test harness runs under `cargo test`; an assertion compares the actual value with a prediction. The sample puts tests beside the implementation in a `#[cfg(test)]` module, which is a good place for small unit tests of edge cases and private helpers. The module is only compiled when testing, so it does not become a normal production code path.

Start with a function that adds two numbers. Test a typical case, zero, and a boundary that might reveal overflow or an incorrect sign. Name tests for the behavior they protect rather than the implementation line they execute. If a test fails, its assertion should tell you what input produced the mismatch. A test that merely repeats the function's code is weak: it can share the same mistake. Prefer a simple expected result you can justify independently.

Integration tests under `tests/` compile as separate crates and call the public library API. They are useful when you want evidence that an external consumer can use the package as intended. A practical suite usually combines focused unit tests with a few end-to-end cases. Tests do not prove an implementation correct for every input, but they make intended behavior executable and guard against later changes. Run the narrowest relevant test while editing and the full suite before shipping; both speeds of feedback matter.

Compare `cargo test` and `cargo test --release`: both execute assertions. Integer overflow checks normally differ between the default dev and release profiles, and projects can override that policy. Write explicit checked arithmetic when overflow is part of the API contract, rather than relying on the test profile.
writing.feedback: A test with no assertion only proves the code did not panic.
writing.question: What is missing from that test?
writing.rule: `#[cfg(test)]` selects test builds, including `cargo test --release`; ordinary builds exclude that module.
writing.success: Both are deterministic and fail for a deliberately broken implementation.
writing.summary: Tests turn behaviour into executable evidence.
writing.task: Add one success case and one boundary case for a pure function.

recall.question: How do unit tests in a `#[cfg(test)]` module differ from integration tests in `tests/` in what they can reach?
recall.answer: Unit tests sit beside the code and, via `use super::*`, can test private helpers. Integration tests compile as separate crates and see only the public API, so they check that an outside consumer can use the package as intended.

recall.question: A test calls `add(u32::MAX, 1)` where `add` returns `a + b`. Why can it behave differently under `cargo test` and `cargo test --release`?
recall.answer: The default dev profile enables integer overflow checks, so the addition panics; the release profile normally disables them, so it wraps to `0`. If overflow is part of the contract, use explicit checked arithmetic rather than relying on the profile.

lessons.title: Error Design

answers: Returns an empty string on failure
Panics; unwinding or process abort depends on the panic configuration
Logs a warning and continues with a default
writing.exampleCaption: The `?` operator returns an `Err` to the caller, which can handle or propagate it.
writing.explanation:
`Result`, custom error types, and ? separate expected failure from programmer mistakes. A panic says this should never happen; a `Result` says the caller has a decision to make — and conflating the two is what makes error handling painful later.

Expected failures should travel through a function's type. Reading a file may fail because it does not exist or cannot be accessed; returning `Result<String, std::io::Error>` tells the caller that a successful string and a recoverable error are both possible. In the sample, `?` returns the I/O error early while leaving the successful path uncluttered. It does not hide the error: the caller must still handle or propagate it.

At the command-line or UI boundary, turn the error into a message with context. “Could not load configuration from settings.toml” is more useful than “file error” because it identifies the attempted operation. Keep the original cause available for diagnostics when possible. A reusable library should avoid panicking for ordinary missing files or invalid input. Reserve panic for violated internal assumptions where the program cannot reasonably continue.

Try calling `load` with an existing file and a missing one. In the caller, match on `Ok(text)` and `Err(error)`, print a helpful message, and decide whether to retry or exit. Then introduce a custom error enum for a workflow that can fail in two different ways, such as I/O and parsing. The type should distinguish those cases without forcing every helper to know about the final presentation. Error handling becomes manageable when each layer adds the context it owns and lets the caller make the next decision.

A caller may attach more context with `map_err` or a custom error type without changing the original low-level fact. That separation keeps errors useful to both programs and people.
writing.feedback: unwrap panics on Err. With unwinding, an appropriate boundary may catch that panic; panic=abort terminates the process. Return Result for expected I/O failures rather than using panic as routine control flow.
writing.question: What does unwrap() do if this file operation returns Err?
writing.rule: Panic for a bug; `Result` for a situation the caller can act on.
writing.success: The caller handles the failure without losing its cause.
writing.summary: Good errors preserve context and keep recovery near the caller.
writing.task: Replace a panic with a `Result` and propagate it through one caller.

recall.question: In `let text = std::fs::read_to_string(path)?;` inside `fn load(path: &str) -> Result<String, std::io::Error>`, what does `?` do when the read fails?
recall.answer: It returns early from `load` with that `Err`, leaving the success path uncluttered. The error is not hidden: the caller still has to handle or propagate it.

recall.question: When should a reusable library panic instead of returning a `Result`?
recall.answer: Only when an internal assumption is violated, a bug, and the program cannot reasonably continue. Ordinary failures such as a missing file or invalid input belong in a `Result`, so the caller can decide to retry, report or exit.

lessons.title: Dependencies

writing.exampleCaption: A requirement, a feature set, and an opt-out of defaults.
writing.exampleCode:
[dependencies]
serde = "=1.0.229"
serde_json = "=1.0.151"
smallvec = "1"
memchr = { version = "2", default-features = false }
writing.explanation:
"1.2" means any 1.x at or above 1.2, because Cargo follows SemVer: patch and minor releases must stay compatible. The resolver picks the highest match and records the exact choice in `Cargo.lock`, and features let one crate ship optional pieces you opt into rather than paying for by default.

A dependency declaration is a compatibility request, not a permanent pin. In Cargo's default caret requirement, `version = "1.2"` accepts compatible 1.x releases from 1.2 upward but not 2.0. `Cargo.lock` records the concrete versions selected for a particular resolution, so two developers can rebuild the same application graph. Read both files when investigating why a new release did or did not appear in your build.

Features let a dependency expose optional capabilities. In the example, `serde` with `derive` enables procedural derives; `default-features = false` on another dependency removes only that dependency edge's default request. Features are unified when the same package is reached through several paths, so another dependency can still turn a feature on. Treat features as additive options, and inspect the resolved feature graph when behavior surprises you.

Before adding a crate, check what problem it solves, whether its API fits the project, and what it brings into the build. A small dependency can be worthwhile, but every dependency adds a maintenance and security surface. Pinning every version forever is not a substitute for tests; compatible updates still need verification. Practice with `cargo tree` to inspect the graph, update one package deliberately, and run tests after the lockfile changes. Keep direct dependency declarations clear and leave transitive selection to the resolver unless a real constraint requires intervention.

When reading a version requirement, pay attention to pre-release versions and major version zero, whose compatibility rules are narrower. Do not infer safety solely from a SemVer range; examine release notes and run meaningful tests after updates.

Execution profile: the Serde: Decode, Validate, Encode lesson contains the qualified, pinned Cargo project for both the app and web Playground. It uses explicit Serde traits. Enabling derive adds a procedural macro dependency and needs separately qualified macro support; downloading serde alone does not provide that capability.
writing.feedback: Below 1.0 the minor number is the breaking one, so 0.4.x only.
writing.practiceCode:
[dependencies]
example = "0.4"
writing.question: Which version can that requirement resolve to?
writing.rule: "1.2" means >=1.2.0 and <2.0.0; the lockfile records what was actually chosen.
writing.success: `Cargo.lock` pins an exact version that satisfies the requirement.
writing.summary: A dependency is a version requirement, not a fixed version.
writing.task: Add a dependency with an explicit feature and resolve it.

recall.question: Which versions can `serde = "=1.0.229"` and `smallvec = "1"` resolve to?
recall.answer: `=1.0.229` allows exactly that version. `"1"` is a caret requirement allowing >=1.0.0 and <2.0.0; the resolver picks the highest compatible release and records the exact choice in `Cargo.lock`.

recall.question: You set `default-features = false` on a dependency, yet one of its default features is still enabled in the build. How can that happen?
recall.answer: Features are unified when the same package is reached through several paths. `default-features = false` removes only your edge's request, so another dependency can still turn the feature on; inspect the resolved feature graph, for example with `cargo tree`.

lessons.title: Workspaces

answers: Nothing, they are independent
One lockfile and one target directory
Their source files
writing.exampleCaption: One root manifest, many members, one shared lockfile.
writing.exampleCode:
# Cargo.toml at the workspace root
[workspace]
resolver = "3"
members = ["core", "cli"]

# cli/Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
core = { path = "../core" }
writing.explanation:
Members share a target directory and lockfile, while the resolver may still select multiple versions of a dependency when requirements are incompatible. Splitting a project into a library plus a thin binary is the usual first move, because it makes the library testable on its own.

A Cargo workspace groups packages that are developed together. A root `Cargo.toml` lists members such as `core` and `cli`; the packages share a lockfile and build output directory, and workspace commands can operate across members. A common design puts reusable behavior in a library and keeps the binary thin: the CLI parses arguments, calls library functions, and prints a result. This makes the core easier to test and reuse.

The example's dependency path from `cli` to `core` is explicit in the CLI manifest. Being in the same workspace does not automatically make every crate visible to every other crate. Nor does it guarantee there is only one version of every external package: incompatible requirements can still resolve to multiple versions. The shared lockfile records the actual graph. Use `cargo tree` when you need to inspect it rather than assuming deduplication.

Create a workspace with two members, add a public function to the library, and call it from the CLI. Run `cargo test --workspace` to exercise all members. Then add a test that calls the library directly and compare it with a CLI-level test. The workspace boundary is a useful organizational choice when packages have separate purposes or release needs. Splitting every file into a crate would add manifest and versioning overhead without improving the design. Start with a clear library/binary split when that split reflects a real responsibility.

A workspace is also a convenient boundary for coordinated checks: formatting, linting, and tests can cover all members together while each package keeps its own public API and dependencies.
writing.feedback: The members resolve together into one `Cargo.lock`, and a shared `target` directory reuses build output. Incompatible requirements can still select two versions of a dependency.
writing.practiceCode:
[workspace]
resolver = "3"
members = ["core", "cli"]
writing.question: What do the members share?
writing.rule: Workspace members share one lockfile, which records every resolved version; incompatible requirements can still select several.
writing.success: The library holds the logic and the binary only wires it up.
writing.summary: A workspace builds several crates against one lockfile.
writing.task: Describe how you would split a project into a library and a binary.

recall.question: `core` and `cli` are members of the same workspace. What must `cli` do before it can call `core`'s functions, and why?
recall.answer: Declare an explicit path dependency in `cli/Cargo.toml`, such as `core = { path = "../core" }`. Membership in a workspace shares the lockfile and target directory but does not make crates visible to each other.

recall.question: Why is splitting a project into a library plus a thin binary a common first move, and when does splitting further become a mistake?
recall.answer: The library holds reusable behaviour that can be tested on its own, while the binary only parses arguments, calls the library and prints. Splitting every file into its own crate adds manifest and versioning overhead without improving the design.

lessons.title: Box<T>

answers: An enum can never refer to itself, boxed or not
The type would have infinite size without an indirection
An i32 payload is not allowed inside an enum
writing.exampleCaption: Without `Box`, this enum would need infinite size.
writing.explanation:
A recursive type has no fixed size, because each level would contain another whole level. `Box` has a known pointer size, so putting the recursive part behind one makes the type representable. `Box` also lets a function return a trait object whose concrete size is not known at the call site.

A recursive enum needs a known size at compile time. If `Tree::Node` directly contained two more `Tree` values, each of those nodes would contain more nodes with no finite size the compiler could lay out. `Box<Tree>` replaces each child with a pointer whose size is known. The actual child values live in separate heap allocations, and the boxes own them. Dropping the root recursively drops the owned children.

The sample's `sum` function borrows `&Tree`, matches on its variants, and reads through the boxes. It does not take ownership of the tree just to traverse it. Trace a root with two leaves and predict the sum before running the code. Then add one nested node and observe how the recursive call follows a box. This exercise shows the separation between the size of the enum variant and the depth of the runtime tree.

A box is also a way to own a value whose concrete type is hidden behind a trait object, `Box<dyn Trait>`. The box does not make every operation faster: following pointers and allocating each node can cost more than a compact flat representation. Use it when indirection expresses a real need, such as recursion or owned dynamic dispatch. For a simple fixed set of values, a `Vec<T>` or plain struct may be clearer. Choose the data shape first, then the pointer type that makes it representable.

The box is an owning pointer, so moving the box moves ownership of the child allocation without copying the entire tree. That makes recursive construction manageable while preserving deterministic cleanup.

writing.rule: `Box` gives a recursive or unsized value a known-size home.
writing.success: It compiles, and you can explain why `Box` is required.

recall.question: When is giving every node its own `Box` a poor choice of representation?
recall.answer: When no recursion or owned dynamic dispatch requires it: allocating each node and following pointers can cost more than a compact flat layout. For a simple fixed set of values, a `Vec<T>` or plain struct is often clearer.

lessons.title: Rc & RefCell

answers: It compiles and works
It panics at runtime
It is a compile error
writing.exampleCaption: Shared ownership on the outside, controlled mutation on the inside.
writing.explanation:
`Rc<T>` keeps a count and frees when it reaches zero, but only hands out shared references. Pairing it with `RefCell<T>` lets you mutate through that shared handle, with the borrow rules checked at runtime instead — a violation panics rather than failing to compile. Neither is thread-safe; that is `Arc` and `Mutex`.

`Rc<T>` provides shared ownership within one thread. Each clone of an `Rc` is another strong handle to the same allocation, not a deep copy of `T`. The allocation is released when its last strong owner disappears. Because multiple owners can access the same value, `Rc<T>` normally provides shared read access. Wrapping the value in `RefCell<T>` permits mutation by checking the borrow rule at runtime.

In the sample, both `shared` and `second` refer to the same cell. A `borrow_mut()` guard grants exclusive access while it is alive; a `borrow()` guard permits reading, possibly alongside other readers. If a writer and reader overlap, `RefCell` panics, or `try_borrow` returns an error. Keep the guard's lifetime short. If the mutation is awkward only because the ownership design is unclear, a simpler owner with explicit mutable borrowing may be preferable.

Use `Rc<RefCell<T>>` for a local graph or UI state where several single-threaded owners truly need to share a mutable value. It is not a concurrency primitive. `Rc` does not implement the thread-safety traits needed for cross-thread sharing, and `RefCell` does not synchronize threads. The rough cross-thread counterparts are `Arc<T>` for shared ownership and a `Mutex<T>` or another synchronization strategy for mutation. Draw each owner and each active borrow separately; counting handles and checking access are two different mechanisms.

If you need only several read-only owners, `Rc<T>` alone is simpler. Add `RefCell` only when mutation behind shared ownership is a real requirement.
writing.feedback: `RefCell` enforces the same rule, just later and with a panic.
writing.question: What happens on the second borrow_mut?
writing.rule: `RefCell` moves the borrow rules to runtime; breaking them panics.
writing.success: Both handles observe the change and the count is correct.
writing.summary: `Rc` shares ownership; `RefCell` moves the borrow check to runtime.
writing.task: Share one vector between two handles and mutate it through both.

recall.question: What does this print, and what did `Rc::clone(&shared)` copy?
recall.answer: It prints `[1, 2, 3, 4]` and then `owners 2`. `Rc::clone` copied only a handle and incremented the strong count; both handles reach the same `RefCell`, so the push through `second` is visible through `shared`.

recall.question: When is `Rc<T>` without `RefCell` enough, and what replaces `Rc<RefCell<T>>` when the state is shared across threads?
recall.answer: Plain `Rc<T>` suffices when several owners only read the value. Across threads, use `Arc<T>` for shared ownership with a `Mutex<T>` or another synchronisation strategy for mutation; neither `Rc` nor `RefCell` is thread-safe.

lessons.title: Deref & Drop

answers: Only when you call drop() on it explicitly
Automatically when the value leaves scope
At program exit, once main has returned
writing.exampleCaption: Deref coercion is why `&MyBox<String>` reaches a `&str` parameter.
writing.explanation:
Implementing Deref lets the compiler insert conversions automatically, which is why `&String` works where `&str` is expected. Drop lets a type run code when it goes out of scope, and the two together are how smart pointers feel built in — a `Box` behaves like the value it holds and cleans up on its own.

`Deref` tells Rust how a pointer-like wrapper exposes a reference to its target. In the example, `MyBox<T>` can return `&T` from its inner field, so code can read the wrapped value through familiar syntax. Deref coercion can adapt `&String` to `&str` through the type's implementations. This convenience should be predictable: implementing `Deref` for a type that is not really pointer-like can make method resolution and ownership harder to understand.

`Drop` describes cleanup when an owner leaves scope. A wrapper around a file or other resource can release it in `drop`, and the caller does not need to remember an explicit cleanup line on every path. You cannot normally call a value's `drop` method directly; `std::mem::drop(value)` consumes it and triggers cleanup early. A moved wrapper is dropped by its new owner, not again at the old binding.

Build a small wrapper, implement `Deref`, and call a method from the inner type through it. Then add a `Drop` implementation that logs when cleanup happens. Place one wrapper in an inner block and predict the log order. Keep the wrapper's behavior unsurprising: `Deref` for transparent access, `Drop` for resource cleanup. If the wrapper needs complex policy or fallible access, explicit methods often communicate more clearly than pretending it is the target value.

Remember that `Drop::drop` receives `&mut self`, so it can inspect and release fields but cannot move arbitrary fields out as if the object were still complete. The compiler still drops fields after the method returns. Avoid panicking in destructors, especially during unwinding, and keep cleanup as reliable as possible.

Test the exact point where each wrapper leaves scope.
writing.feedback: Drop runs at the end of the value's scope; `std::mem::drop` just ends it sooner.
writing.question: When does that Drop message print?
writing.rule: Deref coercion applies repeatedly until the types line up.
writing.success: The call compiles without an explicit conversion.
writing.summary: Deref makes your type usable like a reference to another one.
writing.task: Implement Deref for a wrapper and pass it where the inner type is expected.

recall.question: `greet` takes `&str`, and `boxed` is a `MyBox<String>` whose `Deref` target is `String`. How does `greet(&boxed)` compile?
recall.answer: Deref coercion applies repeatedly until the types match: `&MyBox<String>` becomes `&String` through `MyBox`'s `Deref`, then `&str` through `String`'s `Deref`.

recall.question: In what order does this program print? (`Noisy`'s `Drop` prints `drop <name>`.)
recall.answer: `drop b`, `drop a`, `end`, `drop c`. `_b` is dropped at the end of its block, `std::mem::drop(a)` drops `a` early, and `_c` is dropped when `main` ends. Calling `a.drop()` directly would not compile (E0040).

lessons.title: Reference Cycles

answers: A Weak link is cheaper to clone than an Rc
Two Rc links in a cycle never reach zero, so nothing is freed
The compiler refuses to build a cyclic Rc graph
writing.exampleCaption: The child points back with `Weak`, so the cycle never forms.
writing.explanation:
Two `Rc` handles pointing at each other never reach a count of zero, so neither is freed. `Weak<T>` is the answer: it does not count towards ownership and must be upgraded before use, which turns a parent pointer into something that can legitimately be gone.

Reference counting releases an allocation only when its strong count reaches zero. If node A owns an `Rc` to B and B owns an `Rc` back to A, each keeps the other alive after all outside handles are dropped. Rust prevents memory unsafety here, but the allocations leak. A graph needs a deliberate ownership direction, not strong links in every direction.

A common tree design lets a parent own children through strong `Rc` handles while each child keeps a `Weak` reference back to its parent. A weak reference does not keep the parent alive. `upgrade()` returns an `Option<Rc<T>>`, because the parent may have been dropped. That absence is a normal state to handle, not an exceptional failure. In the sample, `Rc::downgrade` stores the parent link, and the `Option` from `upgrade()` is checked before reading through it.

Draw two nodes and label the strong links before writing code. Remove all external owners on paper: if every node still has an incoming strong link from within the cycle, cleanup cannot begin. Replace one direction with weak links and repeat the count. For practice, create a parent and child, then drop the parent and verify that upgrading the child's weak parent link returns `None` if the child is still held externally. The lesson is not to avoid shared ownership entirely, but to make the owning direction explicit.

Weak references can also be used for caches that should not keep objects alive. The caller must accept that `upgrade()` may return `None`; a weak link is a question about whether the target still exists, not an ownership guarantee. Draw strong and weak edges with different arrows during review.
writing.feedback: Ownership should flow one way; the back-reference observes without owning.
writing.question: Why should that parent link be Weak?
writing.rule: `Weak` does not keep a value alive, so `upgrade()` may return `None`.
writing.success: You can name which direction owns and which merely observes.
writing.summary: Rust prevents data races, not leaks — a cycle can still strand memory.
writing.task: Explain where a parent pointer should be Weak rather than `Rc`.

recall.question: A child holds a `Weak` link to its parent. The parent is dropped while the child is still owned elsewhere. What does `child.parent.borrow().upgrade()` return?
recall.answer: `None`. A `Weak` reference does not keep the parent alive, so once the last strong owner is gone, `upgrade()` reports the absence as an `Option` that the code must handle.

recall.question: How can you tell on paper whether a group of `Rc`-linked nodes will leak?
recall.answer: Remove every external owner. If each node still has an incoming strong link from inside the group, no count can reach zero and nothing is freed. Turning one direction, such as child-to-parent, into `Weak` links breaks the cycle.

writing.exampleCaption: `src/lib.rs` defines the library; `src/main.rs` calls it by its crate name, `demo`.
writing.explanation:
`src/main.rs` defines the default binary and `src/lib.rs` defines the library target. Additional binaries and integration tests have conventional directories that keep tooling automatic.

Cargo recognizes conventional paths, which lets a small project grow without custom build configuration. `src/main.rs` is the default binary entry point. `src/lib.rs` defines a library target that other crates and integration tests can import. Additional binaries can live under `src/bin/`, while external tests live under `tests/`. These paths describe targets, not just folders for tidiness.

In the sample, `demo::answer()` calls the library from the binary. The name before the double colon is the library crate name, normally derived from the package name unless configured otherwise. A binary in the same package still uses the library through its public interface. This is useful discipline: the CLI can remain a thin layer around reusable logic, and integration tests can exercise the same API that a user imports.

Try moving a function from `main.rs` into `lib.rs`, marking it public, and calling it from both the binary and a test in `tests/`. Confirm which imports compile and which private helpers remain inaccessible. Keep module files inside the appropriate target; creating a file by itself does not make Rust compile it unless it is a recognized target or declared from the module tree. A conventional layout reduces configuration surprises, but choose a new crate only when the code deserves its own package boundary.

lessons.title: Check, Build, Run

answers: cargo check
cargo build
cargo run
writing.exampleCaption: Three commands, three levels of evidence: types, an artifact, then a run.
writing.explanation:
`cargo check` proves type correctness without final code generation, build creates artifacts, and run executes a binary after building it. Fast feedback comes from asking only for the evidence you need.

The fastest useful command depends on the question you are asking. After an edit, `cargo check` verifies parsing, types, borrowing, and many other compiler rules without producing a final executable. `cargo test` compiles the test harness and runs tests. `cargo run` builds a binary if needed and executes it. `cargo build` produces an artifact without executing it. `cargo run` reuses what `cargo build` produced, while `cargo check` keeps its own output, and each command provides different evidence.

A productive loop is edit, check, test the changed behavior, then run the whole program when interaction matters. A successful `cargo check` does not prove a function returns the right answer; a passing unit test does not prove the CLI arguments are wired correctly. `cargo build --release` uses the release profile and is appropriate when validating a shippable artifact or measuring optimized performance. It is usually slower than a quick debug check during a small edit.

Try introducing a type mismatch and observe which command catches it first. Fix that, then introduce a logic bug that compiles but fails an assertion. Finally run the application with a representative input. Record what each stage established and what it left untested. This distinction prevents “it compiled” from becoming an overconfident claim. Keep the loop short while developing, and use broader checks at meaningful checkpoints rather than waiting until the end of the project.

For a library-only package, `cargo run` has no default binary to execute; choose an example or add a binary target. In a workspace, a command may need `-p package_name` to identify which member you mean. These small command choices keep feedback focused.
writing.feedback: `cargo check` stops after analysis, so it reports type and borrow errors without producing an executable.
writing.question: Which command skips final code generation?
writing.rule: `cargo check` proves type correctness without final code generation, build creates artifacts, and run executes a binary after building it.
writing.success: You can name the fact each command proved and the fact it left untested.
writing.summary: Choose the cheapest command that proves the next fact.
writing.task: Say which of `cargo check`, `cargo build`, and `cargo run` first reveals that `double(4)` gives 6, not 8. Then break the return type and ask the same question.

recall.answer: A library-only package has no default binary to execute, so run an example or add a binary target. In a workspace, Cargo may need `-p package_name` to know which member you mean.

answers: dev-dependencies
profile.release
