writing.exampleCaption: `log` is part of the normal graph; `pretty_assertions` is available only to tests, examples, and benchmarks.
writing.exampleCode:
[dependencies]
log = "0.4"

[dev-dependencies]
pretty_assertions = "1"
writing.explanation:
Normal dependencies become part of a target graph, build dependencies support build scripts, and dev dependencies exist for tests and examples. The distinction keeps production graphs smaller and clearer.

Cargo separates dependencies by the role they play in a package. Normal `[dependencies]` are needed to build the library or binary target. `[build-dependencies]` are available to a `build.rs` script that runs during the build, often to generate files or detect native libraries. `[dev-dependencies]` support tests, examples, and benchmarks but are not ordinary runtime dependencies of the published library. The distinction helps make a package's requirements understandable.

Read the sample manifest and ask where each crate is used. A logging interface needed by production code belongs under normal dependencies. A prettier assertion formatter used only in tests belongs under dev dependencies. Moving it into normal dependencies may unnecessarily expand consumers' build graphs. Conversely, placing a production import under dev dependencies makes a normal build fail even if tests happen to compile in a different configuration.

Dependency kinds do not by themselves make a crate trustworthy or small. Versions, features, and transitive dependencies still matter. Use `cargo tree` with the relevant target or feature flags to inspect the resolved graph. Add one test-only helper and confirm `cargo build` does not need its API in production code. Then add a build script only if there is a real build-time task; generated code adds another layer to debug. Treat each manifest section as a statement of when that capability is actually required.
writing.feedback: `[dev-dependencies]` are available to tests, examples, and benchmarks, and stay out of what consumers build.

recall.question: What are `[build-dependencies]` for, and who can use them?

answers: Additive capability
Mutual exclusion
Hidden defaults
writing.exampleCaption: Each build compiles exactly one `paint`, chosen by whether `color` is on.
writing.explanation:
Cargo features are unified across a dependency graph, so disabling one consumer's feature may not disable it globally. Prefer additive capabilities and avoid features that make the same API mean incompatible things.

A feature is a named, additive capability a crate can enable at compile time. `#[cfg(feature = "color")]` includes code only when that feature is active; another branch can provide behavior without it. A feature is not a runtime switch, so a binary cannot toggle it after compilation. The public API exposed under different feature sets should be understandable and tested in each supported configuration.

Cargo unifies feature requests for the same package in a dependency graph. If one dependency path asks for feature A and another asks for feature B, the package may be built with both. That makes mutually exclusive features fragile: downstream users can accidentally activate the combination. Prefer features that add independent capabilities and keep a sensible default. If two backends truly cannot coexist, document and enforce that constraint explicitly, or consider a different design.

Create a tiny crate with a `color` feature and compile it with and without `--features color`. Then add two dependents that request different features of the same library and inspect the resulting feature graph with `cargo tree -e features`. Test `--no-default-features` if you claim that mode works. Avoid assuming that setting `default-features = false` at one edge globally disables defaults; another path can enable them. Feature design is part of the compatibility contract, not only a way to reduce compile time.

A feature name should describe the capability it adds. Avoid names that merely encode an internal implementation file, because external users will depend on the public meaning over time.
writing.feedback: Additive capabilities only add code, so the union Cargo builds still compiles. Mutually exclusive features break as soon as two dependents enable both.
writing.question: What style makes features compose well?
writing.rule: Cargo features are unified across a dependency graph, so disabling one consumer's feature may not disable it globally.
writing.success: Every feature combination compiles, including both on together, and you can say why Cargo may ask for that union.
writing.summary: Make optional capability additive and explicit.
writing.task: Declare both features, build with `--features backend_a,backend_b`, and read the error. Then redesign them as additive capabilities that can be on at once.

recall.question: A library offers mutually exclusive features `backend-a` and `backend-b`. Why is that design fragile?
recall.answer: Cargo unifies feature requests for one package across the dependency graph, so if two dependents ask for different backends, the library is built with both. Prefer additive features; if two options truly cannot coexist, document and enforce that explicitly.

recall.question: How does a Cargo feature such as `color` differ from a runtime configuration switch?
recall.answer: It selects code at compile time through `#[cfg(feature = "color")]`; a built binary contains only one branch and cannot toggle it later. Each supported feature combination therefore has to be built and tested separately.

answers: The exact resolved graph
Only the root package name
The Rust edition
writing.exampleCaption: Each registry `[[package]]` entry records one exact name, version, and checksum.
writing.exampleCode:

writing.explanation:
`Cargo.toml` describes allowed versions while `Cargo.lock` records the exact chosen graph. Applications normally commit the lockfile so a later build does not silently select newer compatible releases.

`Cargo.toml` says which versions are acceptable; `Cargo.lock` records which exact package versions the resolver selected. If a manifest permits several compatible releases, the lockfile keeps subsequent ordinary builds on the same chosen graph until an update changes it. This helps a team reproduce a bug and compare results without silently pulling a newer dependency on every checkout.

An application normally commits its lockfile. A library crate may also commit one for its own development and tests, but downstream consumers resolve dependencies using their own lockfiles. The lockfile is therefore not a universal promise that every consumer uses the library author's exact dependency graph. If you are publishing a binary or deploying a service, review lockfile changes along with source changes, because a dependency update can alter behavior even when your own code is unchanged.

Try `cargo update -p package_name` in a disposable branch and inspect the lockfile diff. Run tests and, where relevant, a release build. To check whether a clean machine can reproduce the selected graph without modifying the lockfile, use `cargo build --locked`. Be aware that a lockfile pins versions, not the entire operating environment or external native libraries. Reproducibility improves when toolchain, build flags, and platform assumptions are recorded too.
writing.feedback: `Cargo.lock` records the exact version of every package the resolver selected, not just the root.

# Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
smallvec = "=1.13.1"

# Cargo.lock, from an earlier build
[[package]]
name = "smallvec"
version = "1.13.2"
writing.question: What does Cargo.lock pin?
writing.rule: `Cargo.toml` describes allowed versions while `Cargo.lock` records the exact chosen graph.

recall.answer: None on their resolution: downstream consumers resolve dependencies with their own lockfiles. The library's lockfile only fixes the graph for the library's own development and tests.

recall.question: What does `cargo build --locked` check, and what does a lockfile not pin?
recall.answer: It fails instead of modifying `Cargo.lock`, so it confirms the recorded graph builds as-is on a clean machine. The lockfile pins package versions only, not the toolchain, build flags, platform or external native libraries.

lessons.title: Integration Tests

answers: It is a separate crate
Tests ban privacy
assert_eq! hides them
writing.exampleCaption: The test imports `demo::answer` by crate name, as any outside caller would.
writing.explanation:
Files under `tests/` compile as separate crates and can only use the library's public API. That boundary catches accidental reliance on private implementation details.

An integration test behaves like an external user of your library. Each file under `tests/` is compiled as a separate crate and imports the public API by crate name. It cannot reach private helpers simply because they exist in the same repository. That constraint is valuable: if a test can accomplish a real task through the public interface, downstream callers probably can too.

The sample test imports `demo::answer` and asserts a stable result. Add a second test for a boundary case and a third for an error path. Give each a name that describes the promised behavior. Avoid testing private implementation details through elaborate scaffolding; those tests can become brittle when you refactor without changing the external contract. Unit tests next to the code are still useful for focused private logic. The two test locations serve different levels of confidence.

If an integration test needs a binary or fixture, make setup explicit and keep test cases independent so order does not matter. A test that relies on shared mutable files or network state can fail intermittently and hide real regressions. Run `cargo test --test public_api` while developing that file, then `cargo test` for the full suite. When a test fails, distinguish a library behavior change from a test assumption that was never part of the public contract. A small, representative collection of black-box tests often gives more confidence than many tests coupled to internal functions.
writing.feedback: A file under `tests/` is compiled as its own crate, so it sees only `pub` items, just as a downstream user would.
writing.question: Why can this test not use private items?
writing.rule: Files under `tests/` compile as separate crates and can only use the library's public API.

recall.question: Why are integration tests that share mutable files or network state risky, and what is the remedy?
recall.answer: They can pass or fail depending on run order or the environment, so they fail intermittently and hide real regressions. Make setup explicit and keep each test independent so order does not matter.

lessons.title: Error Context

answers: The original cause
Only a short label
A stack address
writing.exampleCaption: `map_err` adds the operation and the value, and keeps the parser's message in the text.
writing.explanation:
A useful error says what operation failed and retains the original cause. Add context at abstraction boundaries rather than replacing specific information with one vague message.

An error should carry enough information for someone at the boundary to understand what failed. `text.parse::<u16>()` can report a parsing failure, but a caller may need to know that this text was supposed to be a port. The example's `map_err` adds the offending value and the operation while preserving the underlying cause in the formatted message. At a higher layer, you might add which configuration file or command supplied that value.

The useful question is where to add context. A low-level parser knows syntax; a configuration loader knows the field name; a CLI knows what the user was trying to do. Each layer should add only the information it owns. Replacing every error with the same "invalid input" string erases evidence. Duplicating full messages at every layer produces noise. Structured error types or source chains can preserve machine-readable causes until the final presentation layer chooses wording.

Try the port function with valid text, letters, and a number too large for `u16`. Check that the user-facing message distinguishes where the failure occurred without exposing irrelevant internal details. If recovery is possible, return `Result` so the caller can decide. If the error is logged, include enough context to reproduce it while avoiding secrets or full sensitive input. Good diagnostics are a collaboration between error type, call-site context, and final display—not a single catch-all message.
writing.feedback: Context should add what the caller was doing without losing why it failed, so keep the parser's error in the message or as a source.
writing.question: What should context preserve?
writing.rule: A useful error says what operation failed and retains the original cause.
writing.success: Both failures name the value and keep the parser's own reason.
writing.summary: Preserve a cause while explaining the failed operation.
writing.task: Call this `port` with `abc` and with `99999`, then compare the two messages. Rewrite the `map_err` so each one says which value failed and why.

recall.question: What does `port("70000")` return?
recall.answer: `Err("invalid port 70000: number too large to fit in target type")`. The message names the operation and value while keeping the original parse error as its cause.

recall.question: A CLI calls a configuration loader, which calls a number parser. Which context should each layer add to an error?
recall.answer: The parser reports the syntax problem, the loader adds the field name and file, and the CLI adds what the user was trying to do. Each layer adds only what it owns; repeating full messages at every layer creates noise, and secrets should never be included.

cargo clean

writing.exampleCaption: The `assert_eq!` in the doc comment is compiled and run by `cargo test`.
writing.explanation:
Rust documentation examples in Rust code fences can compile and run as tests during `cargo test`, unless their fence attributes opt out or change execution. A small realistic example teaches usage and fails when an API change makes the documentation stale.

A documentation example is a small public usage test. A Rust code block in a `///` comment can be compiled and run by rustdoc during `cargo test`. The sample demonstrates `add_one` with an assertion, so a changed return value can fail the documentation check. In a library crate named `demo`, the example imports the public item as `demo::add_one`; use the actual crate name in a real package. Documentation that calls an item without bringing it into scope can fail even when the function itself is correct.

Keep a doc example focused on the call a user is likely to make, including setup only when needed. Explain the purpose, important input constraints, and meaning of the return value in prose. You can hide incidental setup lines with rustdoc's `#` marker, but the behavior being promised should remain visible. Some fences are marked `no_run` or `ignore` for specific reasons; those attributes affect whether a block executes, so avoid claiming every fenced block is automatically a test.

Run `cargo test --doc` after changing a public API and see whether the example still works. Try deliberately changing the asserted value to observe the failure. Then add an edge-case example if it clarifies behavior, but resist turning documentation into a long test suite. A good example is both readable on the docs page and executable in the test harness. It prevents a common drift: code changes while the published instructions continue teaching an obsolete call.

If a code block requires network access or another external resource, it may be unsuitable as a routine doctest. Show the API in a short self-contained example and put slower environment-dependent checks in integration tests. Keep the documentation honest about what runs automatically.
writing.feedback: `cargo test` runs eligible documentation tests.
writing.question: What checks a Rust doc example?
writing.rule: By default, `cargo test` compiles and runs Rust code fences in library documentation; `no_run` and `ignore` change that behavior.
writing.success: You can identify a failing doc test, repair its assertion, and explain when `no_run` or `ignore` changes execution.

recall.answer: A doctest is compiled like an outside user's program, so the item is not in scope automatically. The example must use the crate path, such as `demo::add_one(4)`, or import it.

recall.question: Why might a doc example be marked `no_run` or `ignore`, and what does that change?
recall.answer: For code that needs network access or another external resource. `no_run` still compiles the block but does not execute it; `ignore` skips it entirely. Either way, not every fenced block is an automatically executed test.

lessons.title: Release Profiles

answers: Measurements
The longest option list
Debug defaults
writing.exampleCaption: A candidate release profile: full optimization, thin LTO, and limited debug information.
writing.exampleCode:
[profile.release]
opt-level = 3
lto = "thin"
debug = 1
writing.explanation:
Cargo profiles configure optimization, debug information, panic strategy, and more. Measure the real workload before trading compile time, binary size, or debuggability for speed.

A Cargo profile controls how a target is compiled. The default development profile favors fast builds and useful diagnostics; the release profile typically enables stronger optimization. Settings such as `opt-level`, `lto`, debug information, and panic behavior change compile time, runtime speed, binary size, or the quality of stack traces. There is no one best combination for every workload.

The sample enables optimization and thin link-time optimization while retaining some debug information. That is a reasonable candidate to measure, not a universal prescription. Compare debug and release builds on a representative task. If a binary is latency-sensitive, measure latency; if it must fit a size limit, measure bytes; if production crashes need investigation, keep enough symbols to diagnose them. A microbenchmark on an empty loop may say little about a real application doing I/O and allocation.

Use `cargo build --release` to create the optimized artifact, and keep tests running in the configurations you support. Some bugs only appear under different optimization or feature combinations, even though safe Rust prevents many memory errors. Record the baseline before changing a profile, change one setting, and compare the same workload. If the result is within noise, prefer the simpler configuration. Release settings should be driven by evidence and operational needs, not by copying every available optimization flag into the manifest.
writing.feedback: Profile settings trade compile time, binary size, and debuggability against speed, so measurements of your own workload decide which to keep.

[profile.release]
opt-level = "s"
lto = "thin"
debug = 1

writing.rule: Cargo profiles configure optimization, debug information, panic strategy, and more.
writing.success: You can report before and after numbers for that one change and justify keeping or rejecting it.

recall.question: A release profile sets `opt-level = 3`, `lto = "thin"` and `debug = 1`. What does each setting trade?
recall.answer: `opt-level = 3` asks for strong optimization at the cost of compile time. Thin LTO allows cross-crate optimization for extra link time. `debug = 1` keeps limited debug info so production crashes can be diagnosed, at the cost of a larger artifact.

recall.question: How should you decide whether to keep a change to a release profile?
recall.answer: Record a baseline on a representative workload, change one setting, and measure the metric that matters (latency, binary size or debuggability) on the same workload. If the difference is within noise, keep the simpler configuration.

writing.summary: Separate a streaming parser from the place its bytes come from.
writing.rule: A reader can fail between records; handle both I/O and parse errors.
writing.explanation:
A file is a source of bytes, not a ready-made collection of valid records. Give the parser a generic `R: BufRead` input so the same function can accept a buffered file, locked stdin, or an in-memory `Cursor`. This separates the data transformation from permissions, paths, and device-specific I/O. It also makes the parser easy to exercise without creating a real file.

The `lines()` iterator yields `io::Result<String>` values. First handle the read result, then decide what a line means. For this small report, trim whitespace, skip blank lines, and parse every other line as `i64`. A malformed nonblank line is an error, not a zero and not a reason to silently discard the record. Include the one-based physical line number in that error, even when earlier lines were blank.

Use `checked_add` when the accepted numeric domain can overflow the accumulator. Returning a clear error preserves the contract instead of making behavior depend on a debug or release overflow setting. Streaming avoids retaining every record, but one unusually long line can still allocate a large string. A production parser needs a separate record-size limit; buffering alone is not a memory quota.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. The lab uses `Cursor` and needs no filesystem permission, package download, network request, or backend execution. Once the parser is correct, a desktop adapter can pass `BufReader::new(File::open(path)?)`. In Crabrix, an adapter must use files granted to its sandbox. Keep the transformation independently testable before adding that adapter.

lessons.title: Paths & Boundaries
lessons.concept: Path, PathBuf, and lexical validation

writing.summary: Treat a path as structured input and keep lexical checks distinct from filesystem authority.
writing.rule: Joining a path is not permission checking, and lexical validation does not resolve symlinks.
writing.explanation:
Use `Path` for a borrowed path and `PathBuf` for an owned path that can be extended. Concatenating strings can mishandle separators and makes it difficult to see which input controls the destination. `root.join(name)` expresses the relationship, but it does not guarantee that the result stays beneath root. In particular, an absolute name can replace the beginning, and parent components can walk upward.

For the lab, accept only a nonempty sequence of normal relative components. Reject an absolute path, any parent component, and a path containing only current-directory components. Joining the accepted components gives a useful lexical rule for an imported project name. Spaces and Unicode are legitimate filename content; do not reject them merely because a shell command would need quoting. No shell command is involved in this operation.

This is deliberately not a complete security boundary for a hostile filesystem. A symlink inside root may point elsewhere, and checking a canonical path before opening it can race with a later replacement. Real authority comes from the host's granted directory handles and platform-specific safe open operations. A WebAssembly guest should not gain access to a user's home directory just because a path string looks harmless.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. The exercise manipulates paths without touching disk. The following file lesson demonstrates a granted sandbox destination. Keep these layers separate: parse a requested relative path, apply the host's access policy, and handle the actual open result. This separation is useful when importing archives or moving project files as well as when writing a command-line report.

writing.task: Accept normal relative components and optional dot components, reject parent/root/prefix components and an empty effective name, then join the trusted root. This is lexical validation, not a symlink security boundary. In the Crabrix app, open the compiler lab and complete the supplied function in solution.rs. The reading question is a separate exercise.

Yes, when the name ends in .txt
No; symlink resolution and authority require separate protection
writing.feedback: The lexical rule rejects obvious traversal but does not establish authority over a changing filesystem.

recall.question: What does `Path::new("/srv/root").join("/etc/passwd")` produce, and what does that mean for validation?
recall.answer: `/etc/passwd`: an absolute argument replaces the base entirely. `join` expresses a relationship but never keeps the result under root, so absolute paths and `..` components must be rejected before joining.

recall.question: Why should a validator accept `my report ü.txt` but reject `../notes.txt`, and what does even a correct lexical check not protect against?
recall.answer: Spaces and Unicode are legitimate filename content, and no shell is involved; `..` is a parent component that walks above root. Lexical checks do not resolve symlinks or prevent races, so real authority must come from granted directory handles.

depth.misconception: A root.join call always stays inside root.
depth.correction: An absolute argument or parent traversal changes the destination; symlinks add another layer.

traceSteps.detail: Refuse roots, prefixes, parents, and an empty effective name.

lessons.title: Save & Read a Text File
lessons.concept: Fallible filesystem effects in a granted directory

writing.summary: Make the file effect explicit, return errors, and verify the bytes that came back.
writing.rule: A successful write is not a promise of crash-safe durability.
writing.explanation:
A small report can keep parsing pure and put file access in a narrow adapter. Accept a borrowed `Path`, write UTF-8 text, read it back, and return `io::Result<String>`. The question mark propagates the real I/O error to the caller. An unreadable destination, missing parent directory, or invalid UTF-8 on a later read is not equivalent to an empty report.

Local compiler profile: standard library with Crabrix's writable `/sandbox` directory. That is a guest path granted by the runtime, not arbitrary access to the iPhone's Files library. The verification harness chooses a sandbox path on wasm32 and a temporary working-directory path for the desktop test. It checks empty text, multiline text, Unicode, and replacement of an existing file. The lesson does not request network or account access.

`fs::write` creates or truncates the target. That is appropriate for this exercise's replace-the-report contract, but it can destroy an older report before a new write finishes. A crash-safe save strategy typically writes a sibling temporary file, flushes and syncs as required, then replaces the destination. Atomic rename and durability details depend on the host filesystem; do not advertise a portable power-loss guarantee from a single write call.

Round-trip equality proves the observed contents for this run. It does not prove every possible failure mode or make concurrent writers safe. If two participants edit a shared Playground, coordinate document updates before asking either participant to save a local copy. A remote output event must never silently trigger the filesystem effect on another device. Keep execution and saving explicit actions owned by the local user.
writing.exampleCaption: Fallible filesystem effects in a granted directory
writing.task: Use fs::write and fs::read_to_string, propagating errors. Return the exact saved text; do not append to an existing file. In the Crabrix app, open the compiler lab and complete the supplied function in solution.rs. The reading question is a separate exercise.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness finishes all normal and boundary cases. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.question: What does fs::write do to an existing target?
answers: It appends automatically
It creates or truncates the file
It guarantees a power-loss-safe transaction
writing.feedback: The target is created or truncated. Crash-safe replacement and durability are separate design requirements.

recall.question: Why is calling `fs::write` straight onto an existing report risky, and what is the usual crash-safer pattern?
recall.answer: `fs::write` truncates the target first, so a crash mid-write can destroy the old report. Write a sibling temporary file, flush and sync as required, then rename it over the destination; atomic rename and durability still depend on the host filesystem.

recall.question: Reading the saved report back hits invalid UTF-8 or a missing parent directory. Why should the function return that error instead of an empty report?
recall.answer: An empty report is a valid result, so substituting it hides a real failure. `fs::read_to_string` on invalid UTF-8 returns an `Err` of kind `InvalidData`; propagating it with `?` lets the caller see what actually went wrong.

depth.misconception: Writing a file automatically makes the save transactional.
depth.correction: Creation/truncation, atomic replacement, and durable persistence are distinct guarantees.

traceSteps.detail: Use only a destination granted by the local runtime.

traceSteps.detail: Propagate write and read errors with question marks.

traceSteps.detail: Compare exact text, including empty input and Unicode.

lessons.title: Validate Data Records

writing.summary: Specify a small input format before implementing its parser.
writing.rule: Malformed records must not disappear from a successful report.
writing.explanation:
The report format in this exercise is intentionally smaller than CSV: one nonblank record per line, exactly two comma-separated fields, a nonempty trimmed name, and an unsigned count. Quoting and escaped commas are unsupported and must be rejected. Calling a split-on-comma parser a complete CSV parser would be misleading; real CSV permits quoted delimiters, embedded newlines, and escaped quote characters.

Parse the entire record before changing the report total. Validate the number of fields, trim both fields, check that the name is nonempty, and parse the count as `u32`. Report a typed or clearly documented error instead of substituting zero. At an application boundary, attach a one-based line number while preserving enough information to explain whether the structure or the number was invalid.

The compiler lab focuses on one record so its contract stays small. A later adapter can reuse the buffered-line reader, skip blank lines, and call this parser. A successful parse returns owned data that can outlive the input buffer. If ownership costs become significant, consider a borrowed intermediate representation, but measure before introducing lifetimes into every public API.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. Tests cover whitespace, zero, extra fields, missing fields, a negative count, overflow, and unsupported quotes. These cases are examples of a broader rule: input validation is a part of the data model, not a cosmetic step at the end. Before extending this format, decide whether an established CSV crate is a better fit than adding another exception to a home-grown grammar.
writing.exampleCaption: A bounded text format with precise errors
writing.task: Return a trimmed owned name and u32 count from exactly two comma-separated fields. Reject quotes, empty names, extra/missing fields, invalid counts and overflow with Err(invalid). This is not a general CSV parser. In the Crabrix app, open the compiler lab and complete the supplied function in solution.rs. The reading question is a separate exercise.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness finishes all normal and boundary cases. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.question: Why is split(',') insufficient for general CSV?
answers: CSV can contain delimiters inside quoted fields
CSV never contains commas
Rust strings cannot contain newlines
writing.feedback: Quoted fields change the grammar. Use a CSV parser for the general format; keep this exercise's restrictions explicit.

recall.question: The format is: one record per line, exactly two comma-separated fields, a nonempty trimmed name and a `u32` count, no quoting. Which of `crab, 3`, `crab,-1`, `crab,3,4`, ` ,3` and `"a,b",3` are accepted?
recall.answer: Only `crab, 3` (name `crab`, count 3). `-1` is not a `u32`, `crab,3,4` has an extra field, ` ,3` has a blank name, and the quoted record is rejected because quoting is unsupported and the split yields three fields.

recall.question: Why should the parser validate a whole record before adding its count to the report total?
recall.answer: So a malformed record can never partly change the report or silently vanish from a successful one. Validate field count, name and count first, then report a clear error with a one-based line number instead of substituting zero.

depth.misconception: Every comma-delimited file can be safely parsed with split.
depth.correction: A simplified grammar is useful only when its accepted and rejected inputs are explicit.

traceSteps.detail: Require a name and a valid unsigned count.

lessons.title: Serde: Decode, Validate, Encode
lessons.concept: Serialization is not domain validation

writing.summary: Turn JSON into a transport type, validate it, and only then create a domain value.
writing.rule: Deserialization checks the transport shape; your domain invariants still need an explicit boundary.
writing.explanation:
JSON describes data exchange, while your application model describes valid state. Deserialize into a small transport structure, then convert it into a domain value whose constructor enforces the rules. A syntactically valid JSON object can still contain a blank display name, a negative quantity, or a count larger than the application supports. Do not spread those checks across every consumer.

Choose an evolution policy. Serde derive normally ignores unknown fields unless configured with `deny_unknown_fields`. This explicit visitor rejects unknown and duplicate fields itself. Neither choice is universally safer: rejecting surprises is useful for a tightly controlled command, while forward-compatible clients may need to tolerate new fields. Document the decision, and use an explicit format version when a later change would reinterpret an existing field.

Compare decoded meaning in a round-trip test rather than relying on object-key order or pretty-print whitespace. Avoid printing full input documents into error logs when they may contain private data. Limit input size before decoding untrusted text, and distinguish a parse error from a domain validation error. The lab in the previous lesson stays dependency-free; this lesson shows how to replace its intentionally restricted transport format with an established serialization library.

The visitor checks duplicate, missing and unknown fields while Serde checks each field type. A u32 rejects negative and overflowing counts. The separate decode function bounds input size and rejects blank names. Main asserts all of those failures as well as a Unicode round-trip; a successful JSON parse alone is not evidence of domain validity.

Local Cargo profile: open the supplied project in Crabrix or the browser Playground. Explicitly prepare its pinned Cargo packages once on each device, then Run and Debug compile and execute on that device without a backend. The project includes Cargo.lock. The lesson question remains the completion exercise; running an unchanged demonstration does not prove a separate programming challenge. This starter uses real serde 1.0.229 and serde_json 1.0.151 with explicit Serialize and Deserialize implementations. That keeps the typed round-trip, strict field policy and domain validation portable without a procedural macro. Derive can generate the same traits on a toolchain with qualified macro support; this lab does not require the experimental macro compiler.
writing.exampleCaption: Real Serde traits: strict typed decoding, separate domain validation and a semantic JSON round-trip.
writing.task: In Crabrix or the web Playground, run the example with the two declared dependencies. Add a domain constructor, then test blank names, missing fields, unknown fields, and an out-of-range count. Open the supplied local Cargo project, prepare packages, then Run or Debug it. Change inputs and examine the assertions. Answer the lesson question separately.
writing.success: A String is structurally valid even when empty. Validate domain invariants after decoding.
writing.question: Does deriving Deserialize guarantee that name is nonblank?
answers: Yes, all String fields are nonblank
No, the application must validate that invariant
Only if JSON keys are sorted
writing.feedback: A String is structurally valid even when empty. Validate domain invariants after decoding.

recall.question: What does Serde derive do by default with an unknown JSON field, and when would you choose to reject unknown fields instead?
recall.answer: Derive ignores unknown fields unless the type uses `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`. Rejecting suits a tightly controlled command; forward-compatible clients may need to tolerate new fields. Use an explicit format version if a change would reinterpret an existing field.

recall.question: Why should a JSON round-trip test compare decoded values rather than the encoded text?
recall.answer: Object-key order and whitespace can differ without any change in meaning, so comparing strings tests formatting, not data. Decode the re-encoded text and compare it with the original domain value.

depth.misconception: Valid JSON is already a valid business record.
depth.correction: The format and type checker do not know application-specific constraints.

traceSteps.detail: Construct domain state only after checking its invariants.

traceSteps.detail: Round-trip meaning and document the schema's evolution policy.

lessons.title: Test Properties, Not Just Examples
lessons.concept: An independent oracle and bounded generated cases

writing.summary: A normalization function should satisfy laws on many inputs, not only one expected output.
writing.rule: Use an independent oracle; repeating the implementation in the assertion repeats its bugs.
writing.explanation:
A few examples help explain a function, while properties describe behavior across a family of inputs. For a canonical set of integer IDs, the output must be sorted, contain no duplicates, preserve membership, and be idempotent. None of those laws alone is enough: a function returning an empty vector is sorted and idempotent but discards every ID.

Compare against an independent model such as BTreeSet rather than copying the same sort-and-deduplicate sequence into the test. Generate bounded combinations from a small domain, including negative values and repeated IDs. Small exhaustive spaces are often excellent at finding boundary mistakes, are deterministic, and require no external dependency. They still establish evidence only for the inputs tested, not a proof for every vector length.

The compiler lab's private harness checks concrete outputs and generated membership behavior. A learner cannot make it pass merely by editing an assertion in the starter. The code under test remains editable; the verdict is produced by a separate harness after calls finish. Treat this as feedback about the exercise contract, not a hostile-code containment guarantee: arbitrary source remains inside the ordinary bounded local runtime.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. On desktop Cargo, property-testing crates such as proptest can generate larger spaces and shrink a failing input into a small counterexample. Preserve the smallest failure as a named regression test even after the generator finds it. Do not call a deterministic loop a fuzzing campaign or claim complete correctness because a finite test suite passed.
writing.exampleCaption: An independent oracle and bounded generated cases
writing.task: Return all distinct input IDs in ascending order. Preserve negative values and integer extremes; empty input stays empty. In the Crabrix app, open the compiler lab and complete the supplied function in solution.rs. The reading question is a separate exercise.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness finishes all normal and boundary cases. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.question: Which property rules out a function that always returns an empty vector?
answers: Idempotence alone
Sorted output alone
Preserving input membership
writing.feedback: Membership preservation catches lost data. Combine it with ordering and uniqueness rather than trusting a single weak property.

recall.question: Why test `canonical` (sort and dedup of IDs) against a `BTreeSet` model rather than repeating `sort_unstable` and `dedup` inside the test?
recall.answer: A test that copies the implementation repeats its bugs and agrees with it whatever it does. A `BTreeSet` is an independent model that yields the sorted, unique members, so a disagreement exposes a real mistake.

recall.question: What do small exhaustive generated input spaces give you, and what can they not establish?
recall.answer: They are deterministic, need no external crate and are good at finding boundary mistakes, including negatives and repeats. They are evidence only for the inputs tested, not proof for every vector length, and are not a fuzzing campaign.

depth.misconception: A single algebraic property proves the whole implementation.
depth.correction: Several incorrect functions satisfy one convenient property; use a complete contract and independent model.

traceSteps.title: Generate

lessons.title: Adversarial Parser Tests
lessons.concept: Reject malformed data without panic or silent truncation

writing.summary: Start with a grammar, then make a test table for the ways input can violate it.
writing.rule: No panic is necessary for an expected invalid input, but success must still mean the whole record was accepted.
writing.explanation:
A parser that never panics can still be wrong if it silently ignores a suffix, rounds an overflowing value, or accepts a missing field. Write down the accepted grammar before writing adversarial cases. This lesson's grammar is exactly two trimmed unsigned decimal byte values separated by one colon. Both values must fit u8. A third field, an empty field, a sign, or nondecimal text is invalid.

Organize tests by failure class instead of adding random strings without a hypothesis. Test a missing delimiter, repeated delimiters, a negative value, a leading plus, overflow, whitespace-only fields, Unicode digits, and the two valid numeric boundaries. Rust's numeric parser may accept syntax you did not intend, so enforce the grammar's ASCII-digit rule before parsing. Return None for this small API; a richer user-facing parser should expose a precise error type.

Avoid `filter_map` on fallible fields: it can turn a three-field record with one bad field into two apparently good values. Do not index a collected vector until its length has been checked. Check complete consumption so a valid prefix cannot conceal trailing junk. These ideas transfer directly to command input, imported project metadata, and network messages.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. The lab uses deterministic hostile cases. Desktop cargo-fuzz is a separate toolchain that can explore byte inputs and save crashes; it does not belong to the browser or iOS run profile merely because the parser itself is portable. A useful fuzz target asserts domain properties after successful parsing and never treats rejection of arbitrary bytes as a bug.
writing.exampleCaption: Reject malformed data without panic or silent truncation
writing.task: Parse exactly two trimmed ASCII-decimal u8 fields separated by one colon. Reject signs, empty fields, extra fields, non-ASCII digits, and overflow. Return None on invalid input. In the Crabrix app, open the compiler lab and complete the supplied function in solution.rs. The reading question is a separate exercise.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness finishes all normal and boundary cases. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.question: Why test a leading plus sign separately from a negative number?
answers: The declared grammar may forbid syntax that a numeric parser accepts
Plus signs always overflow u8
It makes the parser multithreaded
writing.feedback: The application's grammar can be narrower than parse::<u8>(). Test the declared syntax as well as the numeric range.

recall.question: A two-field `a:b` parser collects fields with `filter_map(|f| f.trim().parse::<u8>().ok())`. What does that give for `1:x:2`, and why is it dangerous?
recall.answer: It yields `[1, 2]`: the bad field disappears and the extra field makes up the count, so a malformed three-field record looks like a valid pair. Check the field count and fail on any field that does not parse.

recall.question: What should a fuzz target for this parser assert, and what should it not treat as a bug?
recall.answer: It should assert that parsing never panics and that every successful parse satisfies the domain properties, such as consuming the whole record. Returning `None` for arbitrary garbage bytes is expected rejection, not a bug.

depth.misconception: Anything accepted by parse::<u8>() belongs to my format.
depth.correction: Primitive parsing is a building block; the full record grammar remains your responsibility.

lessons.title: Keep a Unicode Regression
lessons.concept: A minimal failure that survives a refactor

writing.summary: Turn a real boundary failure into a small, named case that protects future changes.
writing.rule: Define the unit before testing a text limit: bytes, scalar values, and grapheme clusters differ.
writing.explanation:
Suppose a preview function once sliced text at a byte offset and panicked on an accented character. Replacing it with a character iterator fixes that specific bug, but keep a regression that would fail under the old implementation. A test named after the behavior, such as truncates_at_scalar_boundary, is more useful than one named after an unrelated ticket number.

The contract here is to keep at most n Unicode scalar values and add no ellipsis. Return all text when it is shorter than n, and an empty string when n is zero. This is not a display-column limit or a grapheme-cluster limit. An e followed by a combining accent consists of two scalar values; stopping after one may produce a visually surprising but contractually valid result. A user-interface preview may need a grapheme-aware library instead.

A strong regression set contains the smallest original failure, zero, an empty input, an oversized limit, and a neighboring ASCII case. Add a property that the result is a prefix at a valid UTF-8 boundary and contains at most the requested number of scalar values. Avoid assuming that String::len counts characters; it counts bytes.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. The lab compiles the changed function and checks the regression cases independently. Before changing the contract to add an ellipsis, decide whether the ellipsis counts toward the limit and whether existing callers depend on exact output. Good tests document that contract; they should not freeze every internal implementation choice or discourage a clearer iterator-based solution.
writing.exampleCaption: A minimal failure that survives a refactor
writing.task: Return at most n Unicode scalar values from the start, with no ellipsis. Never slice at an unchecked byte offset. In the Crabrix app, open the compiler lab and complete the supplied function in solution.rs. The reading question is a separate exercise.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness finishes all normal and boundary cases. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.question: How many Unicode scalar values are in e followed by a combining accent?
answers: One in every representation
Two, although they may render as one grapheme
The UTF-8 byte length is always the scalar count
writing.feedback: A scalar value and a grapheme are different units. State and test the intended unit explicitly.

recall.question: What does `prefix("e\u{301}x", 1)` return, and does it satisfy the contract?
recall.answer: `"e"`, without the combining accent. That meets the contract of at most n Unicode scalar values, though it looks surprising; a user-interface preview that must keep whole letters needs a grapheme-aware approach.

recall.question: Which cases belong in the regression set for a `prefix(text, n)` that once panicked on an accented character?
recall.answer: The smallest original failure, `n = 0`, empty input, a limit larger than the text, and a neighboring ASCII case. Add a property that the result is a prefix ending on a valid UTF-8 boundary with at most n scalar values.

depth.misconception: chars().count() always measures visible character width.
depth.correction: Scalar values can combine into a grapheme and have different display widths.

units.title: Library Contracts
units.subtitle: SemVer, MSRV and unchanged downstream consumers

lessons.title: Evolving a Public API
lessons.concept: Compile the unchanged consumer before calling an API change compatible

writing.summary: Compile the unchanged consumer before calling an API change compatible.
writing.rule: Keep the original caller's signatures and promised behavior across supported releases.
writing.explanation:
A library release is used by code you do not own. Start the review with one unchanged downstream consumer: the original call to `Policy::new(3).unwrap().attempts()` must still compile and return three. A green library test suite is useful but can miss a break if those tests were edited together with the API. Compile the same consumer against both library versions instead of fixing it until it passes.

In the example, `attempts` and `delay_ms` are private. Callers construct `Policy` through `new`, so adding the private delay field does not require them to update a struct literal. The existing constructor keeps its parameter, return type and zero-attempt validation. `with_delay` is a new builder that retains the attempt count; omitting it still selects zero delay. This is a deliberately small compatible evolution of this consumer contract, not a proof that every private representation change is harmless.

An entirely public struct is a different contract. Adding a required field breaks a downstream literal that listed all the previous fields. Adding an enum variant can break an exhaustive downstream match. A `#[non_exhaustive]` design can reserve evolution space when chosen before callers depend on exhaustive construction or matching; adding that restriction later may itself break callers. For a public trait, remember that consumers may implement it as well as call it: a new required method affects those implementations.

Source compatibility is one part of the review. Changing an error condition, normalization rule, panic behavior or ordering can break an application that still compiles. Generic bounds, auto traits such as `Send`, lifetimes and documented layout or FFI promises can also matter. The private-field builder does not grant permission to change these properties silently. Write the behavior you promise, then choose a versioning and migration policy that matches it. Cargo's SemVer guidance describes conventions and caveats; a version number does not establish that an arbitrary change is safe.

Keep a downstream fixture outside the library's own module tests. Pin the consumer source bytes, compile it with the candidate library, run its observable assertions, and retain a deliberately incompatible candidate that the fixture rejects. A changed constructor arity should fail compilation; a constructor that quietly changes the attempt count should compile but fail the consumer assertion. These two failures demonstrate different checks. A finite fixture covers its consumers and inputs, not every possible external program.

Local compiler lab: implement the constructor, getters and builder in `solution.rs` without changing their public signatures. The separate harness calls the API with normal and boundary values and checks that the builder preserves the original attempt count. It does not accept an edited assertion or a printed success string as the implementation. The standard-library example and lab need no server or external crate. Full release CI should additionally test the supported targets, feature sets and compiler versions.
writing.exampleCaption: The original constructor and getter still work; the builder adds delay without changing the old caller.
writing.task: Implement RetryPolicy::new, attempts, delay_ms and the consuming with_delay builder. Reject zero attempts; preserve every positive u8 attempt count. The constructor sets zero delay, and the builder changes only delay, including u32::MAX. Keep the supplied public signatures. Open the compiler lab and edit solution.rs. The reading question is independent.
writing.success: The changed implementation passes the separate normal and boundary harness. MSRV and the full Cargo feature matrix have their own explicit checks.
writing.question: A library adds a required public field to a previously constructible public struct. Which unchanged downstream code can stop compiling?
answers: A struct literal listing only the old fields
Every call to an unchanged getter necessarily fails
Only code using an experimental compiler is affected
writing.feedback: The old literal has no value for the new required field. Constructor-based examples are a different API shape; an unchanged getter alone does not require a downstream literal.

recall.question: Why does adding a private `delay_ms` field to `Policy` leave `Policy::new(3).unwrap().attempts()` working?
recall.answer: Callers cannot write a `Policy` struct literal because its fields are private; they must use `new`, which keeps its parameter, return type and zero-attempt validation. The new `with_delay` builder is optional and defaults to zero delay.

recall.question: The library's own test suite passes after an API change. Why is that weak evidence of compatibility, and what is a better check?
recall.answer: Those tests may have been edited together with the API. Compile an unchanged downstream consumer fixture against both versions and run its assertions; behaviour changes such as a different error condition or ordering can break users even when the code still compiles.

depth.misconception: Private fields make every later library change SemVer-compatible.
depth.correction: Private representation can evolve more easily, but behavior, auto traits, lifetimes and explicit layout promises still need review.

lessons.title: MSRV Is a Tested Promise
lessons.concept: A manifest declaration needs evidence from the minimum supported compiler

writing.summary: A manifest declaration needs evidence from the minimum supported compiler.
writing.rule: Test the actual minimum compiler and supported profiles; metadata alone is not evidence.
writing.explanation:
The minimum supported Rust version, or MSRV, is a support promise about the compiler and Cargo environment your package accepts. A `rust-version = "1.78"` declaration tells Cargo the stated minimum; it does not translate newer syntax or standard-library APIs into older equivalents. A current compiler can compile code that the minimum cannot. A release needs a minimum-version job as well as the ordinary current-version job.

Use a concrete failure. `Option::is_none_or` was stabilized in Rust 1.82. An implementation using that method can pass on a newer compiler while failing on 1.78, even if the manifest still says 1.78. The reading's `match` expresses the same optional-limit rule without that method: no configured value is permitted, zero is rejected, and a positive value must not exceed the ceiling. Check the boundary where the value equals the ceiling, and the case where the ceiling itself is zero.

A useful support record includes the declared compiler, edition, feature sets, targets, dependency resolution and tests performed. This unit's small fixtures use edition 2021 and a dependency-free lockfile understood by both tested toolchains. That keeps a standard-library API failure separate from an unrelated manifest or lockfile-format failure. In a real package, newer Cargo syntax, edition support, build scripts and procedural macros may raise the effective requirement before your own library source is compiled.

Run the actual supported toolchain, for example `cargo +1.78 check --locked` and `cargo +1.78 test --locked`, in an environment that has it installed. Repeat the relevant jobs on the current toolchain and under your documented optional features. A library consumer resolves with its own dependency graph and lockfile, so the author's development lockfile is not evidence for every downstream graph. Review compatible dependency updates and retain a representative consumer fixture. Resolver preferences that consider `rust-version` help select packages, but do not prove the resulting source compiles or that every requested combination has a compatible candidate.

Choose and publish an MSRV-change policy. State when an increase can occur, how it is announced and whether an older release line receives fixes. Different projects choose different policies; do not invent a universal requirement that every MSRV increase must use the same SemVer bump. Cargo's guidance treats these changes as a compatibility concern and recommends documenting the chosen policy. A CI support matrix should express what you actually promise, not the largest list of versions that looks impressive.

Local compiler lab: implement `permits` and satisfy the independent boundary harness. This validates behavior on the compiler installed in Crabrix. Crabrix uses one pinned toolchain, so that result is not an emulated run of Rust 1.78. The accompanying release fixture is tested separately with the real installed old and current compilers, including the deliberately too-new method. Preserve that distinction when reporting compatibility. Neither check needs backend execution.
writing.exampleCaption: A match-based implementation preserves the optional-limit contract on both tested compiler versions.
writing.task: Implement permits(value, ceiling): None is allowed, even with a zero ceiling; Some(n) is allowed exactly when 0 < n <= ceiling. Keep the signature and handle the u16 boundaries. The local grader tests behavior on the installed compiler; use the separate two-toolchain fixture to establish MSRV. Open the compiler lab and edit solution.rs. The reading question is independent.
writing.success: The changed implementation passes the separate normal and boundary harness. MSRV and the full Cargo feature matrix have their own explicit checks.
writing.question: A package declares Rust 1.78 and its only CI job passes on a current compiler. What has that job established?
answers: The declaration guarantees compatibility with Rust 1.78
The tested graph builds on that current compiler; Rust 1.78 remains untested
All optional features and downstream graphs satisfy Rust 1.78
writing.feedback: The declaration is metadata and a support promise. Running the actual minimum toolchain, plus the promised configurations, supplies evidence for the minimum.

recall.question: A crate declares `rust-version = "1.78"` but uses `Option::is_none_or`, stabilized in 1.82. What happens on a current compiler and on 1.78?
recall.answer: The current compiler accepts it, so a current-only CI job passes, while Rust 1.78 fails to compile it. `rust-version` neither rejects newer APIs nor translates them; an equivalent `match` on the `Option` works on both.

recall.question: What gives real evidence for an MSRV promise, and why is the author's lockfile not evidence for downstream users?
recall.answer: Running the actual minimum toolchain, for example `cargo +1.78 check --locked` and `cargo +1.78 test --locked`, alongside current-version jobs and documented features. Consumers resolve their own dependency graph, so the author's lockfile does not cover them.

depth.misconception: Setting rust-version makes the current compiler reject every API newer than the declared minimum.
depth.correction: The current compiler can accept newer APIs. Check the actual minimum compiler and the supported build configuration.

traceSteps.detail: Test absent, zero, equal-to-limit and over-limit values.

traceSteps.detail: The newer method is rejected on 1.78 while the match-based version passes on both.

lessons.title: The Downstream Feature Matrix
lessons.concept: Optional capability must preserve the old consumer across the supported feature sets

writing.summary: Optional capability must preserve the old consumer across the supported feature sets.
writing.rule: Keep the baseline API working with defaults, minimal builds and supported feature unions.
writing.explanation:
A feature is part of a package's public contract when downstream users can request it. This example preserves `label(7) == "core=7"` while adding `details` and `trace` functions. The existing consumer does not change when either feature is enabled. The two features can be requested together, and the base `label` keeps the same signature and behavior. That is the observable promise the matrix checks.

Cargo combines feature requests for a package within the applicable resolution context. One dependency path can request `details` and another can request `trace`, so code that only compiles with exactly one of them is a downstream hazard. Newer resolver versions isolate some contexts, such as certain build or development dependencies; this does not turn ordinary feature requests into global exclusion switches. Keep the example's two functions differently named and additive. A broken alternative that defines the same helper name under both features may pass each individual build and fail their union.

Check a small, explicit matrix rather than trusting `--all-features` alone. Include defaults, `--no-default-features`, each optional feature, and supported combinations. The all-features build can accidentally hide a missing item in the minimal profile. Conversely, checking each feature alone misses collisions when consumers request both. For a large feature set, select combinations from the documented contract and known interactions; checking a few combinations is not a claim to have exhausted an exponential space.

Use a downstream consumer of the library target, not only tests that live inside its private module tree. Keep that consumer's source bytes fixed while changing the requested dependency features. Assert both the baseline rendering and each requested optional API. The accompanying fixture compiles and runs this consumer on the minimum and current compilers. It also checks a candidate that changes baseline rendering only when `details` is enabled, and one whose duplicate helper exists only in the union. Each should fail for a different reason.

`default-features = false` is an edge request to avoid enabling that dependency's defaults; it is not a command to disable defaults that another dependency path requests. The fixture includes two paths to demonstrate this distinction. Be cautious when removing an existing default feature, renaming an optional capability, changing its implied dependencies or increasing the compiler requirement of that feature. Review those changes under the same published compatibility policy as ordinary public methods.

Local compiler lab: implement the baseline `label` function for all `u16` IDs, preserving the exact `core=` prefix and decimal representation. Its independent, manifest-free harness checks the baseline contract only; a passing lab is not evidence that every Cargo feature profile has run. The complete worked example uses ordinary standard-library code and conditional functions. For the actual Cargo matrix, use the accompanying source fixture and run the documented commands with each feature selection. The app's prepared Cargo environment can run supported profiles explicitly; it does not switch to an older compiler. No server, network service or downloaded package is needed for this unit.
writing.exampleCaption: The old consumer always prints core=7; details and trace add independent functions that can coexist.
writing.task: Implement the unchanged baseline label contract: core= followed immediately by the ordinary decimal u16 value, with no padding, spaces or newline. The local harness checks this API only. Then use the accompanying Cargo fixture to test the actual feature profiles and their unchanged downstream consumer. Open the compiler lab and edit solution.rs. The reading question is independent.
writing.success: The changed implementation passes the separate normal and boundary harness. MSRV and the full Cargo feature matrix have their own explicit checks.
writing.question: Why is a successful all-features build insufficient evidence for the documented no-default-features profile?
answers: All-features secretly turns every feature off
The minimal profile always has the same items as all-features
An enabled feature can supply an item missing from the minimal profile
writing.feedback: A large feature set can mask missing minimal-profile items. Test that profile independently, then test unions to catch collisions.

recall.question: Features `details` and `trace` each define `pub fn helper()` under their own `#[cfg(feature = ...)]`. Each feature builds alone. What happens when a downstream graph enables both?
recall.answer: The union fails to compile with E0428, the name `helper` is defined multiple times. Checking each feature separately misses this, and Cargo can unify both requests from different dependency paths, so supported combinations must be built too.

recall.question: Besides compile failures, what kind of downstream break should a feature matrix catch, and how?
recall.answer: A behaviour change in the baseline API that appears only when a feature is enabled, for example `label(7)` no longer returning `core=7` with `details` on. A fixed downstream consumer that asserts the baseline output under every supported feature set catches it.

depth.misconception: Testing each optional feature separately proves that their union is compatible.
depth.correction: The union can expose duplicate definitions or a changed baseline API. Test the combinations your contract supports.

traceSteps.title: Pin the consumer
traceSteps.detail: Call label(7) from a consumer whose source does not change.

traceSteps.title: Vary requests
traceSteps.detail: Run base, no-default, details, trace and both-feature profiles.

traceSteps.title: Observe two failures
traceSteps.detail: A behavior change fails an assertion; a duplicate helper in the union fails compilation.

lessons.title: Review the Exact Change
lessons.concept: Distinguish changed, added and deleted paths

writing.summary: Distinguish changed, added and deleted paths.
writing.rule: Compare source snapshots by path and content before selecting a commit.
writing.explanation:
A worktree is the collection you are editing. A commit records a particular tree; autosave protects edits but does not create a commit. Review both before selecting paths. A file can disappear, appear, or keep its name while its contents change. Looking only for new names misses modifications and deletions.

Build the candidate path set from both trees and compare values. Return each changed path once in lexical order. File ordering is presentation, not Git object identity. This lab models text trees; real Git also stores modes and opaque bytes. In the native terminal, inspect actual history through the existing libgit2-backed commands. The selected-path commit profile commits exactly the reviewed paths, so unrelated edits stay uncommitted.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Run git status and git diff src/main.rs before committing. The terminal uses real Git; the lab isolates the tree-comparison contract.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. A successful unchanged demonstration does not prove your implementation. After the lab, apply the same contract to the route companion project. Its README separates the on-device adapter from the desktop Cargo/TCP profile.
writing.exampleCaption: The worked implementation exercises distinguish changed, added and deleted paths. Its tests demonstrate the stated finite contract.
writing.task: Return the sorted unique paths whose contents differ between two trees; include additions and deletions. Each input has unique paths. Keep the public signature. Open the compiler lab and edit solution.rs; do not edit the private verification caller.
writing.success: The separate caller accepts the changed solution and rejects unchanged TODO, a wrong implementation and a printed success message.
writing.question: An existing file keeps its name but changes content. Should it appear in the review?
answers: Autosave makes the edit a commit
Yes, content is part of the snapshot
Only newly named files belong in a change review
writing.feedback: Comparing only path names misses modified content; comparing only the new tree misses deletions.

recall.question: What does `changed(&[("a", "1"), ("gone", "x")], &[("a", "1"), ("b", "3")])` return?
recall.answer: `["b", "gone"]`: the added path and the deleted path, once each, in lexical order. `a` is omitted because its content is the same in both trees.

recall.question: Why must the candidate path set be built from both the before and after trees, with their contents compared?
recall.answer: Taking names only from the after tree misses deletions, and only from the before tree misses additions. Comparing the values catches files that keep their name but change content.

depth.misconception: Only newly named files belong in a change review
depth.correction: Compare source snapshots by path and content before selecting a commit.

lessons.concept: Construct the selected commit tree

writing.summary: Construct the selected commit tree.
writing.rule: An unselected worktree edit must not silently enter a selected-path commit.
writing.explanation:
Task Ledger changes its CLI and a private scratch note at the same time. A commit intended to fix CLI parsing should contain the CLI change, leaving the note outside history. The tree to commit begins with HEAD, not with every current worktree file. Apply selected additions, modifications and deletions onto that tree.

A selection can include a deleted path: remove it from the commit tree instead of resurrecting its old text. Unknown selected paths have no effect in this model. An actual Git operation additionally validates file paths, expected HEAD and concurrent editor revisions. The terminal deliberately uses selected-path commits rather than pretending to implement an independent staging area. Desktop Git can use its index; distinguish that workflow from this app profile.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Configure git config user.name and user.email, then git commit -m "Validate CLI input" -- src/main.rs; inspect git status afterwards.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. A successful unchanged demonstration does not prove your implementation. After the lab, apply the same contract to the route companion project. Its README separates the on-device adapter from the desktop Cargo/TCP profile.
writing.exampleCaption: The worked implementation exercises construct the selected commit tree. Its tests demonstrate the stated finite contract.
writing.task: Return the HEAD tree with only selected paths replaced from the worktree, or removed if selected and missing. Sort by path; paths are unique in each input. Keep the public signature. Open the compiler lab and edit solution.rs; do not edit the private verification caller.
writing.success: The separate caller accepts the changed solution and rejects unchanged TODO, a wrong implementation and a printed success message.
writing.question: Which tree is the starting point for a selected-path commit?
answers: HEAD, followed by selected changes
The whole current worktree always enters the commit
The selected filenames without their contents
writing.feedback: Starting from the whole worktree includes unrelated edits.

recall.question: HEAD contains `a`, the worktree has deleted `a`, and `a` is selected for the commit. What should the committed tree contain?
recall.answer: No `a`: the selected deletion is applied to the tree built from HEAD rather than resurrecting the old text. With nothing else in HEAD, the committed tree is empty.

recall.question: What does `git commit -m "Validate CLI input" -- src/main.rs` put in the commit, and what happens to an edited scratch note?
recall.answer: The commit is HEAD plus the current contents of `src/main.rs` only. The scratch note's edit stays uncommitted in the worktree, which `git status` afterwards should confirm.

depth.misconception: The whole current worktree always enters the commit
depth.correction: An unselected worktree edit must not silently enter a selected-path commit.

lessons.title: Switch Without Losing Work
lessons.concept: Protect dirty worktrees during checkout

writing.summary: Protect dirty worktrees during checkout.
writing.rule: Require a clean worktree before this profile replaces files from another branch.
writing.explanation:
Branches name positions in history. Creating a branch does not copy a folder, and switching it is not merely changing a label: the target tree can replace editor files. A clean-checkout policy is easy to explain and test. It refuses the operation whenever the current worktree differs from its HEAD, including an untracked file or deletion.

Compare trees without relying on their enumeration order. A new branch can be created while preserving current edits, but switching uses the clean-tree precondition in this terminal. A desktop client may support more nuanced preservation or stash; those are distinct contracts. After committing, refresh status before switching, because a successful commit of one captured snapshot does not prove newer typing was also committed.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Run git branch feature-cli, git status, then git switch feature-cli after the tree is clean.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. A successful unchanged demonstration does not prove your implementation. After the lab, apply the same contract to the route companion project. Its README separates the on-device adapter from the desktop Cargo/TCP profile.

writing.success: The separate caller accepts the changed solution and rejects unchanged TODO, a wrong implementation and a printed success message.
writing.question: Can an untracked file matter to a clean-checkout policy?
answers: Only tracked modifications can make a checkout unsafe
Changing branch names preserves every file automatically
Yes; the worktree differs from HEAD
writing.feedback: An added or deleted file is a tree difference even when tracked file contents match.

recall.question: Under the clean-checkout policy, which of these block a branch switch: a modified tracked file, a new untracked file, a deleted file, the same files listed in a different order?
recall.answer: The first three block it, because each makes the worktree differ from HEAD. Listing order does not, because the trees are compared as path-to-content maps rather than by enumeration order.

recall.question: You just made a commit and want to switch branches. Why refresh status first?
recall.answer: The commit recorded one captured snapshot; anything typed after that snapshot may still be uncommitted. Refreshing status shows whether the worktree is really clean before the switch replaces files.

depth.misconception: Only tracked modifications can make a checkout unsafe
depth.correction: Require a clean worktree before this profile replaces files from another branch.

lessons.title: Recover One Historical File
lessons.concept: Restore narrowly from a known revision

writing.summary: Restore narrowly from a known revision.
writing.rule: A one-file restore must preserve every unrelated current edit.
writing.explanation:
A rollback need not replace a whole project. To recover one file, first inspect its contents at an exact historical commit, compare it with the current file, then confirm the replacement. A full commit identity makes the preview stable while branch names continue moving.

The native git restore command opens a preview; applying the restore remains an explicit UI action. This lab models the resulting tree change: replace just the requested path from the historical tree, or remove it if it did not exist there. Preserve unrelated work and deterministic ordering. Restoring a file is also an uncommitted edit; review and commit it as a new change when it belongs in shared history. Do not rewrite already shared history to hide an ordinary correction.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Use git log, git show <full-commit>:src/main.rs, then git restore --source <full-commit> -- src/main.rs and inspect the preview.

writing.question: After restoring one historical file, what happens to unrelated current edits?
answers: A restore rewrites every previous commit
They stay in the worktree
All files should revert to the historical tree
