recall.question: You restore `a` from a historical commit in which `a` did not exist. What happens to the current `a` and to other edited files?
recall.answer: `a` is removed, because the restore makes that one path match the historical tree. Every other path, including unrelated uncommitted edits, is left as it is.

recall.question: Why preview a historical file by full commit identity rather than a branch name, and what should happen after the restore?
recall.answer: Branch names keep moving, while a full commit identity keeps the preview stable. The restored file is an uncommitted edit, so review and commit it as a new change rather than rewriting shared history.

depth.correction: A one-file restore must preserve every unrelated current edit.

lessons.title: Parse a CLI Contract
lessons.concept: Preserve arguments and reject ambiguous input

writing.summary: Preserve arguments and reject ambiguous input.
writing.rule: Parse the entire invocation before applying any side effect.
writing.explanation:
A shell groups text into arguments before a Rust program sees it. Quotes preserve a space or an empty argument; they are not usually part of the resulting argument. Cargo consumes its options before the double dash and passes the remainder to the executable. The first executable argument is conventionally the program name and is not a user command.

Task Ledger accepts exactly `list` or `add TITLE`. Reject an unknown command, a missing title and extra arguments. Trim the title for domain validation, while retaining internal spaces and Unicode. Do not partially add a task before discovering a later invalid option. The independent lab takes only the already-separated user arguments; the companion main passes `std::env::args().skip(1)`.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Run cargo run -- add "learn Rust" and cargo run -- add "" against the companion CLI.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. A successful unchanged demonstration does not prove your implementation. After the lab, apply the same contract to the route companion project. Its README separates the on-device adapter from the desktop Cargo/TCP profile.

writing.question: Which invocation passes one title containing a space?
answers: cargo run -- add "learn Rust"
cargo run add learn Rust
Quotes always become part of the Rust title
writing.feedback: The shell supplies argument boundaries; Cargo needs the double dash before application arguments.

recall.question: Given `["list"]` or `["add", title]` as the only valid shapes, what do `command(&["add", "  learn Rust 🦀  "])` and `command(&["list", "extra"])` return?
recall.answer: `Ok("add:learn Rust 🦀")`: the title is trimmed but keeps its internal space and Unicode. `Err("usage")`: extra arguments are rejected rather than ignored.

recall.question: In `cargo run -- add "learn Rust"`, what do the `--` and the quotes do, and why does the program use `std::env::args().skip(1)`?
recall.answer: `--` ends Cargo's own options so the rest goes to the executable; the quotes make `learn Rust` one argument and are not part of it. The first argument is conventionally the program name, not a user command, so it is skipped.

depth.misconception: cargo run add learn Rust
depth.correction: Parse the entire invocation before applying any side effect.

lessons.title: Resolve Configuration Once
lessons.concept: Apply explicit configuration precedence

writing.summary: Apply explicit configuration precedence.
writing.rule: Choose flag over environment over default, then validate the chosen value.
writing.explanation:
Configuration can come from a flag, an environment variable or a default. Establish precedence before parsing so a broken lower-priority value does not override an explicit valid flag. Conversely, do not silently fall back when the chosen highest-priority value is malformed: the operator needs to know their request was rejected.

The list limit must be an integer from 1 to 100. Absence selects 20, but an explicitly empty string is an invalid value, not absence. In production, report which configuration source failed without printing secrets. Invocation environment in Crabrix is passed only to the student program; it never changes the compiler or dependency build-script environment. This prevents an educational flag from accidentally reconfiguring the toolchain.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Run env TASK_LIMIT=7 cargo run -- list. Compare with env TASK_LIMIT=bad cargo run -- list.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. A successful unchanged demonstration does not prove your implementation. After the lab, apply the same contract to the route companion project. Its README separates the on-device adapter from the desktop Cargo/TCP profile.

writing.question: An explicit valid flag overrides a malformed environment value. What should happen?
answers: Reject the unrelated lower-priority value
Always use the default
Use the flag
writing.feedback: Precedence decides the authoritative value before validation; invalid authoritative input must still fail.

recall.question: Precedence is flag, then environment, then default 20, with valid values 1 to 100. What do `limit(None, None)` and `limit(Some(""), Some("5"))` return?
recall.answer: `Ok(20)`, since nothing was supplied. `Err("invalid limit")`, because an explicitly empty flag is an invalid value, not absence, so it does not fall back to the environment's 5.

recall.question: Why should a malformed flag value produce an error instead of quietly falling back to the environment variable or default?
recall.answer: The operator explicitly chose that value, and a silent fallback hides that their request was rejected. Report which configuration source failed, without printing secrets.

depth.correction: Choose flag over environment over default, then validate the chosen value.

lessons.title: Process Bounded Standard Input
lessons.concept: Treat input as data with resource limits

writing.summary: Treat input as data with resource limits.
writing.rule: Check byte limits before retaining input and validate complete records.
writing.explanation:
Standard input makes a tool composable: a file can feed the same parser as typed input. Rust strings are UTF-8; byte length and character count answer different questions. A memory budget is measured in bytes, so an emoji can consume several bytes of the budget. A record title is a nonblank line after trimming, with at most 80 Unicode scalar values in this lab.

Reject the complete input if its byte size exceeds the supplied budget or any title is too long. Ignore blank lines and keep record order. A production streaming parser additionally stops accumulation as it reads; this exercise receives an already bounded string to isolate validation. The companion reads through a limited reader and detects one byte beyond its limit. Do not advertise a post-read length check as protection against an unbounded stream.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Create input.txt, then run cargo run -- import < input.txt; inspect stderr for an oversized record.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. A successful unchanged demonstration does not prove your implementation. After the lab, apply the same contract to the route companion project. Its README separates the on-device adapter from the desktop Cargo/TCP profile.

writing.question: Which size controls a UTF-8 input memory budget?
answers: The number of newline separators
Encoded byte length
Only the number of visible characters
writing.feedback: An emoji can fit one scalar position while exceeding a three-byte budget.

recall.question: In the import lab, a line of 81 `x` characters arrives within the byte budget. What happens, and how does the title limit differ from the budget?
recall.answer: The input is rejected with `title too long`. The title limit is 80 Unicode scalar values after trimming, while the memory budget is measured in encoded bytes, so an emoji counts as one character but four bytes.

recall.question: Why is checking the input's length after reading all of standard input not protection against an unbounded stream?
recall.answer: By then the whole stream is already in memory. A streaming reader must stop accumulating as it reads, for example by reading through a limited reader and detecting one byte beyond the limit.

depth.misconception: Only the number of visible characters
depth.correction: Check byte limits before retaining input and validate complete records.

lessons.title: Separate Output from Failure
lessons.concept: Return observable stdout, stderr and exit status

writing.summary: Return observable stdout, stderr and exit status.
writing.rule: Data goes to stdout; a failure has stderr context and a nonzero status.
writing.explanation:
Automation observes a program through more than its printed text. A machine may consume stdout as data and use the exit status to decide whether the next stage may run. Putting an error into stdout while returning success makes a broken command look like a valid empty result.

Use status 0 for a successful task count and 2 for a usage or input error in this CLI contract. Error text belongs on stderr and ends in a newline. Do not add a success banner to machine-readable stdout. A program that crashes or fails compilation is different from a deliberate domain error; retain that distinction when diagnosing the terminal result. The finite lab models the three outputs so tests can assert them separately; the companion uses println, eprintln and process::exit at its actual boundary.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Run a valid and an invalid companion CLI invocation and compare output, error stream and exit result.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. A successful unchanged demonstration does not prove your implementation. After the lab, apply the same contract to the route companion project. Its README separates the on-device adapter from the desktop Cargo/TCP profile.

writing.question: A command prints an error but exits with status 0. What is wrong for automation?
answers: The command reports success through its status
Any text on stderr automatically changes the exit status
Exit codes are only decorative
writing.feedback: Writing stderr does not itself set a nonzero process exit status.

recall.question: Under this CLI contract, what (stdout, stderr, status) does `report(Ok(0))` produce, and how does that differ from `report(Err("missing input"))`?
recall.answer: `("0\n", "", 0)`: a count of zero is valid data. The error gives `("", "error: missing input\n", 2)`, so automation can tell a failure from an empty result by the status and stream, not by guessing from text.

recall.question: Why should a CLI whose stdout is consumed by another program not print a success banner there?
recall.answer: Stdout is the data the next stage parses, so a banner corrupts it. Human-facing diagnostics belong on stderr, and success or failure is signalled by the exit status.

depth.misconception: Any text on stderr automatically changes the exit status
depth.correction: Data goes to stdout; a failure has stderr context and a nonzero status.

lessons.title: Route Method and Path Together
lessons.concept: Separate unknown routes from disallowed methods

writing.summary: Separate unknown routes from disallowed methods.
writing.rule: Resolve the resource first, then the allowed HTTP method.
writing.explanation:
An HTTP method is part of the request contract. GET /tasks lists tasks; POST /tasks creates one. A known resource with a disallowed method is different from a path the application does not own. This lab returns 405 for unsupported methods on /tasks and 404 for unknown paths; GET /health returns 200, while other health methods return 405.

The request target can include a query string. Separate it before matching the path, but do not lowercase the path or decode arbitrary escapes without a policy: route names can be case sensitive. The lab implements literal paths only. A desktop Axum router handles the transport; the on-device adapter passes a bounded real HTTP request to Rust through stdin. It is an HTTP/1.x adapter with one response per connection, not an implementation of every HTTP version or chunked body mode.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Run cargo serve --port 8080 --database tasks.db, then curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/tasks and curl -i -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8080/tasks. Stop with http stop.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. A successful unchanged demonstration does not prove your implementation. After the lab, apply the same contract to the route companion project. An unknown path should return 200 with an empty body

recall.question: In the Task Ledger router, what do `route("GET", "/Tasks")`, `route("GET", "/tasks?limit=5")` and `route("POST", "/health")` return?
recall.answer: 404, 200 and 405. Paths are matched literally and case-sensitively, so `/Tasks` is unknown; the query string is split off before matching; `/health` exists but allows only GET.

recall.question: Why should a router not lowercase the path or decode arbitrary percent-escapes before matching routes?
recall.answer: Route names can be case-sensitive, and decoding without a policy can make different request targets match the same route unexpectedly. Separate the query string, then match the literal path.

depth.misconception: Both statuses always mean the same thing
depth.correction: Resolve the resource first, then the allowed HTTP method.

lessons.title: Validate Before Applying Effects
lessons.concept: Check declared and actual request size

writing.summary: Check declared and actual request size.
writing.rule: A body-length mismatch is a framing error; an exceeded limit is a resource error.
writing.explanation:
A request can advertise one size and deliver another. A server needs limits on both the declared size and accumulated bytes. Check limits before parsing the domain object or applying writes, otherwise an oversized request can consume unbounded resources or leave partial state.

This function receives an optional parsed Content-Length, actual byte count and maximum. Return 413 if either known size exceeds the maximum. Otherwise a present length that differs from actual input returns 400; valid bounded input returns 200. Missing length is accepted by this isolated policy when transport framing has already supplied a complete body. The native HTTP adapter has a stricter framing profile: it rejects chunked transfer, duplicate lengths and pipelined bytes. Never use this size-only policy as a complete HTTP parser.

This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Use curl -i -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @request.json http://127.0.0.1:8080/tasks and compare a rejected oversized title with a valid request.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. A successful unchanged demonstration does not prove your implementation. After the lab, apply the same contract to the route companion project. Its README separates the on-device adapter from the desktop Cargo/TCP profile.

writing.question: Can a small declared length replace a limit on actual bytes?
answers: Only decoded character count matters
No, actual bytes also need a bound
Yes, clients always report an accurate size
writing.feedback: Clients can lie or disconnect mid-body, so declared size alone is insufficient.

recall.question: What do `body_status(Some(20), 0, 10)`, `body_status(Some(5), 4, 10)` and `body_status(None, 11, 10)` return, given (declared length, actual bytes, maximum)?
recall.answer: 413, 400 and 413. Any known size above the maximum is a resource error and is checked first; a declared length that disagrees with the actual bytes is a framing error (400); a missing length is still bounded by the actual byte count.

recall.question: Why must request size be checked before parsing the domain object or applying any write?
recall.answer: Otherwise an oversized request can consume unbounded memory or CPU, or a write can start and leave partial state before the problem is noticed. Limits on both the declared and the accumulated size come first.

depth.misconception: Yes, clients always report an accurate size
depth.correction: A body-length mismatch is a framing error; an exceeded limit is a resource error.

lessons.title: Encode a Valid JSON Boundary
lessons.concept: Escape JSON strings without corrupting Unicode

writing.summary: Escape JSON strings without corrupting Unicode.
writing.rule: Escape control characters, quotes and backslashes while preserving Unicode data.
writing.explanation:
JSON is a wire format, not arbitrary quoted text. A title containing a quote or newline must remain one string value. Direct interpolation can terminate a string or create a response that no client can decode. Escape the JSON control set while retaining the original Unicode scalar values.

The exercise builds one JSON string value, including its surrounding quotes. It is deliberately small enough to inspect; the desktop service should use Serde instead of maintaining a general JSON implementation. Do not treat this function as a parser, canonical JSON signer or complete serializer. HTTP response byte lengths must be computed from encoded UTF-8 bytes after serialization, not from character count. The local adapter recalculates Content-Length and closes each connection so an edited response cannot smuggle a second framed response.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Inspect curl -i output for a title containing quotes. Compare the response Content-Length with its encoded body.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. recall.answer: `\t`, `\u0001` and the emoji unchanged, all inside surrounding quotes: control characters are escaped while ordinary Unicode scalar values are kept as they are. Content-Length must then use the encoded byte length.

lessons.title: Retry Without Duplicating Tasks
lessons.concept: Bind an idempotency key to one request payload

writing.summary: Bind an idempotency key to one request payload.
writing.rule: Reuse a stored result only when the key and original payload agree.
writing.explanation:
A timeout does not prove that the server performed no work. It can commit a task and lose the response. An unconditional retry then creates a duplicate. Store a stable request key with the original payload and result; on a repeated request, compare the payload before reusing that result.

This lab models the decision without claiming an in-memory map is durable. A new key creates once, the same key and payload replays, and the same key with a different payload conflicts. Missing or blank keys are invalid. Production storage must enforce the key uniqueness and the business write in one transaction. Set an explicit retention policy; expiring a key changes how late retries behave. The SQL and capstone stages demonstrate that the deduplication record belongs beside the committed task.

writing.summary: Enforce domain invariants in a real database.
writing.rule: Validate in Rust for helpful errors and in SQL for every writer.
writing.explanation:
Task Ledger must not accept empty titles just because a caller bypasses the API. A database schema is an independent enforcement boundary. Give each task an integer primary key, require a title whose trimmed length is between 1 and 80, and constrain done to exactly 0 or 1 with a default of 0.

A CHECK returning null can behave differently from a false expression; NOT NULL remains a separate requirement. A default applies when a column is omitted, not when a caller explicitly sends null. SQLite trim without a second argument removes ordinary spaces, rather than Rust's full Unicode whitespace set. Store canonical titles and keep that policy explicit. Migration history belongs in version control. Once a production schema exists, changing CREATE TABLE text does not update an existing database: write and test a migration. This lab starts from a fresh SQLite database and executes your DDL, then tries valid, null, empty, duplicate and out-of-domain writes. It does not merely compare the SQL text.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Run sqlite3 tasks.db .read migrations/001.sql, then attempt valid and invalid INSERT statements. The compiler lab executes your DDL against fresh real SQLite.

writing.summary: Filter, join and order by the intended relationship.
writing.rule: Specify both the inclusion rule and deterministic ordering.
writing.explanation:
A task report joins tasks to projects and lists unfinished tasks in active projects. Joining by a coincidentally equal name or forgetting the done filter may pass a tiny happy-path fixture. Seed unrelated, archived and completed records so each predicate has observable consequences.

SQL does not promise result ordering without ORDER BY. Sort by project name and then task ID to break ties. A LEFT JOIN and an INNER JOIN have different contracts: this report includes only tasks with an existing active project. The task title does not participate in grouping or identity. Inspect the query plan after establishing correctness, then consider an index on the actual filter/join keys. An index is not permission to change which rows appear. The independent checker rebuilds fixtures and executes your query, allowing different correct SQL formulations.

writing.summary: Keep untrusted text in a parameter slot.
writing.rule: A title is data even when it contains quotes or SQL-looking text.
writing.explanation:
A title can contain an apostrophe or text that resembles SQL. Concatenating it into a WHERE clause turns data into syntax and makes quoting rules part of the security boundary. Bind the title into a placeholder instead; the database receives the statement structure separately from the value.

The local bridge accepts JSON with sql and params fields. The desktop SQLx profile uses its own bind API; placeholders differ across drivers, so SQLite ?1 is not PostgreSQL $1. This lesson grades a read-only SQLite query with exactly one positional title parameter. Fixtures include an apostrophe, Unicode, and an injection-shaped title that must match only itself. LIKE is a different search contract and should not replace exact equality. Parameterization does not grant access control: the application must still decide which caller is allowed to read a project.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

writing.summary: Roll back a failed multi-write operation.
writing.rule: All related writes belong to one transaction with an observable failure path.
writing.explanation:
A transfer debits one account and credits another. If the debit succeeds while the credit fails, the database has lost value. Enclose both writes in one explicit transaction. Constrain balances to remain nonnegative and make a rejected debit fail before any durable credit occurs.

The exercise transfers an integer amount from account 1 to account 2. A zero transfer leaves balances unchanged. A transfer larger than the source balance triggers the database CHECK and must leave both accounts unchanged. The local SQL host rolls back any open transaction when a statement fails, and refuses a script that ends with an open transaction. SQLx on desktop normally uses a transaction value with explicit commit and rollback behavior. Concurrency isolation, lock timeouts and retry policy need separate tests; this single-connection lab proves only the finite atomicity cases it executes.

recall.question: A transfer runs its debit and credit as two separate UPDATE statements with no explicit transaction. The debit succeeds and the credit fails. What state is left?
recall.answer: The debit stays committed and the credit never happens, so value is lost. Both writes belong in one explicit transaction that is rolled back when either statement fails.

recall.question: Inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT` in SQLite, one UPDATE fails its CHECK constraint. What does SQLite do by default, and what must the caller therefore do?
recall.answer: SQLite aborts only the failing statement; the transaction stays open with earlier writes intact, and a following `COMMIT` would keep them. The caller or host must issue `ROLLBACK` on any failure so both balances stay unchanged.

writing.summary: Redact sensitive diagnostic fields.
writing.rule: An error should identify the operation without copying credentials into logs.
writing.explanation:
A bare connection failed message loses the operation and request that failed. Add bounded structured context: operation name, request ID and a stable error category. Keep secret fields out of the event. Redacting only one capitalization of Authorization is insufficient when headers are case insensitive.

This lab preserves field order while replacing authorization, cookie, password, token and api_key values with [REDACTED], case insensitively. It does not claim that this small allowlist finds every possible secret in free text. Production code should prefer explicitly selected safe fields and never dump arbitrary request bodies or connection URLs. Diagnostic context is useful only when a person can connect it to a specific operation; a giant unstructured debug print can be harder to use than a short event with a correlation ID.

This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

lessons.title: Propagate One Request Identity
lessons.concept: Validate a bounded correlation ID

writing.summary: Validate a bounded correlation ID.
writing.rule: Use the same validated ID across a request and its child operations.
writing.explanation:
Async work interleaves. Two requests can emit similar messages on one thread, so thread identity alone does not connect the messages that belong together. Give an operation one request ID, propagate it through database calls and retries, and record child work under the same parent context.

An incoming ID is untrusted data. Accept only a bounded ASCII token here, using letters, digits, dash and underscore; otherwise use a generated fallback supplied by the caller. Reject line breaks so an identifier cannot inject a fake log record. Do not treat a correlation ID as authentication or an idempotency key. Clients can choose or repeat it, and tracing systems have their own full trace-context format. This exercise isolates a small application request-ID policy rather than pretending to implement W3C traceparent.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Send curl -i -H "X-Request-ID: req_42" http://127.0.0.1:8080/health and follow the same ID through the diagnostic output.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. recall.question: Why can't thread identity link together the log messages of one async request?
recall.answer: Async tasks interleave, so messages from different requests can come from the same thread, and one request can run on several threads. Give the operation one request ID and propagate it through database calls, retries and child work.

recall.question: The request-ID policy accepts only 1 to 64 ASCII letters, digits, `-` and `_`. Why reject an incoming ID containing a line break, and what is it still not?
recall.answer: A line break could inject a fake record into line-based logs, so any invalid ID is replaced with the generated fallback. Even a valid ID is client-chosen diagnostic context, not authentication or an idempotency key.

writing.summary: Compute an explicitly defined latency percentile.
writing.rule: State the percentile convention and preserve the original measurements.
writing.explanation:
Averages can hide slow requests. A service with many quick responses and a few multi-second waits may have an acceptable mean while some users regularly time out. Record a latency distribution and inspect tail behavior alongside throughput and error rate.

This exercise defines p95 using the nearest-rank rule: sort a copy of the positive or zero millisecond observations, choose rank ceil(0.95*n), and return that element. Return None for an empty sample. Do not mutate the caller's measurements or invent interpolated values. A percentile from a small sample has limited statistical precision; the exact calculation is not evidence that the load generator or measurement conditions were realistic. The desktop companion keeps raw samples, concurrency and toolchain identity with a before/after report.

writing.summary: Retry transient failures within attempt and time limits.
writing.rule: A retry needs a transient failure, remaining attempts and a deadline budget.
writing.explanation:
Retries amplify load when a dependency is already failing. Decide whether an error is transient, cap total attempts, and stop when the proposed delay plus one minimum operation budget no longer fits the deadline. Retrying authentication failures or malformed input does not repair them.

Here failed_attempts counts attempts already made, including the one that just failed. Retry only transient failures after at least one attempt, while the count is below the total maximum. Require delay + operation_budget to fit in remaining time, using checked arithmetic so an overflow cannot create a false large budget. Jitter and exponential delay selection are separate policies. Before retrying a write, use the idempotency contract from the HTTP stage; a timing budget does not prevent duplicated effects.

writing.summary: Require all declared release checks.
writing.rule: An absent or failed required check cannot be treated as a green release.
writing.explanation:
A reproducible release pipeline connects source checks to a specific revision. Formatting, compilation and tests answer different questions. A successful build does not establish that tests ran, and a test job from an older revision does not approve newer source.

The release policy requires fmt, test and build exactly once with successful results; extra unrelated checks may be present. Duplicate required records are ambiguous and should refuse delivery rather than choosing whichever result looks better. This lab models gate aggregation, while the companion workflow runs the actual commands in a clean checkout with Cargo.lock retained. The iOS terminal runs its supported Cargo profile; the desktop CI workflow exercises the server target, SQL migrations and integration requests. Keep those receipts separate instead of claiming one target qualifies the other.

This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Run cargo fmt --check, cargo test and cargo build. Inspect the companion GitHub workflow for desktop integration checks.

A successful unchanged demonstration does not prove your implementation. After the lab, apply the same contract to the route companion project. Its README separates the on-device adapter from the desktop Cargo/TCP profile.

writing.summary: Reject invalid deployment configuration.
writing.rule: A deployment configuration must fail before the service accepts traffic.
writing.explanation:
A service can compile correctly and still fail because its deployment configuration is wrong. Parse the bind port, database address and operational limits before opening a listener. Report the failed field without echoing a password-bearing connection URL.

This lab accepts decimal ports from 1024 to 65535 and a nonempty database setting containing no whitespace. It rejects signed port syntax, surrounding whitespace and malformed numbers so accepted configuration is predictable. The database check here is intentionally syntactic; it does not prove connectivity, credentials or migration compatibility. The desktop service should perform those separate startup checks and expose readiness only after required initialization. A liveness endpoint and a readiness endpoint answer different operational questions.

writing.summary: Verify release identity and digest metadata.
writing.rule: A filename or version label does not prove which bytes were tested.
writing.explanation:
A release artifact should have an identity that can be compared with the tested source and the expected content digest. Reusing a mutable latest filename makes rollback and incident investigation harder. Retain the source revision, exact target, digest and verification receipt beside immutable artifact bytes.

The lab validates metadata: a full lowercase 40-hex Git object ID, a lowercase 64-hex SHA-256 digest and an exact match with an independently supplied expected digest. It does not calculate SHA-256 or prove the claim by validating string shape. The actual delivery script computes the digest from built bytes with a standard tool, then compares it before promotion. A digest detects changed bytes when the expected digest is trusted; it is not an author signature. Keep signing and provenance decisions explicit rather than calling a checksum an authenticity guarantee.

writing.summary: Keep a known-good version until the candidate is healthy.
writing.rule: A failed readiness check preserves the previous active version.
writing.explanation:
Delivery continues after uploading bytes. A candidate can build successfully and fail a migration or readiness check in the target environment. Retain the previous active version while preparing the candidate, promote only after the required health evidence, and preserve a concrete recovery path.

The state transition in this lab receives the current version, candidate and readiness observations. Reject a blank candidate, an unchanged version or a candidate without successful required checks. On every rejection return the original active version; a partially configured candidate is not an active release. A real database migration may be irreversible, so reverting an executable is not automatically a schema rollback. Prefer compatible expand/contract changes and test recovery against actual persistent state. The capstone asks for an incident record showing the failing condition, observed data and successful recovery rather than a screenshot of a green pipeline.

lessons.title: Threads

answers: A return type so the thread can report back
move, so the closure owns data rather than borrowing it
The captured data has to be declared mut
writing.exampleCaption: `move` gives the closure ownership so it can outlive this scope.
writing.explanation:
`thread::spawn` requires a `Send + 'static` closure. Owning captured data is a common way to satisfy this, which is why `move` appears often. Borrowing static data is also possible; moving a short-lived reference into the closure does not make it static. `join` waits for a result. Rust moves many data races from runtime accidents to compile-time errors, because a type that isn't `Send` cannot be moved to a thread, and one that isn't `Sync` cannot be shared with one.

Concurrency means several tasks can make progress during overlapping periods; it does not automatically mean every task runs on a separate CPU core. `thread::spawn` starts an operating-system thread and returns a handle. A `move` closure often transfers owned data into that thread so the worker cannot outlive a borrowed local variable. `join()` waits for the worker and returns its result or a panic payload. Decide what to do with a panic rather than blindly assuming success.

Trace a small program with two workers, each owning a different input. The main thread starts both before joining either, so their work can overlap. If you join the first immediately before spawning the second, you have written a mostly sequential workflow. Move a `String` into one worker and try to use the original binding afterward; the compiler points to the ownership transfer. Clone only when both threads truly need independent owned data, or share through a deliberate thread-safe abstraction.

Rust's type system rules out many unsynchronized shared-memory data races by enforcing `Send`, `Sync`, and borrowing. It does not guarantee your result is logically correct: ordering bugs, deadlocks, and missed messages are still possible. Write down which thread owns each value and how the results meet again. Test with different scheduling, but rely on an explicit synchronization design rather than hoping a test run visits every interleaving. A clear spawn/join boundary makes the lifetime of the work visible.

Before adding workers, identify whether the task is CPU-bound or waiting on I/O. Threads can overlap both kinds of work, but overhead and shared-state contention may erase the benefit for tiny tasks. Measure a realistic workload and verify that results remain deterministic where your application requires it.
writing.feedback: The thread may outlive this scope, so a borrow is not enough.

std::thread::spawn(|| println!("{data:?}"));

writing.rule: `thread::spawn` requires a `Send + 'static` closure; `move` captures by value and does not extend borrowed lifetimes.
writing.success: The value is computed off the main thread and joined back.
writing.summary: Threads run in parallel, and ownership decides what may cross.
writing.task: Spawn a thread that owns its data and return a result with join.

recall.answer: `join` blocks the main thread until that worker finishes, so `b` is not even spawned until `a` is done. To let them overlap, spawn both first and then join both.

recall.question: What does this print, and why shouldn't you just `unwrap()` a `join()` without thinking?
recall.answer: The worker's panic message appears on stderr, then `true`. A panic in a spawned thread doesn't crash `main`; `join` returns `Err` with the panic payload. `unwrap()` would re-panic in `main`, so decide on a policy for it.

lessons.title: Channels

answers: A channel receiver loops forever by design
tx and its clone worker are still alive, so the channel never closes
The receiver has to be declared mut to iterate
writing.exampleCaption: Ownership transfers with the message, so no lock is needed.
writing.explanation:
An mpsc channel moves values from many producers to one consumer, and the move is what makes it safe — once sent, the sender no longer owns the value. After every sender is dropped, the receiver drains queued messages and then its iterator ends, so no sentinel message is required.

A channel separates the producer of a value from its consumer. In a multi-producer, single-consumer channel, several senders can submit messages to one receiver. Sending an owned `String` moves it into the channel; the sender cannot keep changing the same object afterward. That ownership transfer is a simple way to avoid sharing mutable state. If the sender needs its own copy too, make that duplication explicit.

The receiver loop can continue until every sender handle is dropped. A cloned sender counts as another live producer, even when it never sends anything. Accidentally keeping one clone in the main thread can make a receiving loop wait forever, because the channel is still open. Track sender ownership on paper and drop unused handles deliberately. Also handle `send` failure: the receiver may already be gone, and the failed send can return the unsent value to the caller.

Try spawning two producers that each send a labeled message. Do not assume which message arrives first unless you add an ordering mechanism. The receiver should process both and then finish once all senders are gone. Next, leave a sender clone alive and observe why the loop does not terminate; remove it and rerun. Channels work well when a task can be expressed as a stream of owned messages. A mutex is more suitable when workers truly need coordinated access to one shared object. Choose the communication shape before choosing the primitive.

If the consumer is slower than producers, an unbounded channel can accumulate messages and memory. A bounded channel gives backpressure: senders wait or receive an error when capacity is exhausted. Choose a capacity by measuring the burst you can afford to buffer and the latency you can tolerate.
writing.feedback: Every live sender keeps the channel open; drop the ones you do not use.
writing.question: Why might that loop never end?

writing.explanation:
`Arc<T>` is `Rc` with an atomic count so it can cross threads. `Mutex<T>` holds the data itself rather than guarding it by convention, so the only way to reach the value is to lock — and the guard unlocks when it drops, which means a forgotten unlock is not a bug you can write.

`Arc<T>` is an atomically reference-counted owner that can be cloned across threads when the contained type permits it. `Mutex<T>` protects mutable data with a lock. Together, `Arc<Mutex<T>>` lets workers own handles to one allocation while only one guard at a time accesses the protected value. Cloning an `Arc` clones a handle, not the inner data. The guard from `lock()` releases the lock when it leaves scope. `RwLock<T>` is a close relative: it allows many readers or one writer at a time, which can help when reads far outnumber writes.

In a counter example, each worker clones the `Arc`, locks the mutex, increments the count, and drops the guard. If a worker holds the guard while doing slow I/O, every other worker waits unnecessarily. Keep the critical section small and do unrelated work before or after it. Treat `lock()` as fallible because a panic while holding the lock can poison a standard mutex; decide how the application handles that state.

Try writing the counter first without synchronization and read the compiler error rather than fighting it. Add `Arc<Mutex<_>>`, start several workers, join them, and compare the final count with the predicted sum. Then move a long sleep inside the lock and measure the slowdown. The type system prevents an unsynchronized data race, but the lock still has performance and deadlock costs. Use a channel when workers can hand off owned messages instead of editing shared state; use a mutex when a shared invariant must be updated atomically.

Beware of hidden lock retention: a guard stored in a local variable stays live until it is dropped or leaves scope. Explicitly shorten its scope before calling another function that may need the same lock. This is both a responsiveness issue and a common path to self-deadlock.

A closure is not allowed to capture a cell type

writing.exampleCaption: The bound is what the thread API asks for, spelled out.
writing.explanation:
`Send` means a value can be moved to another thread; `Sync` means `&T` can be shared with one. Both are inferred from a type's fields, so you rarely write them — but they are why `Rc` is rejected at compile time while `Arc` is accepted, and why a whole class of race is a type error.

`Send` and `Sync` are marker traits describing safe movement and sharing across threads. A `Send` value may transfer ownership to another thread. A `Sync` type may be accessed through shared references from multiple threads; equivalently, `&T` can be `Send` when `T` is `Sync`. These properties are usually derived automatically from fields, so the type composition communicates the safety constraint.

`Rc<T>` changes a non-atomic reference count, so it is unsuitable for sharing between threads. `Arc<T>` uses an atomic count, but that does not make arbitrary inner mutation safe. If workers must change the contained value, combine it with a suitable synchronization primitive such as `Mutex<T>`, or use atomics for a very narrow operation. The compiler rejecting `Rc` in a spawned thread is evidence of a missing thread-safety guarantee, not an invitation to add `unsafe impl` casually.

Test this by capturing an `Rc<String>` in a thread closure and reading the diagnostic. Replace it with `Arc<String>` for read-only sharing. Then try to mutate a shared counter and choose `Arc<Mutex<i32>>` or `Arc<AtomicUsize>` based on the operation. Ask separately whether ownership crosses threads and whether references may be shared. `Send` and `Sync` answer those two different questions; they do not promise freedom from deadlocks, starvation, or application-level ordering mistakes.

A value can be `Send` without being `Sync`, so moving it exclusively to another thread may work even when simultaneous shared references would not. Check the precise compiler bound at the thread or library boundary. This tells you whether to change ownership, add synchronization, or redesign the data flow. Never assert these marker traits manually unless you can prove the `unsafe` contract for every field and operation.
writing.feedback: The closure captures `&RefCell<i32>`, and `&T` is `Send` only when `T` is `Sync`. `RefCell`'s borrow flag is not synchronised, so the shared borrow is rejected; moving the cell instead compiles, because `RefCell<i32>` is `Send`.

writing.rule: `T` is `Sync` exactly when `&T` is `Send`.

recall.question: `Arc<T>` lets several threads hold handles to one value. Why does that make `Arc<T>: Send` require `T: Sync`, not just `T: Send`?

writing.exampleCaption: Nothing happens until the future is awaited or spawned.
writing.explanation:
Calling an `async fn` does nothing on its own: it builds a state machine that makes progress only when polled. `.await` yields at that point, letting the executor run something else while the operation is pending — which is how one thread can service thousands of waits.

Calling an `async fn` creates a future that represents work to be performed. It does not run the body to completion immediately. An executor polls the future; it may return `Poll::Pending`, register a way to be woken, and yield the thread to other tasks. When the awaited operation can make progress, the waker schedules another poll. Eventually the future returns `Poll::Ready(value)`. This is why many I/O waits can share a small number of threads.

An `.await` marks a point where the task may suspend. Local values that are needed afterward become part of the future's state, which affects memory usage and whether the future can be safely sent between executor threads. Code between `await` points still runs synchronously until it yields or completes, so a long CPU loop can monopolize an executor worker even though it sits inside an `async` function.

Write a short `async` function that logs before and after an awaited timer. Observe that constructing its future does not print the whole sequence; running it on an executor does. Then launch two timer futures concurrently and compare the elapsed time with running them one after the other. Avoid thinking of each future as a thread. A future is a state machine plus a polling contract; the runtime decides when and where to poll it. That distinction helps you choose between `async` waiting, blocking work, and true parallel computation.

A future normally needs to be polled by an executor to make progress. Merely storing it in a variable does not schedule it. That is a common source of confusion when an `async` call appears to do nothing. Trace where the future is awaited, spawned, or otherwise polled.
writing.feedback: The future is created and dropped without ever being polled.
writing.question: What does that print with no `await`?
writing.rule: Futures are lazy: no poll, no progress.

recall.answer: Code between await points runs synchronously, so the loop holds the worker thread until it finishes; other tasks scheduled there can't be polled. Being `async` doesn't make the computation yield. Move heavy work to a blocking or compute thread.

writing.exampleCaption: A synchronous main explicitly asks a current-thread executor to poll the future.
writing.explanation:
The language defines `Future` and `.await`; polling, timers, and I/O readiness come from a runtime you choose, such as tokio or smol. That keeps `async` usable on an embedded target with no allocator, at the cost of one decision you have to make per project.

Rust's language and standard library define `Future` and `.await`, but a program needs an executor to poll futures and often a runtime to provide timers, sockets, and task spawning. Tokio is a common choice, but an `async` function is not inherently tied to one runtime. A library should be clear about whether it uses runtime-specific I/O types or exposes runtime-neutral futures. The decision affects how easily callers can integrate it.

The runtime schedules ready tasks; it cannot make blocking code magically nonblocking. A synchronous file operation or long CPU loop inside an `async` task can occupy an executor worker and delay unrelated tasks. Use the runtime's dedicated blocking facility for genuinely blocking work, and measure when offloading is worthwhile. Also know who owns spawned tasks: dropping a join handle does not necessarily cancel the task, depending on the runtime API. Cancellation and shutdown behavior belong in the program's design.

Create a minimal program with an `async` entry point and an awaited timer. Then remove the runtime wrapper and inspect the compiler or execution setup needed to drive the future. Add a second task and observe that scheduling depends on `await` points. When choosing a runtime for a project, check required I/O, platform support, footprint, and shutdown semantics. For embedded or restricted targets, the executor can be much smaller than a server runtime, but you still need a concrete way to poll and wake futures.

An executor and an operating-system event source solve different problems: one chooses which ready future to poll, while the other reports that I/O is ready. A runtime often bundles both. This separation explains why creating a future is cheap but actually driving a network request requires runtime services.

Local Cargo profile: open the supplied project in Crabrix or the browser Playground. Explicitly prepare its pinned Cargo packages once on each device, then Run and Debug compile and execute on that device without a backend. The project includes Cargo.lock. The lesson question remains the completion exercise; running an unchanged demonstration does not prove a separate programming challenge. Tokio 1.54.1 is built with default-features=false and only rt/sync. The current-thread builder needs no runtime attribute macro. JoinSet, Semaphore, watch and yield_now are real Tokio APIs. This profile supplies cooperative concurrency, not native threads, sockets, OS signals or CPU parallelism.
writing.feedback: Something has to drive the future, and that something is the runtime.
writing.question: Why is that not a valid program entry point?
writing.rule: std defines `Future`; the executor is a library decision.
writing.success: You can name polling, waking, and I/O readiness as runtime concerns.
writing.summary: Rust ships the `async` syntax but not the engine that drives it.

recall.question: Why might a reusable async library avoid exposing runtime-specific I/O types in its public API?
recall.answer: `Future` and `.await` belong to the language, but the executor, timers and sockets come from whichever runtime the application picks. If the library's API uses one runtime's types, every caller is tied to that runtime; runtime-neutral futures let the application decide.

writing.exampleCaption: join overlaps the waits instead of adding them up.
writing.explanation:
join runs futures at the same time and waits for all of them; select takes whichever finishes first. Dropping an owned operation future stops polling that operation, but completed external effects remain. A handle to independently spawned work is different: dropping a Tokio `JoinHandle` detaches the task rather than stopping it.

`join!` polls several futures concurrently and waits for all of them; it does not imply they run on separate threads. `select!` waits for one branch to become ready and then proceeds with that branch. The other in-progress branch futures may be dropped when the selection expression ends, depending on how they are owned. Dropping the actual operation future prevents its later polls; cleanup of owned values runs, but ordinary code after its suspension point does not. External effects already performed are not automatically rolled back.

In the example, loading a user and loading orders are independent, so `join!` can overlap their waits. If one result is enough, `select!` might reduce latency, but the losing operation must be safe to stop or resume. A database write followed by an acknowledgement is a dangerous candidate if cancellation can occur between them. Place durable state changes and retries behind an idempotent operation or an explicit transaction where appropriate.

Try timing two independent sleeps with sequential awaits and then with `join!`. Predict the total duration. Next, use `select!` between a timer and a slow operation, and record which cleanup code runs when the slow future loses. Do not assume `async` cancellation works like killing an OS thread; it occurs when an owned future is dropped, usually at a suspension boundary. Choose the combinator from the result you need and the cancellation guarantees of each branch.

When using a timeout wrapper, inspect whether it owns the inner future or only borrows it. That determines whether the timed-out operation is dropped or can continue elsewhere. In either case, record which effects are safe to repeat. If independent operations can fail separately, also decide whether `join!` should wait for every outcome or stop early through a different combinator.

Task ownership matters in timeouts: `timeout(limit, operation())` owns the operation, while timing out a spawned task’s owned `JoinHandle` can merely drop the handle and leave the task running. To request cancellation of an async Tokio task, retain the handle, call `abort()`, and await it to observe termination. Cancellation is cooperative and cannot interrupt a poll that never yields; an already running `spawn_blocking` closure cannot be stopped this way. Use a shutdown protocol for work with effects that must finish or roll back explicitly.

recall.question: In Tokio, what happens to a spawned task when you drop its `JoinHandle`, and how do you actually stop it?
recall.answer: Dropping the handle detaches the task, and it keeps running to completion. To cancel it, keep the handle, call `abort()`, and await the handle: it returns a `JoinError` whose `is_cancelled()` is true. Abort only takes effect at an await point.

writing.exampleCaption: Every scoped thread finishes before `scope` returns, so borrowing `values` is allowed.
writing.explanation:
`thread::scope` proves every spawned thread finishes before borrowed stack data disappears. It avoids unnecessary `Arc` or cloning when concurrency stays inside one lexical operation.

Ordinary `thread::spawn` may outlive the function that created it, so its closure generally needs owned, thread-safe data. `thread::scope` sets a tighter boundary: every scoped thread finishes before the scope returns. Within that boundary, a worker can borrow local values that remain alive until all workers join. This is useful for parallel processing of disjoint parts of a collection without cloning the entire collection into `Arc`.

The safety promise is about lifetime, not completion without failure. A scoped worker can still panic; the scope joins all its workers and can propagate an unhandled panic. Write the error policy explicitly if a worker result matters. Also avoid making the borrow invalid yourself: if one worker reads a value, the usual borrowing rules still prevent an overlapping mutable borrow of that same value. A scope is no shortcut around aliasing or synchronization.

Try dividing a slice into two non-overlapping mutable halves with `split_at_mut`, then process one half in each scoped worker. Predict why the compiler accepts those two borrows. Change the code so both workers try to mutate the entire slice and read the rejection. Finally compare the scoped form with an owned `Vec` moved into an ordinary spawned thread. Use the scope when the work naturally ends inside the current operation; use detached or longer-lived tasks only when you have an explicit ownership and shutdown plan.

answers: A thread panicked while holding the lock
The lock is slow

writing.exampleCaption: `lock` returns `Err` after a holder panicked, and `into_inner` still gives access to the guard.
writing.explanation:
A standard `Mutex` becomes poisoned when a holder panics. Recovery is possible, but code must decide whether the protected invariant is still trustworthy instead of blindly ignoring the signal.

A standard-library `Mutex` becomes poisoned if a thread panics while holding its guard. A subsequent `lock()` returns a `PoisonError` rather than silently claiming the protected state is sound. The bytes are still there, and the error can give access to the guard, but the application must decide whether its invariant survived. Poisoning is a warning about a possible inconsistency, not proof that the data is corrupt.

Imagine a bank ledger with two fields updated under one lock. If a panic occurs after subtracting from one field but before adding to the other, a future reader must not pretend the transfer completed. Recover only after checking or rebuilding the invariant. A cache whose entries are independently replaceable might be safe to clear and rebuild. A process-wide critical invariant may justify failing the operation instead. The right choice comes from the meaning of the state, not from a universal `unwrap()` habit.

Write a test in which a worker acquires a mutex and deliberately panics. Join that worker, then inspect the result of the next `lock()`. Separate the panic returned by `join()` from the poison returned by `lock()`: they are two observable events. Add a recovery branch that validates the stored data before clearing poison or continuing. Avoid putting fallible, unrelated work inside a critical section so the chance of leaving a half-updated invariant is smaller. Different mutex implementations have different poison semantics, so verify the actual API you use.
writing.feedback: `lock` returns `Err` because a thread panicked while holding the guard. The value is still there, but its invariant may be incomplete.
writing.question: What does poisoning report?
writing.rule: A standard `Mutex` becomes poisoned when a holder panics.
writing.success: You can separate the panic returned by `join` from the poison returned by `lock`, and say when recovery is justified.
writing.summary: Notice a panic that may leave state inconsistent.

recall.question: When is it reasonable to recover from a poisoned mutex, and when should the operation fail instead?
recall.answer: Recover when the protected state can be checked or rebuilt, such as a cache whose entries can be cleared. If a panic could have left a multi-field invariant half updated, like a ledger transfer, validate it first or fail rather than unwrapping the poison away.

answers: What other memory effects become visible
The size of the integer

writing.exampleCaption: `fetch_add` updates the count as one indivisible step; `Relaxed` orders no other memory.
writing.explanation:
Atomic operations are indivisible but still need an ordering that describes cross-thread visibility. Use the weakest ordering justified by a written synchronization argument, not by habit.

An atomic value supports operations that are indivisible with respect to competing threads. `fetch_add` on `AtomicUsize`, for example, prevents two workers from losing an increment by reading and writing the same stale count. This makes atomics a good fit for simple counters, flags, and some carefully designed state machines. It does not turn a sequence of several atomic operations into one transaction. If two fields must change together, a mutex may express the invariant more clearly.

Memory ordering answers a second question: when another thread sees an atomic change, which ordinary memory writes are guaranteed visible too? `Relaxed` is enough for a count whose only requirement is an accurate final total after workers join. A flag that publishes prepared data generally needs a release store and an acquire load, or another synchronization design. `SeqCst` gives a stronger global ordering model, but choosing it blindly does not fix a flawed state machine.

Start with several threads incrementing a shared atomic counter and compare `fetch_add` with a failed idea built from separate `load` and `store` calls. Then draw a producer that fills a buffer and sets a ready flag; explain why the consumer must not read the buffer before it observes readiness through an appropriate synchronization operation. Keep `unsafe` shared-memory examples out of an introductory exercise. State the invariant first, pick the weakest ordering you can justify only after understanding it, and prefer a mutex if the proof is hard to explain.
writing.feedback: An ordering says which other memory effects become visible with an atomic change. Here, the `Acquire` load that sees `true` is also guaranteed to see the store of 42.
writing.question: What does an atomic ordering describe?
writing.rule: Atomic operations are indivisible but still need an ordering that describes cross-thread visibility.
writing.success: You can say why `Relaxed` is enough for a count and why this ready flag needs more.

recall.question: Why can incrementing a shared counter with `let v = c.load(..); c.store(v + 1, ..);` lose updates, while `c.fetch_add(1, ..)` cannot?
recall.answer: Between one thread's `load` and `store`, another thread can store its own increment, which is then overwritten with a stale value. `fetch_add` is one indivisible read-modify-write, so no other thread can slip in between.

recall.question: Why is `Ordering::Relaxed` fine for a hit counter read after all workers are joined, but not for a `ready` flag that tells a consumer a buffer is filled?
recall.answer: For the counter, only the atomic value itself matters, and `join` already synchronises the final read. The flag must also make the buffer writes visible, which needs a `Release` store paired with an `Acquire` load; `Relaxed` makes no such promise.

lessons.title: Deadlock Avoidance

answers: Both workers lock in one order
Running more threads
A mutable borrow
writing.exampleCaption: Sorting by id gives every transfer the same first lock, so two transfers cannot wait on each other.
writing.explanation:
Rust prevents data races, not deadlocks. A consistent order for acquiring multiple locks and avoiding calls into unknown code while locked remove common wait cycles.

A deadlock can arise when worker A holds lock X while waiting for Y and worker B holds Y while waiting for X. Both workers may be perfectly data-race-free, yet neither can move. Rust's ownership rules do not decide a global lock order for your program. The simplest prevention is often a consistent acquisition order: if every path takes X before Y, the cycle cannot form from those two locks.

Draw a wait-for graph with one node per task and an arrow when it waits for a resource held by another task. A cycle is the warning sign. Reduce the number of locks held at once, move expensive work outside locked sections, or combine related fields under a single mutex when the data model allows it. `try_lock` can avoid indefinite waiting in some designs, but a retry loop without backoff can livelock or waste CPU. Timeouts help detection and recovery; they do not automatically make a transfer atomic.

Build two workers that each need two locks. First write the unsafe ordering on paper, then rewrite both workers to acquire locks in the same order. Ask what happens if a callback called while holding X attempts to acquire X again: a non-reentrant mutex may self-deadlock. Avoid invoking unknown callbacks while a guard is alive. When reviewing a codebase, document the lock hierarchy near the shared state, not only in one caller. Tests can expose some schedules; a clear acquisition rule is the stronger argument that a cycle cannot occur.
writing.feedback: Both workers take `X` before `Y`, so neither can hold `Y` while waiting for `X`, and that cycle cannot form.
writing.question: What prevents the wait cycle here?
writing.rule: Rust prevents data races, not deadlocks.
writing.success: You can point to the cycle in the swapped version and to the lock order that removes it.
writing.summary: Keep a global lock order and short critical sections.
writing.task: Swap the two `lock` lines in `worker_b` and draw the wait-for graph. Say which schedule hangs, and check that the compiler still accepts the code.

recall.question: Why is replacing `lock()` with a loop of `try_lock()` retries not automatically a deadlock fix?
recall.answer: Without backoff, threads can keep failing and retrying in step (livelock) and burn CPU, and progress still isn't guaranteed. A timeout or `try_lock` helps detect contention; it doesn't make a two-lock transfer atomic. A consistent lock order is the stronger fix.

recall.question: Why is calling an unknown callback while holding a `MutexGuard` risky?
recall.answer: The callback might lock the same mutex; `std::sync::Mutex` is not re-entrant, so the thread waits on itself and deadlocks. It might also take other locks in a different order. Drop the guard, or copy the needed data out, before calling unknown code.

lessons.title: Pinning Intuition

answers: String implements Unpin, so this pinning wrapper does not forbid the move
Pin makes String thread safe
Pin gives the borrowed String a static lifetime
writing.exampleCaption: This complete safe program moves a String out through Pin because String implements Unpin. It contrasts with a location-sensitive !Unpin pointee.
writing.explanation:
`Pin` protects location-sensitive values after they are pinned; it does not make every value immovable from creation. Most users interact through pinned futures while libraries handle the `unsafe` construction details. Some future state machines can contain references into their own stored state while suspended. Moving such a value after those references become valid could invalidate them. `Pin

` is a contract that the value reached through pointer `P` will not be moved again if the value's type relies on pinning. It is not a magical freeze of every value from birth, and it does not mean the surrounding pointer variable can never move. Many ordinary types are `Unpin`, so pinning adds no movement restriction for them. A type that is `!Unpin` needs more care: once pinned, safe code must not move its inner value out through the pinned pointer. APIs that project pinned fields or construct self-referential structures carry subtle invariants. At this stage, use library-provided safe pinning helpers and avoid writing `unsafe` projections to make a compiler error disappear. Compare a plain `String`, which can be moved between bindings, with a future that a runtime stores and polls repeatedly. Think of pinning as protecting the address of the future's internal state across polls. Then read an API signature accepting `Pin<&mut F>` and identify what it promises to the future implementation. Do not infer that every `async` function creates self-references or that `Box::pin` is required for every future. The practical rule is to follow the executor and library API, and to treat `Pin` as a movement guarantee with a precisely defined start.
writing.feedback: Unpin opts a type out of pinning movement restrictions. The guarantee for an address-sensitive !Unpin pointee does not apply to this String.
writing.question: Why is moving the String out through Pin safe in this example?
writing.rule: `Pin` constrains moves of a pointee that relies on pinning. `Unpin` types such as `String` opt out of that restriction; moving the pointer wrapper itself is a separate matter.
writing.success: You can say why this safe move works for `String` and why it is unavailable for a `!Unpin` pointee.
writing.summary: Promise that a value will not move in memory.
writing.task: Run the safe String example, then explain why the same safe extraction API is unavailable for an address-sensitive !Unpin pointee. Do not use unsafe code to bypass its contract.

recall.question: `Pin::new(&mut text)` works for a `String`. Why is `Pin::new(&mut fut)` rejected for an async block, and what should you use?
recall.answer: `Pin::new` is only safe for `Unpin` types, and an async block's state machine is `!Unpin` because it may hold references into itself (E0277: the async block cannot be unpinned). Pin it in place with `std::pin::pin!` or on the heap with `Box::pin`.

recall.question: `Future::poll` takes `self: Pin<&mut Self>`. What does that guarantee give a `!Unpin` future?
recall.answer: That once it has been pinned, it will not be moved again, so any references its suspended state holds into itself stay valid across polls. It is a promise about the value's address from pinning onwards, not that the pointer variable can't move.

lessons.title: Cancellation Safety

answers: Dropping that future; its body may not have started or may have suspended
Only reaching the end of the async body
Dropping any runtime join handle always cancels its task
writing.exampleCaption: One explicit poll saves state and then suspends. Dropping the future cancels the remaining acknowledgement, while saved=true remains observable.
writing.explanation:
Selecting or timing out a future may drop it before completion. Keep partial state consistent across `await` points, or wrap the operation so retrying cannot duplicate or lose external effects.

An owned future can be cancelled by dropping it before its first poll, before its body has run, or between polls after it has suspended. Work already completed before that point remains completed. A dropped future does not reverse a file write, database transaction, sent message, or charge to an external service. This creates a gap between “the caller did not receive a result” and “nothing happened.” Retry logic must account for that gap.

Consider `save_record().await` followed by `send_ack().await`. If the task stops between the two awaits, the record exists but the acknowledgement may not. Repeating the whole operation could create a duplicate record. Give each request a stable identifier and design the save as idempotent, or use a transaction/outbox pattern when the storage and notification must coordinate. Store enough progress that a restarted worker can decide what remains. A timeout tells the caller how long it waited, not whether the remote side performed the action.

Draw cancellation points on a three-step operation: prepare, commit, notify. At each point, list which externally visible effects already happened and what a retry would do. Test by injecting cancellation after the commit boundary. A guard can release an in-process mutex when dropped, but it cannot roll back arbitrary external effects. For spawned tasks, also check the runtime's ownership rules: dropping a handle may detach rather than cancel. Define both the cancellation path and the normal completion path before selecting a timeout or `select!` branch.
writing.feedback: A future can be dropped before its first poll or between polls. Dropping a task handle has separate runtime-specific semantics and may detach its task. Cancellation does not undo effects already performed.
writing.question: What cancels an ordinary owned future, including one that has not been polled?
writing.rule: Selecting or timing out a future may drop it before completion.
writing.success: You can point to where each flag is set and say why a retry must be idempotent after a drop.
writing.summary: Expect a future to be dropped at any `await` point.

recall.question: A task runs `save_record().await` then `send_ack().await` and may be cancelled between them. Why is a plain retry dangerous, and what helps?
recall.answer: The record may already be saved without an ack, and dropping the future doesn't undo it, so retrying the whole operation can create a duplicate. Give each request a stable ID and make the save idempotent, or use a transaction or outbox pattern.

answers: It stalls an executor worker
It moves the future
It poisons a lock
writing.exampleCaption: `.await` on a timer gives the thread back to the executor; `std::thread::sleep` would not.
writing.explanation:
A blocking call occupies an executor worker without yielding, so unrelated tasks can stall. Move CPU-heavy or blocking work to a dedicated pool and `await` its result.

An executor worker can poll many `async` tasks because each task yields while waiting for nonblocking I/O. A synchronous `sleep`, filesystem call, expensive compression loop, or blocking foreign-library call can occupy that worker instead. Other ready tasks then wait even though they could run. Putting `async` on a function signature does not change a blocking call inside it into cooperative work.

Use the runtime's blocking pool or a dedicated worker thread for truly blocking operations, and pass owned input into it. The offload has overhead, so a tiny calculation may be cheaper to perform directly; measure the latency of other tasks under realistic load. CPU-heavy jobs can saturate even a blocking pool, so consider a bounded queue or a separate compute service when throughput matters. Think about shutdown too: a blocking call may not stop simply because its `async` caller was cancelled.

Create one task that repeatedly awaits a short timer and logs the delay. Alongside it, run a second task with a long synchronous sleep. Observe the timer stalls when both compete for an executor worker, then move the blocking operation to the runtime's blocking facility and compare. Change the sleep to a CPU loop and watch the same scheduling issue. Keep track of where the result and error travel back to the `async` caller. The goal is predictable responsiveness, not merely making code compile inside an `async` block.
writing.feedback: There is no `.await` in that wait, so the task cannot yield. The worker is held for the full second, and other ready tasks on it wait too.
writing.question: Why is a blocking sleep harmful here?
writing.rule: A blocking call occupies an executor worker without yielding, so unrelated tasks can stall.
writing.success: The second task keeps its schedule, and you can say why `sleep` inside an `async fn` delayed it.

writing.task: Rewrite `handler` so the wait yields, using your runtime's async timer. Then run it beside a second task and compare how late that task's timer fires.

recall.question: On a Tokio current-thread runtime, task A wakes every 50 ms from `tokio::time::sleep`; at about 60 ms task B calls `std::thread::sleep(300 ms)`. What happens to A's ticks?
recall.answer: A ticks at about 50 ms, then nothing until B's blocking sleep ends; the next tick comes at roughly 360 ms. The runtime's only worker thread is blocked and can't poll A, even though A's timer is ready.

recall.question: You move blocking work into `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`. What happens if you `abort()` that handle while the closure is running?
recall.answer: Nothing stops the closure: it runs to completion on the blocking pool, because abort only works at async await points. The awaited handle simply reports completion. Blocking work needs its own stop mechanism, and it should take owned input since it runs on another thread.
