lessons.concept: Borrowing iteration, consuming iteration and deliberate collection

writing.summary: An iterator pipeline describes work; the item type and terminal operation determine ownership and execution.
writing.explanation:
For a `Vec<T>`, `iter` normally yields `&T`, `iter_mut` yields `&mut T` and `into_iter` on an owned vector yields `T`. The chosen receiver matters: `into_iter` on a reference can still borrow. Read the actual item type before deciding whether an operation moves, copies or clones values.

Most iterator adapters are lazy. `map` describes a transformation, while a consumer such as `collect` or `sum` drives it. Returning an iterator can avoid collecting an intermediate vector, but keeps any captured input borrows alive for the returned iterator’s lifetime. Calling `cloned` on an iterator of references requests `Clone` on its items; it is not a free conversion for every `T`.

The example computes lengths by borrowing the strings and then proves the original vector remains usable. A second pipeline consumes it into another collection. Explain both the data flow and when work occurs. In an interview, follow up by returning an `impl Iterator<Item = &str>` tied to the input. That exposes lifetime reasoning more clearly than naming adapter methods from memory.
writing.exampleCaption: Borrowing iteration preserves the input; owned `into_iter` consumes this vector.
writing.rule: Trace the receiver, iterator item type and consumer before making a move or allocation claim.
writing.task: Explain the example, predict the result, and justify your answer to the follow-up.
writing.success: Identify the relevant ownership or API contract and test the changed constraint.
writing.question: Why can `words` still be read after collecting these lengths?
answers: collect implicitly clones every String in the source vector.
iter yields shared references and the map produces lengths without moving strings.
Every iterator pipeline automatically returns ownership to its original container.
writing.feedback: The pipeline borrows `&String` values and collects `usize` results. A consuming receiver or a different adapter can change the ownership contract.

recall.question: For `v: Vec<String>`, what item types do `v.iter()`, `v.iter_mut()`, `v.into_iter()` and `(&v).into_iter()` yield?
recall.answer: `&String`, `&mut String`, `String` and `&String`. Only `into_iter` on the owned vector consumes `v`; called on a reference, `into_iter` still just borrows.

recall.question: In what order does this code print, and why?
recall.answer: `built` first, then `visit 1`, `visit 2`, `visit 3`, then `12`. `map` is lazy and only describes the work; the `sum` consumer drives the iterator.

depth.misconception: Every iterator pipeline automatically returns ownership to its original container.
depth.correction: Nothing is returned, because nothing left. `iter` only lends references; `into_iter` on an owned `Vec` consumes it and never gives it back.

writing.summary: The call trait follows what the closure does with captures, not just whether `move` appears.
writing.explanation:
`Fn` closures can be called through a shared reference, `FnMut` permits a mutable receiver, and `FnOnce` consumes its receiver. The traits form a hierarchy: a closure that implements `Fn` also works where `FnMut` or `FnOnce` is required. Every closure supports at least `FnOnce`, but consuming a captured non-`Copy` value can make a closure callable only once.

The `move` keyword determines how captures enter the closure. It does not alone make the closure `FnOnce`-only. A `move` closure that merely reads owned data may still implement `Fn`. Conversely, mutating captured state generally requires `FnMut`. The example borrows a counter mutably, calls the closure twice, then ends its scope before reading the counter directly.

Read the implementation and the caller’s intended use together. A callback stored for repeated notifications needs a repeated-call contract, while a one-shot cleanup callback can accept `FnOnce`. If the callback crosses a thread or task boundary, `Send` and lifetime bounds are additional questions. In an interview, expect to change only the closure body from reading a `String` to returning the owned `String` and explain which call capability is lost.
writing.exampleCaption: A mutating callback runs twice, while a read-only `move` closure remains repeatedly callable.
writing.rule: `move` controls capture ownership; the closure body determines its call-trait capabilities.
writing.task: Explain the example, predict the result, and justify your answer to the follow-up.
writing.success: Identify the relevant ownership or API contract and test the changed constraint.
writing.question: Why can this `move` closure be called twice?
answers: move makes every captured String implicitly Copy.
The captured String is recreated before every call.
The body reads the owned capture without consuming it.
writing.feedback: The closure owns `text` but only borrows it during each call. Returning `text` by value instead would consume that capture.

recall.question: Why does the second call to `give` fail to compile?
recall.answer: The body returns the captured `String` by value, which consumes the capture, so the closure implements only `FnOnce`. The first call moves `give` itself; the second is E0382, use of moved value: `give`.

recall.question: What happens when `|| count += 1` is passed to `fn call(f: impl Fn())`?
recall.answer: It is rejected (E0594, cannot assign to `count` in a `Fn` closure). Mutating captured state makes the closure `FnMut`, not `Fn`; the function must accept `impl FnMut()` (and take `mut f`) instead.

depth.misconception: move makes every captured String implicitly Copy.
depth.correction: `String` never becomes `Copy`. `move` transfers the one `String` into the closure, and calls stay repeatable because the body only reads it.

lessons.title: Pin, Unpin and Future Polling
lessons.concept: Stable pointees without confusing the pointer with its allocation

writing.summary: `Pin` constrains moving a pointee through a pointer; moving that pointer can remain valid.
writing.explanation:
A future’s `poll` method receives `Pin<&mut Self>`. Some futures may have address-sensitive state, so the polling interface must not allow callers to move that state out after pinning. `Unpin` marks types for which the pinning restriction can be relaxed. `Pin` is not a mutex and does not itself provide synchronization or permanent storage.

The example pins a compiler-generated async future in a `Box`, records the pointee’s address, moves the `Pin<Box<_>>` handle and polls through its pinned mutable reference. Moving the handle does not relocate its heap pointee. A noop waker is adequate only because this particular future completes immediately; it is not a general executor for I/O or pending tasks.

Safe code should use supported pinning constructors and projection APIs instead of inventing unchecked pointer manipulations. A self-referential structure or pinned field needs a careful destruction and projection contract. In an interview, distinguish moving a pointer from moving the pointee, then explain why `get_mut` requires `Unpin`. Do not promise that every future is self-referential or that boxing every future is universally necessary.
writing.exampleCaption: Moving the pinned `Box` handle retains its pointee’s address and permits pinned polling.
writing.rule: `Pin` protects the pointee’s address-sensitive contract; `Unpin` governs safe access that can move it.
writing.task: Explain the example, predict the result, and justify your answer to the follow-up.
writing.success: Identify the relevant ownership or API contract and test the changed constraint.
writing.question: Which operation is demonstrated by moving `first` into `second`?
answers: The Pin<Box<_>> handle moves while the pinned allocation stays at its address.
The future becomes Unpin because its Box handle was moved.
Pin copies the future into a new allocation on every assignment.
writing.feedback: The handle’s move does not move its pointee. The example does not establish `Unpin` for a compiler-generated async future.

recall.question: Why does `Pin::get_mut` require `T: Unpin`, and what happens if you call it on a pinned `async` block?
recall.answer: `get_mut` hands out `&mut T`, through which the pointee could be moved, for example with `mem::swap`; that is only safe for types whose address does not matter. An `async` block's future is not `Unpin`, so the call fails to compile (E0277, cannot be unpinned).

recall.question: What does `Pin` not provide, despite guarding a future's address?
recall.answer: It is not a mutex, so it gives no synchronisation, and it does not provide permanent storage. It only constrains moving the pointee through that pointer; moving the `Pin<Box<_>>` handle itself is fine.

depth.misconception: The future becomes Unpin because its Box handle was moved.
depth.correction: Moving a handle does not change the pointee’s type, so the future’s `Unpin` status is unaffected. Only the pointer moved.

lessons.concept: Task state, 'static bounds and non-Send locals

writing.summary: Inspect which values survive a suspension before deciding whether a future satisfies `Send`.
writing.explanation:
A suspended async computation stores the state needed for a later poll. If that state contains an `Rc` or another non-`Send` value, the future may fail a `Send` bound. A non-`Send` temporary can still be used inside a future when it does not survive a suspension. The example places `Rc` in a lexical scope that ends before `await` and asks the compiler to verify `Send` on the resulting future.

`tokio::spawn` requires a `Send + 'static` future and a `Send + 'static` output even on a current-thread runtime. A separate local-task API supports a different contract; changing the executor’s thread count does not silently change the signature of `spawn`. `'static` on an owned task does not mean it must run forever: it means the value contains no shorter-lived borrows that would make this use invalid.

The standard-library example checks a type bound without starting Tokio or a network server. It can therefore isolate a compiler error from runtime setup. For an interview follow-up, keep `Rc` in scope across `await`, observe the compiler rejection and identify the retained state. A plain `drop(local)` before `await` is not always enough: once `local` has been borrowed, as `println!` does, rustc 1.99 still rejects the future, while a block scope passes. `async move` can own captured values, but ownership alone does not make every captured type `Send`.

Execution detail: `require_send` consumes and drops this unpolled future after checking its type. This program does not execute the async body. Polling the future in a suitable executor is a separate operation; an `await` expression is not itself proof that polling happened.
writing.exampleCaption: `Rc` is gone before suspension; this compile-time probe requires the future to be `Send`.
writing.rule: `Send` is determined by the future’s actual retained state; `async move` does not upgrade non-`Send` types.

writing.question: Why does this intentionally failing `Send` check reject the future?
answers: Every async function requires an operating-system thread for its whole lifetime.
Rc remains part of the future’s state across await and is not Send.
The ready future’s unit output is not Send on any runtime.
writing.feedback: `local` stays in scope across the `await`, so the `Rc` is part of the future’s state even with no later use. End its scope before the `await`, as the example does.

recall.question: This future still fails a `Send` check, although `local` is dropped before the `.await`. Why, and what does pass?
recall.answer: Once `local` has been borrowed (as `println!` does), rustc still treats the `Rc` as possibly held across the `await`, so the future is not `Send`. Putting the `Rc` in a block that ends before the `await` passes the check.

recall.question: `tokio::spawn` requires a `'static` future. What does `'static` mean here, and what does it not mean?
recall.answer: The future must contain no borrows shorter-lived than the task, so it owns its data or borrows only `'static` data. It does not mean the task runs forever.

depth.misconception: The ready future’s unit output is not Send on any runtime.
depth.correction: `()` is `Send`, and so is `ready(())`. The state that fails the check is the `Rc` still in scope across the `await`.

lessons.concept: Synchronous blocking, suspension and cancellation-safe critical sections

writing.summary: Keep synchronous critical sections short and make suspension while holding a guard an explicit design decision.
writing.explanation:
A standard mutex can be a reasonable choice for a short critical section that does not cross `await`. Acquiring a contended synchronous mutex can block the executor worker. Holding its guard while a future suspends is a separate problem: it keeps the lock unavailable and can violate a `Send` bound or participate in a deadlock.

The example updates a counter inside a lexical scope, drops the guard and only then awaits. A compile-time `Send` check confirms this particular future does not retain the standard `MutexGuard` across suspension. A plain `drop(guard)` before `await` is not a substitute here: after `*guard += 1` has borrowed the guard, rustc 1.99 still rejects the future, while the block scope passes. The check does not prove absence of every deadlock or that every acquisition is cheap.

An async mutex can yield while waiting for its lock, but it does not make arbitrary guarded work nonblocking. Avoid awaiting a child task that needs the same lock you hold. For cancellation, define what state is left behind when a task drops after a partial update; lock release is not a business transaction rollback. In an interview, draw lock acquisition, state update, guard drop and each suspension point before arguing about mutex brands.

Execution detail: `require_send` consumes and drops this unpolled future after checking its type. This program does not execute the async body. Polling the future in a suitable executor is a separate operation; an `await` expression is not itself proof that polling happened.
writing.exampleCaption: The synchronous guard’s scope ends before `await`; the future passes this `Send` check.
writing.rule: Waiting for a lock, holding a lock during suspension and doing CPU work are separate concerns.

writing.question: Why does this future keep the standard `MutexGuard` across `await`?
answers: The standard Mutex is not Send, so any future using it fails this check.
await releases the lock, then the future reacquires a new guard on resume.
The guard’s scope still spans await, so its non-Send state stays in the future.
writing.feedback: `guard` stays in scope across the `await`, so the lock and its non-`Send` guard are part of the future’s state. Moving the later use before the `await` is not enough; end the guard’s scope first when the design permits it.

recall.question: Why can a task deadlock if it awaits a child task while still holding a mutex guard?
recall.answer: The parent suspends while keeping the lock, and the child needs that same lock to finish, so each waits for the other. Release the guard before awaiting work that may need the lock.

recall.question: Compared with `std::sync::Mutex`, what does an async mutex change, and what does it not fix?
recall.answer: Waiting for the lock yields to the executor instead of blocking the worker thread. It does not make slow guarded work nonblocking, and if the task is cancelled mid-update, releasing the lock does not roll back the partial state.

depth.misconception: The standard Mutex is not Send, so any future using it fails this check.
depth.correction: `Mutex<i32>` is `Send`, and the example’s future uses one and passes this check. The non-`Send` part is `MutexGuard`, and only while its scope spans an `await`.

lessons.concept: Native async methods, returned futures and explicit type erasure

writing.summary: Native async trait methods and dynamic dispatch are separate interface choices.
writing.explanation:
Rust supports async methods in traits, but a method returning a hidden future is not directly dispatchable through a trait object under the current dyn-compatibility rules. A generic caller can retain the concrete implementation and future type. A dynamic interface can instead return an explicitly erased future, commonly behind `Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = T> + Send + '_>>`.

The example deliberately writes that erased interface rather than relying on an attribute macro. Its returned future borrows `self`, so the lifetime is explicit. `Send` is also an explicit promise in the returned future type; it is not implied for every native async trait method. Boxing adds an ownership/allocation choice whose tradeoff should match the workload.

A simple noop-waker poll demonstrates only the immediately ready example. Real pending work needs a runtime that arranges wakeups. In an interview, compare a generic implementation, an enum of a closed implementation set and a trait object for an open set. Ask which bounds callers need before choosing an async-trait macro or a boxed interface. Native support does not mean every trait is dyn-compatible, and dynamic dispatch does not inherently require every possible receiver to be heap allocated.
writing.exampleCaption: The trait-object method returns one explicit erased future interface with a borrowing lifetime.
writing.rule: Check dyn compatibility, future lifetime and `Send` bounds independently.
writing.task: Explain the example, predict the result, and justify your answer to the follow-up.
writing.success: Identify the relevant ownership or API contract and test the changed constraint.
writing.question: Why does this native async method prevent using this trait directly as `dyn NativeSource`?
answers: The async method has a hidden future return type that is not dyn-dispatchable here.
Rust forbids async methods in every trait declaration.
The trait becomes dyn-compatible solely by adding Send as a supertrait.
writing.feedback: Native async traits are supported, but this method is not directly dyn-dispatchable. Use a suitable generic, enum or explicit erased-future interface.

recall.question: In `fn value(&self) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = u32> + Send + '_>>`, why are `+ Send` and `+ '_` written out, and what happens if `'_` is left off while the body is `Box::pin(async move { self.0 })`?
recall.answer: `'_` says the future borrows `self`; `Send` is an explicit promise so callers can move the future across threads, and it is not implied for every async method. Without `'_` the boxed future defaults to `'static` but captures `&self`, so it fails with "lifetime may not live long enough".

recall.question: Several types provide an async operation. Compare calling it through a generic, an enum and a trait object returning a boxed future.
recall.answer: A generic keeps the concrete type and future type, with static dispatch and no boxing. An enum suits a closed, known set with exhaustive matching. A trait object with an explicitly boxed future suits an open set of implementations, at the cost of an allocation per call.

depth.misconception: Rust forbids async methods in every trait declaration.
depth.correction: `NativeSource` compiles, so async methods in traits are allowed. What the hidden future type rules out is dyn dispatch, not the method.

lessons.concept: Absence, invalid input and contextual failure

writing.summary: An error type should preserve the distinctions the caller needs to handle.
writing.explanation:
A missing optional value and an invalid supplied value describe different outcomes. `Result<Option<T>, E>` can express success with absence, success with a value, or failure. The example converts `Option<Result<u16, ParseIntError>>` using `transpose`, preserving all three cases without manufacturing a default port.

At an application boundary you may add contextual information such as a safe field name or a public operation ID. Preserve a useful source error when appropriate and avoid depending on human-readable error strings for control flow. A library can expose typed error cases, while an executable may aggregate errors for reporting. Type erasure through a trait object trades some structured matching for flexibility and may need `Send + Sync` bounds if the value crosses task boundaries.

In an interview, begin with what the caller can reasonably do: retry, prompt for input, treat absence as normal, or stop. A retry policy also needs to know whether an earlier effect may have committed. Returning `Result` alone does not make a side effect transactional or idempotent. Do not leak credentials or private paths into a shared diagnostic merely because an error type can store them.
writing.exampleCaption: `transpose` preserves absence separately from a supplied value that fails to parse.
writing.rule: Choose error structure from caller decisions; absence, failure and defaulting are different policies.
writing.task: Explain the example, predict the result, and justify your answer to the follow-up.
writing.success: Identify the relevant ownership or API contract and test the changed constraint.
writing.question: Which outcome should `optional_port(Some("bad"))` produce under this contract?
answers: Ok(None), because every parse failure means the field was absent.
Err carrying the parse error, because the supplied value is invalid.
Ok(Some(0)), because Result automatically chooses a numeric default.
writing.feedback: `None` represents absence; malformed supplied input follows the error path. Defaults require a separate documented policy.

recall.question: Why is `fn optional_port(raw: Option<&str>) -> Result<Option<u16>, ParseIntError>` better than returning a default port whenever the value is missing or invalid?
recall.answer: It keeps three cases apart: `Ok(None)` means nothing was supplied, so the caller applies its own policy; `Ok(Some(port))` is a valid value; `Err` means the supplied value was invalid, so the caller can report it. A silent default would hide a typo.

recall.question: Why should callers not branch on an error's human-readable message, and what should go into error context at a boundary?
recall.answer: Message strings are for people and can change; expose typed error cases for control flow. Context should add safe facts such as a field name or public operation ID, never credentials or private paths.

depth.misconception: Ok(Some(0)), because Result automatically chooses a numeric default.
depth.correction: `Result` chooses no defaults. `parse` returns `Err` for `bad`, and `transpose` carries it out unchanged. A default needs explicit code such as `unwrap_or`.

lessons.concept: Implementing foreign traits without conflicting implementations

writing.summary: A local wrapper creates a distinct type whose behaviour your crate can own.
writing.explanation:
Rust’s coherence rules restrict trait implementations so that implementations can be selected consistently across crates. The orphan rules broadly require the trait or a relevant implementing type to be local, with additional rules for generic parameters and fundamental types. A type alias does not create a new local type for this purpose.

The example wraps `Vec<u8>` in a local `Bytes` type and implements the standard `Display` trait for that wrapper. It does not attempt to implement `Display` directly for `Vec<u8>`. The wrapper also creates an explicit API boundary: you can restrict construction, choose formatting and control which capabilities are exposed. Delegation is a design choice rather than an automatic consequence of wrapping.

In an interview, contrast a local trait implemented for a foreign type with a foreign trait implemented for a local wrapper. Explain why a type alias cannot make an otherwise conflicting implementation valid. Then discuss what a blanket implementation can prevent downstream crates from adding later. The rule is about which implementations exist and can coexist, not a runtime performance penalty. A newtype’s layout or FFI suitability still requires the relevant representation and ABI contract.
writing.exampleCaption: `Display` is implemented for a local wrapper, not directly for a foreign `Vec` type.
writing.rule: A newtype creates a distinct local type; an alias only gives an existing type another name.

writing.success: Identify the relevant ownership or API contract and test the changed constraint.
writing.question: Why does this local `Bytes` wrapper permit the shown `Display` implementation?
answers: The wrapper makes the standard Display trait local to this crate.
Any alias of Vec<u8> would create the same local implementation identity.
Bytes is a distinct local implementing type, satisfying the relevant orphan requirement.
writing.feedback: The trait remains foreign; the implementing wrapper is local. Generic coverage and overlap still need to satisfy coherence rules.

recall.question: Why does this fail to compile, and what is the fix?
recall.answer: A type alias is only another name for `Vec<u8>`, so this implements a foreign trait for a foreign type, which the orphan rule forbids (E0117). Use a newtype such as `struct Bytes(Vec<u8>);`, a distinct local type.

recall.question: Which of these does the orphan rule allow: your own trait for `Vec<u8>`, `Display` for your own struct, `Display` for `Vec<u8>`?
recall.answer: The first two: either the trait or the implementing type is local to your crate. `Display` for `Vec<u8>` is rejected because both are foreign, which keeps implementations consistent across crates.

depth.misconception: The wrapper makes the standard Display trait local to this crate.
depth.correction: `Display` stays foreign. The orphan rule is satisfied because the implementing type, `Bytes`, is local.

lessons.title: Integer Boundaries and Conversion
lessons.concept: Checked arithmetic and deliberate narrowing policies

writing.summary: Input bounds and arithmetic policy are part of the algorithm’s contract.
writing.explanation:
Integer operations need a policy when the mathematical result is outside the destination range. `checked_add` returns `None` on overflow, `wrapping_add` uses modular arithmetic, and `saturating_add` clamps at a boundary. A lossy `as` conversion can discard information; `TryFrom` can reject an out-of-range conversion. Choose behaviour that matches the domain instead of depending on the build’s overflow-check settings.

The example checks an addition at `u32::MAX` and rejects narrowing 300 to `u8`. It also widens `i32` operands before computing their difference. Widening after an overflowing operation is too late. A wider type is sufficient only when the full input-domain calculation fits it; replacing `u64` arithmetic with `i64` is not a general widening strategy.

In an interview, ask for the input range, the result range and the required failure behaviour. A sum over many elements may overflow even if each element is valid, while a length cast can truncate on large inputs. Boundary tests should cover both sides of a conversion and the exact maximum or minimum. Explain the correctness argument separately from performance measurements and from memory safety: losing numeric information is not automatically undefined behaviour.
writing.exampleCaption: Checked operations report overflow and conversion failure; widening happens before subtraction.
writing.rule: Choose the numeric domain and overflow policy explicitly, and widen before the operation when that is the proof.
writing.task: Explain the example, predict the result, and justify your answer to the follow-up.
writing.success: Identify the relevant ownership or API contract and test the changed constraint.
writing.question: Which result does `u8::try_from(300u16)` report?
answers: An error, because 300 cannot be represented as u8.
Ok(44), because TryFrom always uses modular narrowing.
A compile error, because integers cannot be converted at runtime.
writing.feedback: `TryFrom` checks representability. An `as` cast follows a different conversion contract and can lose numeric information.

recall.question: What do `u32::MAX.checked_add(1)`, `u32::MAX.wrapping_add(1)` and `u32::MAX.saturating_add(1)` return?
recall.answer: `None`, `0` and `u32::MAX` (4294967295). Each method states an overflow policy explicitly, so the result does not depend on whether the build has overflow checks enabled.

recall.question: With `a` and `b` of type `i32`, why does `i64::from(a + b)` not prevent overflow, while `i64::from(a) + i64::from(b)` does?
recall.answer: In the first, the `i32` addition overflows before the conversion: it panics with overflow checks on or wraps without them. Widening must happen before the operation, and only works if the full calculation fits the wider type.

depth.misconception: Ok(44), because TryFrom always uses modular narrowing.
depth.correction: 44 is what `300u16 as u8` gives. `TryFrom` is the checked path and returns `Err` instead of wrapping.

lessons.title: What Rust Is, from C

writing.summary: Rust compiles to native code like C, with no garbage collector and no virtual machine; what changes is that rustc proves memory safety for safe code before the program runs.
writing.rule: Rust is a compiled, statically typed language without a garbage collector: rustc checks types, ownership and borrowing before the program runs, then produces a native executable.
writing.explanation:
From a C programmer's seat, most of the toolchain looks familiar. `rustc` is an ahead-of-time compiler: it parses and type-checks the program, lowers it to LLVM IR, and LLVM, the same optimiser and code generator family that clang uses, emits machine code that the platform linker turns into an ordinary executable. There is no interpreter, no virtual machine and no garbage collector. The standard library is linked into the binary by default, and its start-up work before `main` is small, comparable to what the C runtime and libc already do; `#![no_std]` code for kernels and microcontrollers drops even that and keeps only `core`.

The machine model is the same as C's. Locals live in stack frames, `Box`, `Vec` and `String` allocate on the heap through the system allocator, references and raw pointers are addresses, integers have fixed widths, and structs have a size you can ask for: `size_of::<Point>()` is 8, like `sizeof(struct point)`. You reason about performance the way you do in C, and Rust can call C and be called from C.

The difference is what the compiler checks. Besides static types, rustc tracks ownership (which binding frees each value) and borrowing (which references may read or write it, and for how long). For safe code it proves, before the program runs, that no value is used after it is freed, freed twice, or written while another reference reads it, and that no data race is possible. Those checks happen at compile time and cost nothing at run time; the remaining run-time checks, such as array bounds, are explicit and cheap.

The price is that rustc rejects programs it cannot prove safe, even some that would happen to work. The C program frees `on_heap` while `alias` still holds its address, and clang accepts any later use of `alias`; the same shape in Rust is error `E0505`, because `on_heap` cannot be moved into `drop` while `alias` still borrows it. When safe Rust cannot express a design, `unsafe` lets you take over specific proofs yourself, as C always required.
writing.exampleCaption: The same stack value, heap copy and pointer as in C; the `Box` frees its memory when its owner goes out of scope, and the borrow `alias` is checked.
writing.task: Compile the practice program, read why rustc refuses it, and say where the equivalent C program would fail instead.
writing.success: You can explain that the C version compiles and is undefined at run time, while rustc rejects the Rust version with `E0505` before any code runs.
writing.question: Where does Rust's memory safety come from, compared with C?
answers: A garbage collector that frees unreachable memory at run time
rustc checks types, ownership and borrowing at compile time and then emits a native executable through LLVM
A virtual machine that checks every pointer access while the program runs
Every pointer is reference-counted automatically
writing.feedback: The checks are static: rustc proves them while compiling, then produces ordinary machine code. There is no collector, VM or hidden reference counting.

recall.question: Does a Rust program need a runtime installed on the target machine, the way Java needs a JVM or JavaScript needs Node.js?
recall.answer: No. rustc produces a native executable linked against the platform's C library, as clang does, and the Rust standard library is linked into the binary by default. There is no VM, interpreter or garbage collector to install.

recall.question: Which line does rustc reject, and when?
recall.answer: `drop(v)`, at compile time: `v` cannot be moved into `drop` while `first` still borrows it (`E0505`). The C equivalent, `free` followed by a read through a stale pointer, compiles and is undefined behaviour at run time.

bridge.fromCaption: Stack value, heap copy and an aliasing pointer; after `free`, nothing stops a later use of `alias`.

contrasts.from: clang compiles C ahead of time through LLVM to a native executable.
contrasts.rust: rustc also compiles ahead of time through LLVM to a native executable.

contrasts.from: No garbage collector; memory is freed by explicit `free` calls.
contrasts.rust: No garbage collector; the compiler inserts the free where the owner goes out of scope.

contrasts.from: The compiler accepts any pointer use that type-checks.
contrasts.rust: rustc also checks ownership and borrowing, and rejects what it cannot prove safe.

lessons.title: What Safe Rust Rules Out

writing.summary: Safe Rust rules out the memory and thread bugs that are undefined behaviour in C, but not leaks, deadlocks, panics or wrong logic.
writing.rule: Safe Rust has no undefined behaviour: use after free, double free, dangling references, out-of-bounds access, null dereference, uninitialised reads and data races are rejected or checked; leaks, deadlocks, panics, logic errors and wrapping arithmetic in release builds are not.
writing.explanation:
In C, executing an undefined operation makes the whole program meaningless, and the optimiser is allowed to assume it never happens. The example's four cases compile without a single warning under `-Wall -Wextra`; each one fails only when it runs, and only a sanitizer build says why: `stack-buffer-overflow`, `heap-use-after-free`, a load of a null pointer and `attempting double-free`.

Safe Rust closes each of these by construction. Ownership means one owner frees each value once, so double free and use after free cannot be written. Borrow checking means a reference cannot outlive its value or overlap a writer. References are never null; absence is `Option`. A binding must be initialised on every path before it is read, or the program is rejected with `E0381`. `Send` and `Sync`, together with borrowing, make data races a compile error. Indexing is the one run-time check: `xs[i]` with a bad index panics, and `xs.get(i)` returns `None`, so an out-of-bounds read never touches the neighbouring memory.

"Safe" means free of undefined behaviour, not correct. Safe Rust can still leak memory (`Box::leak`, `mem::forget` and `Rc` cycles are all safe), deadlock on two `Mutex`es taken in different orders, compute the wrong answer, run out of memory or stack, and panic. A panic is defined behaviour: the thread unwinds and runs destructors, or the process aborts if it is configured to. Integer overflow is defined too, but in release builds it wraps unless you choose `checked_` or keep `overflow-checks` on.

`unsafe` re-enables specific powers that safe code lacks: dereferencing raw pointers, calling `unsafe` functions including every C function, accessing mutable statics, implementing `unsafe` traits and reading `union` fields. Inside those blocks every C undefined behaviour is possible again, and the guarantee for the whole program rests on each `unsafe` block being right. That is why such blocks are kept small and documented; a later lesson shows how.
writing.exampleCaption: A checked index, a move instead of a second owner, `Option` instead of null, explicit wrapping, and a leak that is wasteful but safe.
writing.task: Run the C program's cases under a sanitizer in your head, match each one to the Rust rule that excludes it, then decide what the practice program needs before it compiles.
writing.success: You can name the Rust mechanism behind each excluded C bug, and list three kinds of bug safe Rust still allows.
writing.question: Which of these can a program written entirely in safe Rust still do?
answers: Read a freed heap buffer through a stale reference
Index one element past the end of an array without being stopped
Dereference a null reference
Leak memory with `Box::leak` or deadlock on two `Mutex`es
writing.feedback: Leaks and deadlocks are bugs, not undefined behaviour, so safe Rust allows them. The other three are rejected at compile time or stopped by a bounds-check panic.

recall.question: Is a panic in Rust undefined behaviour, like an out-of-bounds read in C?
recall.answer: No. A panic is defined: by default the thread unwinds, runs destructors and reports the message, and with `panic = "abort"` the process stops immediately. A bad index in safe Rust becomes this defined panic instead of a read of neighbouring memory.

recall.question: Does this compile, and is it safe?
recall.answer: Yes and yes: it prints `done`. Leaking is not undefined behaviour, so `mem::forget`, `Box::leak` and `Rc` cycles are all safe. The memory is never returned to the allocator, which wastes it but cannot corrupt anything.

bridge.fromCaption: Four undefined behaviours that compile without a warning; sanitizers report a stack overflow, a use after free, a null load and a double free.

contrasts.from: Use after free, double free and dangling pointers compile and are undefined.
contrasts.rust: Ownership and borrow checking reject them at compile time.

contrasts.from: Out-of-bounds reads and NULL dereferences are undefined.
contrasts.rust: Indexing is bounds-checked (a defined panic); absence is `Option`, never a null reference.

contrasts.from: Reading an uninitialised variable is at most a warning.
contrasts.rust: Every binding must be initialised on every path before it is read (`E0381`).

contrasts.from: Leaks, deadlocks and logic errors are the programmer's problem.
contrasts.rust: They still are: safe Rust excludes undefined behaviour, not bugs.

depth.misconception: “The `help:` line is the fix; apply it and move on.”
depth.correction: A `help:` line is one change that would compile. It may cost a copy (`clone`) or turn a compile error into a run-time panic (`unwrap`). Decide what the program should mean first; the notes often point to a better fix.

lessons.title: Reading rustc Diagnostics

writing.summary: Where a C program compiles and crashes later, rustc stops with an error code, the exact spans involved and a suggested fix; reading them in order is a skill worth learning first.
writing.rule: Repair the first causal error before chasing its downstream messages: read its code and primary span, then the labels, notes and help, fix the cause and recompile.
writing.explanation:
In C the compiler's main job is translation, and whole classes of bugs produce no diagnostic at all. The example's use after free compiles silently even with `-Wall -Wextra`; the only warning is about `count`, which may be used uninitialised. `-Werror` turns that warning into a build failure, and the use after free surfaces only at run time, as `heap-use-after-free` under AddressSanitizer.

rustc refuses the equivalent program instead, and its diagnostic has a fixed anatomy. The first line gives the severity, the error code and the rule: `error[E0382]: borrow of moved value`. The `-->` line gives the file, line and column. Under the source, `^^^` marks the primary span, the place where the rule is broken (`value borrowed here after move`), and `---` marks secondary spans that explain why: where the value moved, and that `Vec<i32>` does not implement `Copy`. `note:` lines add context, here pointing at the parameter that takes ownership, and `help:` lines propose a change.

Read in that order and fix the first error first. One root mistake can produce several later errors, so recompile after each fix before reading the rest. Treat `help:` as evidence, not a command: `consider cloning the value` would compile, but the note's suggestion to borrow, `values: &[i32]`, matches what the program means and copies nothing. For any code, `rustc --explain E0382` prints the rule with examples, offline.

Errors and warnings are separate in Rust. An error, such as a move, a type mismatch or a possibly uninitialised read (`E0381`), means no program is built; there is no flag that lets it through. Lints such as unused variables are warnings by default, and `#![deny(warnings)]` in the crate, or `RUSTFLAGS="-D warnings"` in CI, is the equivalent of `-Werror`. `cargo clippy` adds further lints, much as extra `-W` flags do for clang.
writing.exampleCaption: Following the note rather than the `clone` help: `total` borrows a slice, so `readings` is still usable afterwards.
writing.task: Compile the practice program, label each part of the diagnostic (code, primary span, secondary spans, note, help), then choose between the `clone` help and the borrowing note.
writing.success: You can point to the `^^^` span that breaks the rule, the `---` span that explains it, and explain why borrowing is a better fix than cloning here.
writing.question: After one edit, rustc reports three errors: `E0308` at a call to `total`, then two more in later lines that use its result. What do you do first?
answers: Fix the first error at its primary span, recompile, and then see which later errors remain
Fix the last error first, because it is closest to the end of `main`
Apply every `help:` suggestion in the order printed
Silence the errors with `#[allow(...)]` attributes
writing.feedback: Later errors are often consequences of the first. Its primary span shows where the rule breaks; fix that cause, rebuild, and only then read what is left.

recall.question: In a rustc diagnostic, what do the `^^^` and `---` markers under the source mean?
recall.answer: `^^^` marks the primary span, the place where the rule is broken, with the main label (for example `value borrowed here after move`). `---` marks secondary spans that explain why, such as `value moved here`. Read the primary span first, then the labels.

recall.question: Does this compile? What plays the role of `gcc -Wall -Werror` here?
recall.answer: No. Warnings are on by default, and `#![deny(warnings)]`, or `RUSTFLAGS="-D warnings"` in CI, turns them into errors, so the unused variable stops the build. Errors such as `E0382` were never optional in the first place.

bridge.fromCaption: `-Wall` warns only about `count`; the use after free compiles silently and is found at run time by AddressSanitizer.

contrasts.from: A use after free compiles without a diagnostic, even with `-Wall -Wextra`.
contrasts.rust: A use after move is error `E0382`, with spans for where the value moved and where it was used.

contrasts.from: `-Wall` warns about a possibly uninitialised variable; `-Werror` makes it fatal.
contrasts.rust: Reading a possibly uninitialised binding is always error `E0381`.

contrasts.from: Warning flags are looked up in the compiler manual.
contrasts.rust: `rustc --explain E0382` prints the rule with examples, offline.

contrasts.from: `-Werror` promotes warnings to errors.
contrasts.rust: `#![deny(warnings)]` or `-D warnings` does the same for rustc lints.

depth.misconception: “`println!` is Rust's `printf`, so a wrong argument shows up as garbage output.”
depth.correction: `println!` is a macro that rustc expands and type-checks. A missing argument, an extra argument or a value without the requested trait (for example `{}` on a type without `Display`) stops the build. Garbage output from a mismatched format is not possible in safe Rust.

lessons.title: From printf to println!

writing.summary: `println!` checks its format string against its arguments while compiling; `printf` trusts you until run time.
writing.rule: `println!` is a macro: placeholders and arguments are matched during compilation, so a missing or mistyped argument is a compile error, not undefined behaviour.
writing.explanation:
`printf` is an ordinary variadic function. The compiler passes whatever arguments you wrote, and the C library reads them back according to the format string at run time. Clang and GCC compare the two as a courtesy (`-Wformat`), but a mismatch is still valid C with undefined behaviour: the second `%u` in the example reads an argument that was never passed.

`println!`, `print!`, `eprintln!` and `format!` are macros, which is what the `!` means. They expand during compilation, so rustc sees the format string and every argument together. One placeholder too many is a compile error. Each value must also implement the trait its placeholder asks for: `Display` for `{}`, `Debug` for `{:?}`, `LowerHex` for `{:x}`. There are no length modifiers such as `%ld` or `%zu`, because the argument's type already says how wide it is.

The flags map closely: `{:>8}` is `%8s`, `{:03}` is `%03u`, `{:#06x}` is `%#06x` and `{:.2}` is `%.2f`. Two defaults differ. A bare width pads text on the right (`{:8}` behaves like `%-8s`) while numbers still pad on the left, and `#` always prints the `0x` prefix, even for zero, where C prints plain `0`. A variable in scope can be named inside the braces, as in `{qty}`.

Execution still starts in `fn main()`. `println!` writes a line to stdout and `eprintln!` to stderr. `format!` returns the text as an owned `String` instead of filling a caller-sized buffer, so there is no `snprintf` truncation to check.
writing.exampleCaption: The same lines as the C program, plus `eprintln!` for stderr and `format!`, which returns a `String` instead of writing into a buffer.
writing.task: Port the commented C `snprintf` call: `label` returns the name right-aligned in 8 columns, the quantity zero-padded to 3 digits and the code as `0x`-prefixed hex zero-padded to width 6, separated by `|`. Keep Rust's prefix for zero (`0x0000`).
writing.success: `label("bolt", 7, 255)` returns `    bolt|007|0x00ff`, longer names are never cut, and a zero code prints as `0x0000`.
writing.question: The practice program has two `{}` placeholders and one argument. What happens?
answers: It prints `7 items,  left` and continues
It compiles with a warning, like `-Wformat`
rustc rejects it while expanding the macro, before any code runs
It panics at run time when it reaches the second placeholder
writing.feedback: `println!` is expanded during compilation, so rustc counts placeholders against arguments and stops with `2 positional arguments in format string, but there is 1 argument`.

recall.question: Why does `{:8}` give a different result for `"bolt"` than `%8s` does in C?
recall.answer: Rust pads non-numeric values on the right by default, so `{:8}` gives `bolt    `, like `%-8s`. Numbers still pad on the left. Write `{:>8}` to right-align text the way `%8s` does.

recall.question: What do these two lines print?
recall.answer: `0x0` and `0x00ff`. With `#`, Rust always prints the `0x` prefix, even for zero, and the width counts the prefix. C's `%#x` prints plain `0` for zero.

bridge.fromCaption: Correct output for matching arguments; the last call compiles with only a `-Wformat` warning and reads an argument that was never passed.

contrasts.from: `printf` checks nothing itself; `-Wformat` is an optional compiler warning.
contrasts.rust: `println!` expands at compile time; a missing argument is a compile error.

contrasts.from: `%ld`, `%zu` and `%u` must match each argument's exact type.
contrasts.rust: The argument's type decides; the placeholder picks a trait: `{}`, `{:?}`, `{:x}`.

contrasts.from: `%8s` right-aligns text; `%#x` prints `0` for zero.
contrasts.rust: `{:8}` left-aligns text; `{:#x}` prints `0x0`.

contrasts.from: `snprintf` truncates into a buffer the caller must size.
contrasts.rust: `format!` returns an owned `String` that grows as needed.

lessons.title: const by Default

writing.summary: In Rust a binding is immutable unless you write `mut`, and a new `let` can reuse a name for a new value or even a new type.
writing.rule: `let` bindings are immutable by default; `mut` opts in to mutation, and shadowing with a new `let` creates a new binding instead of changing the old one.
writing.explanation:
In C every object is writable unless you add `const`, and `const` means read-only through this name, not constant: `const int limit = 3` is not an integer constant expression, and a `const T *` parameter says nothing about whether someone else changes the object. Rust flips the default. `let total = 0;` can never be reassigned; trying is error `E0384`. Write `let mut total = 0;` when the value really changes.

Immutability belongs to the binding, which makes it cheap to check and useful to read: a binding without `mut` names the same value for its whole scope. Mutable state stands out because every mutable binding is marked, and rustc warns when a `mut` turns out to be unnecessary.

Shadowing has no C equivalent. `let width = width.trim();` declares a new binding called `width` that hides the previous one, and it may have a different type. C code usually invents a name per stage (`raw_width`, `trimmed`, `width_value`); Rust code often reuses one, because the earlier stage can then no longer be used by mistake. Shadowing is not mutation: the old value is unchanged, and a reference that borrowed it still sees it.

Rust's `const LIMIT: u32 = 3;` is what C programmers usually want from `#define` or `enum { LIMIT = 3 }`: a typed compile-time constant, copied into each use. `static` is the item with one fixed address, the closer match to a C global. A mutable `static` needs `unsafe` to access, so shared counters use an atomic or a `Mutex` instead.
writing.exampleCaption: `width` is shadowed twice, from `&str` to a trimmed `&str` to a `u32`; only `total` needs `mut`.
writing.task: Predict which statement in the quiz rustc rejects, then fix the practice program with the smallest possible change.
writing.success: You can explain why a shadowing `let` compiles while `+=` on a binding without `mut` is error `E0384`.
writing.question: In `let total = 0; let total = total + 5; total += 1;`, which statement does rustc reject?
answers: `let total = total + 5;`: a name cannot be declared twice
`total += 1;`: the second `total` is a new binding, and it is not `mut`
None of them: the second `let` made `total` mutable
`let total = 0;`: an integer literal needs a type suffix
writing.feedback: Shadowing declared a new immutable `total` with the value 5. `+=` would change it, so rustc reports `E0384` and suggests `let mut total`.

recall.question: What does this print?
recall.answer: `10` then `5`. The inner `let` shadows `x` only inside the block. The outer binding was never changed, so it is visible again after the closing brace.

recall.question: When should a C programmer reach for `const` and when for `static` in Rust?
recall.answer: `const` for a typed compile-time value that is copied into each use, like `#define LIMIT 3` with a type. `static` for one item with a fixed address that lives for the whole program, like a C global. Mutable statics need `unsafe`, so shared mutable state usually goes in an atomic or a `Mutex`.

bridge.fromCaption: C mutates by default, needs a new name per parsing stage, and its `const` means read-only rather than constant.

contrasts.from: Objects are writable unless declared `const`.
contrasts.rust: Bindings are immutable unless declared `mut`; reassignment is error `E0384`.

contrasts.from: `const int` means read-only, not a compile-time constant.
contrasts.rust: `const` is a typed compile-time constant; `static` has one address.

contrasts.from: Each processing stage needs a new variable name.
contrasts.rust: A new `let` can shadow the name, even with a different type.

traceSteps.detail: For each `+`, `*` or `-` that can exceed the type, choose `checked_`, `wrapping_` or `saturating_`, or prove the bound.

traceSteps.title: Separate casts from conversions

depth.misconception: “Overflow in Rust is like unsigned overflow in C: it silently wraps.”
depth.correction: Only in release builds with the default profile, and even there it is a defined wrap rather than undefined behaviour. Debug builds panic. Code that needs wrapping should call `wrapping_*` so it does not depend on the build profile.

lessons.title: Integer Overflow and Casts

writing.summary: Rust never converts between integer types silently, and overflow is always defined: a panic in debug builds, wrapping in release builds, or exactly the policy you call.
writing.rule: Integer types never mix implicitly; choose the overflow policy (`checked_`, `wrapping_`, `saturating_`) and the conversion (`From`, `TryFrom`, `as`) explicitly.
writing.explanation:
C's usual arithmetic conversions decide behind your back: in `-1 < 3u` the `int` becomes `UINT_MAX` and the comparison is false, and clang's `-Wsign-compare` is the only hint. Rust has no integer promotion and no implicit conversion between `i32`, `u32`, `usize` or any other pair. Comparing or adding mixed types is error `E0308`. Widen with `i64::from(d)`, which cannot fail, or convert with `u8::try_from(x)`, which returns a `Result` when the value might not fit.

Signed overflow in C is undefined behaviour: UBSan reports `signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int32_t'`, and the optimiser may assume it never happens. In Rust overflow is always defined. In the default debug profile arithmetic is checked, and overflow panics with `attempt to add with overflow`. The release profile turns `overflow-checks` off, and the same expression wraps in two's complement. Neither is undefined, but a program that depends on either for ordinary values has a bug.

When overflow is possible, say what you want. `checked_mul` returns `None`, `wrapping_mul` wraps on purpose (hashes, checksums), `saturating_add` clamps at the limit, and `overflowing_add` returns the wrapped value with a flag. The policy is then visible in the code instead of depending on the build profile.

`as` remains for deliberate, lossy casts. Between integers it truncates or extends like a C cast: `300_i32 as u8` is 44. From floating point it saturates, and NaN becomes 0, where C is undefined for out-of-range values. Use `as` when you mean exactly that, and `TryFrom` when a value that does not fit is an error.
writing.exampleCaption: Each line chooses its policy: `None` from `checked_mul`, deliberate wrapping, a truncating `as`, a checked conversion, a saturating float cast and an explicit widening.
writing.task: Port the commented C functions without their silent wrap and truncation: `total_bytes` returns `None` when `count * size` does not fit in `u32`, and `to_byte` returns `None` for values outside `0..=255`.
writing.success: `total_bytes(65_536, 65_536)` is `None`, `to_byte(300)` and `to_byte(-1)` are `None`, and values that fit come back unchanged.
writing.question: In C, `d < u` with `int d = -1` and `unsigned u = 3` is false. What does rustc do with the same comparison on an `i32` and a `u32`?
answers: Rejects it with `E0308`: you must convert one side yourself
Converts `d` to `u32` and returns `false`, like C
Converts both to `i64` and returns `true`
Compiles, then panics at run time because `d` is negative
writing.feedback: Rust has no usual arithmetic conversions. `i64::from(d) < i64::from(u)` states the widening and evaluates to `true`.

recall.question: A debug build panics with `attempt to multiply with overflow`. Does the release build of the same code have undefined behaviour?
recall.answer: No. With the default release profile, `overflow-checks` is off and the multiplication wraps in two's complement, which is defined but almost certainly wrong. Call `checked_mul`, or `wrapping_mul` if wrapping is intended, so both builds behave the same.

recall.question: What do these four casts produce?
recall.answer: `44 4294967295 2147483647 0`. Integer casts keep or reinterpret the low bits as in C. Float-to-integer casts saturate and map NaN to 0; in C those two out-of-range conversions are undefined.

bridge.fromCaption: Unsigned overflow wraps to 0, `(uint8_t)300` keeps the low byte, `-1 < 3u` is false, and `add(INT32_MAX, 1)` is undefined behaviour that UBSan reports.

contrasts.from: Signed overflow is undefined; unsigned overflow wraps silently.
contrasts.rust: Overflow panics in debug builds and wraps in release; `checked_*` makes it a value.

contrasts.from: Usual arithmetic conversions mix signed and unsigned silently.
contrasts.rust: Mixed integer types do not compile (`E0308`); convert with `From`, `TryFrom` or `as`.

contrasts.from: An out-of-range float-to-integer conversion is undefined.
contrasts.rust: `f64 as i32` saturates, and NaN becomes 0.

depth.correction: Using the result of a non-`void` C function that falls off its end is undefined. In Rust the end of the body is the return value; if that value is `()` but the signature promises another type, the program does not compile.

lessons.title: Functions Are Expressions

writing.summary: A Rust block evaluates to its last expression, so functions return without `return`, and `if` replaces the ternary operator.
writing.rule: A block's value is its final expression without a semicolon; adding the semicolon turns it into a statement, and the block evaluates to `()`.
writing.explanation:
C separates statements from expressions: `if` is a statement, so choosing a value needs `?:`, and a function hands back a value only through `return`. In Rust almost everything is an expression. A block `{ ... }` evaluates to its last expression, and a function body is a block, so `fn is_even(x: i32) -> bool` can end with the comparison itself. `return` still exists for early exits.

`if` is an expression too, which is why Rust has no ternary operator: `if v < lo { lo } else { v }` is the value. Both branches must have the same type, and the condition must be a `bool`. C's habit of testing an integer, `if (flags & MASK)`, is a type error; write `flags & MASK != 0`. Unlike C, `&` binds tighter than `!=` in Rust, so that expression means what it says.

The semicolon is significant. `x + 1` at the end of a block is the block's value; `x + 1;` is a statement that discards it, and the block then evaluates to `()`, the unit type. In a function that promises `u32`, that is error `E0308`, and rustc's help points at the semicolon to remove. Read semicolons this way and the rule becomes mechanical.

Parameters need full types, and arguments are never converted to fit them: passing an `i32` where a `u32` is expected does not compile. There are no prototypes and no forward declarations; functions in a module can be defined in any order.
writing.exampleCaption: `clamp` is one `if` expression, `sign` mixes an early `return` with a tail `if`, and `is_even` ends with its comparison.
writing.task: Port the commented C functions: `is_leap` applies the Gregorian rule (divisible by 4, except centuries, except every 400th year) and `days_in_february` returns 29 or 28.
writing.success: 2024 and 2000 are leap years, 1900 and 2023 are not, and February has 29 days only in leap years.
writing.question: Why does rustc reject `fn days(leap: bool) -> u32 { if leap { 29 } else { 28 }; }`?
answers: `if` cannot produce a value; use a `match`
The function is missing `return`
The semicolon makes the `if` a statement, so the body evaluates to `()`
writing.feedback: Remove the semicolon and the `if` expression becomes the body's value. The literals take the type `u32` from the signature.

recall.question: What does this print?
recall.answer: `()`. The semicolon after `x * 3` discards the product, so the block has no tail expression and evaluates to the unit value.

recall.question: In C, `flags & MASK == 0` is a classic precedence bug. What does this Rust version print?
recall.answer: `false`. In C, `==` binds tighter than `&`, so the expression computes `flags & (MASK == 0)`. In Rust, `&` binds tighter than comparisons, so this is `(flags & MASK) == 0`, a `bool` that `if` accepts.

bridge.fromCaption: C needs `return`, a nested ternary and an `int` that stands in for a boolean.

contrasts.from: A value comes back only through `return`.

lessons.title: From for(;;) to Ranges

writing.summary: `for` iterates over ranges and collections, `..=` includes the end safely, and `loop` can hand a value out with `break`.
writing.rule: `for` iterates over a range or collection; `a..b` excludes `b`, `a..=b` includes it, and `loop` with `break value` replaces sentinel variables.
writing.explanation:
Rust has no `for (init; cond; step)`. `for` takes anything iterable: a range such as `0..n`, an array, a `Vec` or an iterator chain. The loop variable is a fresh binding in each iteration, and the range is built once before the loop starts. `for x in xs` visits values directly, so there is no index to get wrong; when you need the index as well, `for (i, x) in xs.iter().enumerate()` gives both.

`a..b` is half-open, like `i < b`; `a..=b` is closed, like `i <= b`. The inclusive form matters at type limits. In C, `for (unsigned char i = lo; i <= hi; i++)` never ends when `hi` is 255, because `i` wraps to 0. A Rust port written as `lo..hi + 1` panics in a debug build when `hi + 1` overflows. `lo..=hi` visits 255 and stops, because the range records that it has produced its last element instead of computing `hi + 1`.

Reverse iteration is `.rev()`, which replaces the `for (size_t i = n; i-- > 0;)` idiom that avoids an unsigned underflow. `while cond { }` works as in C. `loop { }` is an unconditional loop, and it is an expression: `break value` ends it and becomes its value, which replaces the sentinel pattern where `first_big = n` means not found.

Labels such as `'outer: for ...` with `break 'outer` replace a `goto` out of nested loops. Most index searches also have iterator methods (`position`, `find`, `any`), but a clear `for` or `loop` is equally idiomatic when it reads better.
writing.exampleCaption: Values instead of indices, an inclusive range, `.rev()` instead of the underflow idiom, and a `loop` whose `break` yields `Some(4)` or `None`.
writing.task: Port the commented C functions: `count_multiples` counts the multiples of `k` in `lo..=hi` (zero when `lo > hi`, and `k` is at least 1), and `first_power_at_least` returns the smallest power of two that is at least `n` (1 for 0 and 1; `n` is at most 2^31).
writing.success: `count_multiples(250, 255, 5)` is 2 without overflow, `count_multiples(7, 3, 2)` is 0, and `first_power_at_least(5)` is 8.
writing.question: What is `total` after `let mut n = 1; let found = loop { if n * n > 20 { break n; } n += 1; }; let total: u32 = (found..=7).sum();`?
answers: It does not compile: `loop` has no value
writing.feedback: `loop` ends with `break n` when `n` is 5, so `found` is 5, and `5..=7` includes 7: 5 + 6 + 7 = 18.

recall.question: Why does `for i in 0..=u8::MAX` terminate while the C loop `for (unsigned char i = 0; i <= 255; i++)` does not?
recall.answer: The C counter wraps from 255 to 0, so `i <= 255` is always true. A Rust `RangeInclusive` records when it has yielded its last element, so it produces 0 through 255 and then stops without ever computing 256.

recall.question: What does this print?
recall.answer: `Some(2) None`. The `loop` breaks with `Some(2)` at the first 4, and `position` runs the same kind of search with an iterator and finds no 9.

bridge.fromCaption: Index loops, an inclusive bound, the `i-- > 0` reverse idiom and a sentinel value that means not found.

contrasts.from: `for (i = 0; i < n; i++)` with an index you manage.
contrasts.rust: `for x in xs` or `for i in 0..n`; the loop variable is a new binding each time.

contrasts.from: `i <= hi` never ends when `hi` is the type's maximum.
contrasts.rust: `lo..=hi` includes `hi` and terminates, even at `u8::MAX`.

contrasts.from: A sentinel such as `n` means not found.
contrasts.rust: `loop { ... break Some(i) ... }` returns the result directly.

depth.misconception: “Rust frees memory with a garbage collector, so cleanup happens at some later time.”
depth.correction: There is no collector. The compiler inserts the drop at a known point: the end of the final owner's scope, or the call to `drop`. That point is visible in the source, exactly where a careful C programmer would have called `free`.

lessons.title: From malloc/free to Ownership

writing.summary: Every heap value in Rust has exactly one owner; passing it by value moves ownership, and the end of the owner's scope frees it exactly once.
writing.rule: One value has one owner; a move transfers ownership and ends the old binding, and the remaining owners drop in reverse declaration order at the end of their scope.
writing.explanation:
In C, ownership of a `malloc` result is a convention written in comments: who frees it, and when. Getting it wrong has three outcomes: a leak, a use after free or a double free. The example's `archive()` frees its argument and the caller frees it again. Nothing in `void archive(char *)` says the pointer is consumed, so the compiler cannot help; AddressSanitizer reports `attempting double-free`, and a plain macOS build is killed by a trap inside `free`.

Rust makes the convention part of the type. `String`, `Vec<T>` and `Box<T>` own their heap memory. A parameter of type `String` takes ownership: after `archive(report)` the value has moved, and any later use of `report` is error `E0382`, borrow of moved value. The value is freed once, by its final owner, when that owner goes out of scope. There is no `free` to call and none to forget on an early return.

A move copies only the handle (pointer, length and capacity) and then treats the source as uninitialised; nothing is deep-copied unless you call `.clone()`. Returning a value moves it out to the caller, which is how a Rust function hands back ownership, like a C function returning a pointer the caller must free.

Cleanup order is defined. At the end of a scope, the remaining locals drop in reverse declaration order, the order a careful `goto cleanup` chain releases resources. The `Drop` trait runs code at that point, so the same mechanism closes files and releases locks. `drop(x)` ends a value early by moving it into a function that does nothing with it.
writing.exampleCaption: `archive` consumes `report`; the three `Noisy` values drop in reverse order (`file`, `lock`, `log`) after `end of main`.
writing.task: Port the commented C function: `take_largest` returns the longest buffer (the first one on a tie) without copying it, drops all the others, and returns `None` for an empty list.
writing.success: The returned `Vec` has the same heap pointer as the buffer it came from, a tie returns the first longest buffer, and an empty list gives `None`.
writing.question: A function declares `let _log = Noisy("log"); let _lock = Noisy("lock"); let _file = Noisy("file");`. In which order do their `Drop` implementations run at its closing brace?
answers: `log`, `lock`, `file`: declaration order
In an unspecified order, as with a garbage collector
`file`, `lock`, `log`: reverse declaration order
None of them run there: names starting with `_` are dropped immediately
writing.feedback: Remaining locals drop in reverse declaration order. A leading underscore only silences the unused-variable warning; `_log` still owns its value until the scope ends.

recall.question: How does a Rust function return ownership of a heap buffer, the way a C function returns a pointer the caller must free?
recall.answer: It returns the owning type by value, such as `Vec<u8>` or `String`. The return moves the handle to the caller, who becomes the owner and frees it by letting it go out of scope. The heap data is not copied.

recall.question: Does this compile? If not, what is the smallest fix?
recall.answer: No: `data` moved into `consume`, so `data.len()` is error `E0382`. Read the length before the call, or change `consume` to borrow (`v: &[u8]`) and call `consume(&data)`.

bridge.fromCaption: `archive()` frees its argument, so the caller's `free` is a double free that AddressSanitizer reports.

contrasts.from: Who calls `free` is a comment-level convention.
contrasts.rust: The owner frees; ownership is in the type: `String`, `Vec<T>`, `Box<T>`.

contrasts.from: Using a pointer after the callee freed it compiles.
contrasts.rust: Using a moved value is error `E0382`.

contrasts.from: Cleanup on every exit path, often `goto cleanup` in reverse order.
contrasts.rust: Locals drop in reverse declaration order on every exit path.

depth.misconception: “A shared reference is just `const T *`.”
depth.correction: `const T *` only stops you writing through that pointer; other code may still change the value. `&T` also guarantees that nothing mutates the value while the borrow is in use (outside interior-mutability types such as `Cell`), which is why the compiler can reject the `push`.

lessons.title: Pointers to References

writing.summary: A reference is a pointer the compiler checks: shared `&T` for reading, or one exclusive `&mut T` for writing, never both at once.
writing.rule: At any point a value has either any number of shared borrows `&T` or exactly one mutable borrow `&mut T`, never both; a borrow lends access without transferring ownership.
writing.explanation:
The C program keeps `int *first` into a dynamic array and then pushes. `realloc` may move the buffer, so `first` can dangle: AddressSanitizer reports `heap-use-after-free`, while a plain build may print the right number by luck. The bug is not the pointer itself but the combination of a reader that keeps a pointer and a writer that changes the buffer it points into.

Rust references are pointers with two rules that the compiler enforces. `&T` is shared: any number may exist, and none of them can mutate the value. It is like `const T *`, plus the guarantee that nobody else mutates the value while the borrow is in use. `&mut T` is exclusive: while it is in use, no other reference to the value may be used, which is what C's `restrict` promises and never checks. `v.push(2)` needs `&mut v`, so with `first = &v[0]` still in use, rustc reports `E0502`.

A borrow lasts until its last use, not until the end of the scope. Moving the `println!` above the push, or copying the `i32` out with `let first = v[0];`, removes the conflict. References are never null and always point at a live value, so the defensive `if (!p) return -1;` at the top of a C function disappears for references; `Option<&T>` is the type when absence is possible.

Borrowing is also how a function reads data without taking ownership: `fn sum(values: &[i32])` reads the caller's vector and leaves it with the caller. The aliasing bug in the challenge's C original, `append_doubled(v, v->data, v->len)`, cannot be written in Rust: a `&mut dst` and a `&dst` in the same call are rejected.
writing.exampleCaption: The value is copied out before `push`, and `sum` borrows `v` for reading only, so the later `push` is allowed.
writing.task: Port the commented C function: `append_doubled` pushes twice each value of `src` onto the end of `dst` and leaves `src` with the caller.
writing.success: Values are appended after the existing ones, an empty `src` changes nothing, and `src` is still usable after the call.
writing.question: Why does rustc reject `let first = &v[0]; v.push(2); println!("{first}");`?
answers: `v[0]` cannot be borrowed because `i32` is `Copy`
`first` is a shared borrow still in use when `push` needs a mutable borrow of `v`
`push` takes `v` by value, so `v` has moved
Elements of a vector cannot be borrowed; you must use an index
writing.feedback: The shared borrow lives until the `println!`. Print before pushing, or copy the value out with `let first = v[0];`, and the mutable borrow no longer overlaps it.

recall.question: Does this compile?
recall.answer: Yes, and it prints `1` and `[1, 2, 3]`. The shared borrow `first` is last used in the first `println!`, so it has ended before `push` takes `&mut v`. Borrows last until their last use, not until the end of the scope.

recall.question: What contract does `fn fill(dst: &mut [u8], src: &[u8])` state that the C prototype `void fill(uint8_t *dst, const uint8_t *src, size_t n)` does not?
recall.answer: That `dst` and `src` do not overlap and that each is valid for its own length. A caller cannot pass the same buffer as both, because a `&mut` and a `&` to it cannot coexist. In C that takes `restrict` plus documentation, and nothing checks it.

bridge.fromCaption: `first` points into the old buffer after `realloc`; AddressSanitizer reports a heap use after free.

contrasts.from: Any number of `T *` may read and write at the same time.
contrasts.rust: Many `&T` readers or one `&mut T` writer at a time; a conflict is `E0502`.

contrasts.from: `restrict` promises no aliasing, unchecked.
contrasts.rust: `&mut T` is exclusive, and the compiler checks it.

contrasts.from: A pointer may be NULL or dangle; callers check by hand.
contrasts.rust: A reference is never null and cannot outlive its value.

lessons.title: Pointer + Length to Slices

writing.summary: A slice `&[T]` is a pointer and a length in one value, so functions receive their bounds and every index is checked.
writing.rule: A slice borrows a contiguous range of another value's elements; it allocates nothing, and indexing past its length panics instead of reading out of bounds.
writing.explanation:
C arrays decay to pointers at a function boundary, so the length has to travel separately and nothing ties the two together. Inside `max_in`, `sizeof xs` is the size of a pointer, which clang flags with `-Wsizeof-array-argument`, and the `i <= n` off-by-one reads one element past the array: AddressSanitizer reports a `stack-buffer-overflow`.

A Rust slice `&[i32]` is a fat pointer: the address and the length together. `xs.len()` is always right, and `xs[i]` checks `i < len` and panics with `index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 3` instead of reading the neighbour. When an index may be out of range, `xs.get(i)` returns an `Option`. Arrays, vectors and other slices all coerce to `&[T]`, so one function serves all of them.

Slicing creates a view, not a copy: `&xs[1..]`, `xs.split_at(mid)` and `xs.windows(2)` borrow the same memory with different bounds. A function that returns a `&[i32]` derived from its `&[i32]` argument is returning a range of the caller's data, and the compiler ties the result's validity to that input, so it cannot outlive the buffer. `&str` is the same idea for UTF-8 text.

Bounds checks are cheap and are often removed when the compiler can see the index stays in range, which is common in iterator loops. When profiling shows a real cost, iterate instead of indexing, or slice once up front so the later indexes are provably in bounds.
writing.exampleCaption: `max_in` takes a slice, so the length cannot be wrong; an empty slice gives `None`, and `get(3)` is `None` instead of a read past the end.
writing.task: Port the commented C function: `longest_run` returns the longest run of equal neighbouring values as a subslice of `xs`, the first one on a tie, and an empty slice for empty input.
writing.success: `[5, 5, 1, 7, 7, 7]` gives `[7, 7, 7]` even though that run ends the slice, a tie returns the first run, and the result points into the input.
writing.question: What does the return type of `fn longest_run(xs: &[i32]) -> &[i32]` promise?
answers: A new heap-allocated copy of the run
A pointer that may outlive `xs`
A fixed-size array of the run's length
A borrowed view into `xs`, valid only while `xs` is
writing.feedback: With one reference input, the result borrows from it: a range of the caller's elements, with no allocation, tied to the input's lifetime.

recall.question: What does this print, and does it panic?
recall.answer: `0 None Some(10)`, without a panic. A range that starts at the length is valid and gives an empty slice; only an index such as `xs[3]`, or a range that starts past the length, panics.

recall.question: Why can one function `fn total(xs: &[u32]) -> u32` accept an array, a `Vec` and part of either?
recall.answer: `&[u32; N]` and `&Vec<u32>` coerce to `&[u32]`, and `&v[a..b]` already is a slice. Every caller passes a pointer and a length the compiler knows, unlike a C `const unsigned *` whose length is passed and trusted separately.

bridge.fromCaption: `sizeof` on an array parameter gives the pointer size, and `i <= n` reads past the end, which AddressSanitizer reports as a stack buffer overflow.

contrasts.from: Pointer and length are separate arguments that can disagree.
contrasts.rust: `&[T]` carries both; `len()` is always the real length.

contrasts.from: `xs[n]` reads past the end without a check.
contrasts.rust: `xs[n]` panics; `xs.get(n)` returns `None`.

contrasts.from: Arrays decay; `sizeof` inside the callee is the pointer size.
contrasts.rust: Arrays and `Vec`s coerce to `&[T]` and keep their length.
