lessons.title: Dangling Pointers and Lifetimes

writing.summary: A lifetime names how long a reference is valid, so the compiler rejects the dangling pointer that a C comment could only warn about.
writing.rule: A lifetime annotation relates the output borrow to the input borrows; it never extends how long any value lives.
writing.explanation:
A C function that returns a pointer into one of its arguments documents the relationship in a comment: the result points into `a` or `b`. The caller in the example frees `b` and then prints the result, and AddressSanitizer reports `heap-use-after-free`. Nothing in `const char *longer(const char *, const char *)` carries the fact that matters.

Rust writes that fact into the signature. `fn longer<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str` says the result borrows from the inputs and may be used only while both borrows are valid. The compiler then checks every caller: using `result` after `b` has been dropped is error `E0597`, `b` does not live long enough.

Most signatures need no annotation, because of elision. With exactly one reference input, the output borrows from it: `fn first_word(line: &str) -> &str`. With a `&self` method, the output borrows from `self`. With two reference inputs and a reference output there is no default, so rustc asks with `E0106`, missing lifetime specifier, because it cannot know which input you return.

An annotation describes a relationship. It does not make anything live longer and cannot turn a dangling pointer into a valid one; returning a reference to a local, like `return buf;` for a stack array, is still rejected. Choose lifetimes that state what the code really does: if the result only ever points into `line`, only `line` should share `'a`. Tying `prefix` to it as well would force callers to keep `prefix` alive for no reason.
writing.exampleCaption: `longer` needs `'a` because it has two reference inputs; `first_word` has one, so elision ties its result to `line`.
writing.task: Port the commented C functions, keeping the lifetimes in the starter: `after_prefix` returns the rest of `line` after `prefix`, or `None`, and borrows only from `line`; `longer` returns the input with more bytes, `a` on a tie.
writing.success: The result of `after_prefix` stays usable after `prefix` is dropped, a line shorter than its prefix gives `None` instead of a panic, and a tie in `longer` returns `a`.
writing.question: Why does `fn longer(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str` need a lifetime annotation when `fn first_word(line: &str) -> &str` does not?
answers: With two reference inputs, the compiler cannot tell which one the result borrows from
Functions that compare lengths always need annotations
The annotation keeps `a` and `b` alive until the end of `main`
A `&str` result always needs `'static`
writing.feedback: Elision covers one reference input, and `&self` methods. With two, you state the relationship; the annotation constrains callers and never extends a value's life.

recall.question: Does annotating the return type as `&'static str` make this compile?
recall.answer: No. `'static` claims the text lives for the whole program, but `s` is dropped when `make` returns, so rustc rejects `&s` with `E0515`, cannot return a reference to a local variable. Return the `String` itself to hand over ownership.

recall.question: Which inputs should share `'a` in a function that returns the part of `line` after `prefix`, and why does it matter to callers?
recall.answer: Only `line`, because the result is part of `line` and never of `prefix`. `fn after_prefix<'a>(line: &'a str, prefix: &str) -> Option<&'a str>` lets a caller drop `prefix` and keep using the result; tying `prefix` to `'a` would force it to stay alive as long as the result.

bridge.fromCaption: The result points into `b`; after `free(b)`, printing it is a heap use after free that AddressSanitizer reports.

contrasts.from: Which argument a returned pointer refers to lives in a comment.
contrasts.rust: The signature's lifetimes say it, and the compiler checks every caller.

contrasts.from: Freeing the source while a pointer into it remains compiles.
contrasts.rust: Using a borrow after its source is dropped is error `E0597`.

contrasts.from: Returning the address of a local is only a warning.
contrasts.rust: Returning a reference to a local is always an error.

traceSteps.title: Classify each field
traceSteps.detail: Integers and plain structs are `Copy`; any `Vec`, `String`, `Box` or file handle makes the type move-only.

traceSteps.detail: Derive `Copy` for plain data you would pass by value in C; derive only `Clone` for types that own resources.

lessons.title: Struct Copies: Copy and Clone

writing.summary: Rust copies a struct implicitly only when it is plain data marked `Copy`; anything that owns a resource moves, and a deep copy is an explicit `.clone()`.
writing.rule: `Copy` permits implicit bitwise duplication for types that own no resources; `Clone` is an explicit duplication whose cost depends on the type.
writing.explanation:
C struct assignment always copies bytes. For `struct point` that is exactly right. For `struct path`, which holds a pointer, `b = a` copies the pointer and not the points: the two structs share one buffer, a write through `b` changes `a`, and freeing both is a double free, which AddressSanitizer reports.

Rust splits this in two. A type can be `Copy` only if all of its fields are `Copy`, which means it owns nothing: integers, `char`, `bool`, shared references, and structs or tuples made of those. Assignment and by-value calls then duplicate the bytes and the source stays usable, exactly like C's `struct point`. `#[derive(Clone, Copy)]` opts a type in.

A type with a `Vec`, `String` or `Box` field cannot be `Copy`; deriving it is error `E0204`. Assigning such a value moves it: still a bitwise copy of the handle, but the source becomes unusable, so one buffer keeps one owner. When you really want a second, independent buffer, call `.clone()`. The cost is visible at the call site, the opposite of a C struct assignment that may quietly make a shallow copy.

`Clone` is a trait you derive or implement. For `Vec<Point>` it allocates and copies every element; for `Rc<T>` it only increments a count. Reading `.clone()` tells you that a duplication happens, and the type tells you its price.
writing.exampleCaption: `Point` is `Copy`, so `p` survives `let mut q = p`; `Path` owns a `Vec`, so `b` is an explicit `clone` and `let c = a` is a move.
writing.task: Port the commented C functions: `translated` returns a new `Path` with every point moved by `dx` and `dy` and leaves the input unchanged; `first_point` returns a copy of the first point, or `None`.
writing.success: `translated` returns new points while the original `Path` is unchanged, and `first_point` returns `Some(Point)`, or `None` for an empty path.
writing.question: Why can `Point { x: i32, y: i32 }` derive `Copy` while `Path { points: Vec<Point> }` cannot?
answers: `Copy` is limited to structs with at most two fields
`Vec<Point>` is too large to copy
A bitwise copy of a `Vec` would make two owners of one heap buffer, so `Vec` is not `Copy`
`Path` would need `#[repr(C)]` first
writing.feedback: `Copy` requires every field to be `Copy`. `Vec` owns heap memory, so `Path` gets `Clone` for explicit deep copies and moves otherwise.

recall.question: Does this compile, and what does it print?
recall.answer: Yes: `Rgb(1, 2, 3) Rgb(9, 2, 3)`. `Rgb` is `Copy`, so `let mut b = a` duplicates the bytes and `a` stays usable and unchanged.

recall.question: What is the difference in cost between `rc.clone()` on an `Rc<Vec<u8>>` and `v.clone()` on a `Vec<u8>`?
recall.answer: `rc.clone()` increments a reference count and shares the same vector; `v.clone()` allocates a new buffer and copies every byte. Both are explicit `.clone()` calls; the type tells you which cost you pay.

bridge.fromCaption: Struct assignment copies the pointer, so `b` and `a` share one buffer, and freeing both is a double free.

contrasts.from: Struct assignment always copies bytes, pointers included.
contrasts.rust: Only `Copy` types copy implicitly; other types move to a single owner.

contrasts.from: A shallow copy of a struct with a pointer creates two owners.
contrasts.rust: A type that owns a `Vec` or `String` cannot be `Copy` (`E0204`).

contrasts.from: A deep copy is a hand-written function.
contrasts.rust: `.clone()` is the explicit deep copy, visible at every call site.

lessons.title: Structs and Methods

writing.summary: Methods live in an `impl` block, and the receiver (`&self`, `&mut self` or `self`) states what C expressed with `const` pointers and comments.
writing.rule: `&self` reads, `&mut self` modifies, and `self` consumes the value; read a method's receiver to learn its ownership effect.
writing.explanation:
C groups behaviour by naming convention: `counter_hit(struct counter *)`, `counter_hits(const struct counter *)` and `counter_finish(...)`, with a comment that says not to use the counter afterwards. The `const` documents read-only access, and the do-not-use-after rule is not checked at all: the example calls `counter_hit` after `counter_finish`, and it compiles.

In Rust, functions associated with a type go in `impl Counter { ... }`. The receiver is the first parameter and carries the contract. `fn hits(&self)` is a shared borrow, like a `const` pointer with the stronger guarantee that nobody mutates the value during the call. `fn hit(&mut self)` is an exclusive borrow. `fn finish(self)` takes the value itself: after `c.finish()`, `c` has moved, and calling `c.hit()` is error `E0382`.

Method calls borrow automatically: `c.hit()` means `Counter::hit(&mut c)`, so there is no `&` at the call site and no `->` operator; `.` works through references. A function without a receiver, such as `Counter::new`, is an associated function, the idiomatic replacement for `counter_init`, and it returns the initialised value instead of filling memory the caller provides.

Fields are private to the module unless marked `pub`, so the invariants behind methods such as `spend` and `remaining` can only be broken by code inside that module. That replaces the opaque-pointer pattern, `struct budget;` in the header, for most C APIs.
writing.exampleCaption: `hit` takes `&mut self`, `hits` takes `&self`, and `finish` takes `self`, so the counter cannot be used after it.
writing.task: Port the commented C budget: `spend` refuses an amount larger than what remains and then changes nothing, `remaining` reports the rest, and `close` consumes the budget and returns the amount spent. Avoid the C version's wrapping sum.
writing.success: Spending exactly the remainder succeeds, a refused spend leaves the state unchanged, and `spend(u32::MAX)` is refused without overflowing.
writing.question: Which receiver should `close` take so that using the budget after `budget.close()` is a compile error?
answers: `&self`
`self`
`&mut self`
`&'static self`
writing.feedback: `self` moves the value into the method. The caller's binding has moved, so any later method call on it is `E0382`.

recall.question: Which receivers match these C prototypes: `size_t buf_len(const struct buf *)`, `void buf_push(struct buf *, uint8_t)` and `uint8_t *buf_into_raw(struct buf *)`, after which the buffer must not be used?
recall.answer: `fn len(&self) -> usize`, `fn push(&mut self, byte: u8)` and `fn into_raw(self) -> ...`. The `into_` prefix is the Rust naming convention for a method that consumes `self`.

recall.question: Why is `budget.spend(5)` allowed on `let mut budget` but not on `let budget`?
recall.answer: `spend` takes `&mut self`, so the call borrows `budget` mutably, and that needs a `mut` binding. `remaining(&self)` works on either.

bridge.fromCaption: The receiver contract is a naming convention plus `const`; using the counter after `counter_finish` compiles.

contrasts.from: `const struct counter *` documents read-only access.
contrasts.rust: `&self` is a shared borrow; no one mutates the value during the call.

contrasts.from: Do not use the counter after `counter_finish` is a comment.
contrasts.rust: `fn finish(self)` consumes the value; a later use is `E0382`.

contrasts.from: `counter_init(&c)` fills memory the caller provides.
contrasts.rust: `Counter::new()` returns an initialised value; `c.hit()` borrows automatically.

lessons.title: Tagged Unions to Enums

writing.summary: A Rust `enum` is a tagged union whose tag and payload cannot disagree, and `match` must handle every variant.
writing.rule: `match` must be exhaustive: every variant has to be handled, and an arm with a guard does not count as covering its pattern.
writing.explanation:
The C tagged union is a discipline: an `enum` tag next to a `union`, and every reader checks the tag before touching the matching member. Nothing enforces it. `{EV_CLICK, .as.key = 'q'}` compiles, reading the wrong member is not diagnosed, and a `default:` arm silently absorbs kinds added later, with no `-Wswitch` warning because a default exists.

A Rust `enum` makes the pairing part of the type. `Key(char)`, `Click { x, y }` and `Quit` are variants, each with its own data, and the only way to reach that data is to match the variant; you cannot build a `Click` that holds a `char`. The compiler chooses the tag and the layout, and uses invalid bit patterns (niches) where it can, which is why `Option<&T>` is the size of a pointer.

`match` is a `switch` that destructures and is checked for completeness. Leave a variant out and the program does not compile (`E0004`, non-exhaustive patterns), so adding a variant produces a list of every place that must handle it. A `_` arm opts back into C's `default:` behaviour; use it only when new variants really should fall through. Arms never fall through to each other, so there is no `break` to forget.

Arms can bind fields (`Event::Click { x, y }`), match literals and ranges, and add a guard such as `if *x < 0`. A guard narrows its arm, but exhaustiveness checking ignores guard conditions, so a guarded arm still needs an unguarded arm, or a wildcard, for the same variant. `match` is also an expression whose arms produce one type, which replaces a `switch` that assigns a variable in every case.
writing.exampleCaption: Each variant carries only its own data; the guarded `Click` arm is backed by an unguarded one, and the `match` lists every variant.
writing.task: Port the commented C `area`, including the forgotten triangle: return the area rounded down for every variant without overflowing, and make `is_degenerate` return true when any dimension is zero.
writing.success: `Square { side: u32::MAX }` gives the exact `u64` area, a 3 × 3 triangle gives 4, and zero-sized shapes are degenerate.
writing.question: In the practice code every variant appears in the `match`. Why does rustc still reject it?
answers: The `Click` arm has a guard, and guards do not count toward exhaustiveness, so a click with a negative coordinate is unhandled
`match` needs a `default` arm, like a C `switch`
Struct-like variants cannot have guards
`Quit` carries no data, so it must be listed first
writing.feedback: Add an unguarded `Event::Click { .. }` arm after the guarded one. The compiler checks patterns, not the conditions in guards.

recall.question: Why is a `_ => ...` arm in a `match` over your own enum often a mistake?
recall.answer: It turns off the check that makes enums safer than a C `switch`: a variant added later falls into `_` silently instead of producing `E0004` at every `match` that must handle it. List the variants unless falling through really is the intended behaviour.

recall.question: What does this print?
recall.answer: `small large huge`. Arms are tried in order: `Large(3)` fails the guard and reaches the unguarded `Large(_)` arm, while `Large(12)` matches the guarded arm first.

bridge.fromCaption: The tag and the union member are kept in sync by hand, and `default:` absorbs any kind added later.

contrasts.from: Tag and union member can disagree; nothing checks the pairing.
contrasts.rust: A variant and its data are one value; the data is reached only by matching.

contrasts.from: `default:` silently handles kinds added later.
contrasts.rust: A missing variant is error `E0004`; `_` is an explicit opt-in.

contrasts.from: Cases fall through unless you write `break`.
contrasts.rust: Arms never fall through, and each `match` arm is an expression.

lessons.title: NULL and errno to Option and Result

writing.summary: Absence is `Option<T>` and failure is `Result<T, E>`, both in the return type, so a caller cannot use the value without handling the other case.
writing.rule: Return `Option<T>` when a value may simply be absent and `Result<T, E>` when the caller needs to know why an operation failed.
writing.explanation:
C signals trouble out of band. A pointer return uses `NULL` for absent, as `getenv` and `strchr` do. An integer return reserves a value such as `-1` and leaves the reason in `errno`, which must be cleared before calls such as `strtol` and read before the next library call can overwrite it. In the example, `-1` means failure and is also a valid parsed value, so the caller has to inspect `errno` to tell them apart.

Rust puts both into the type. `Option<T>` is `Some(value)` or `None`; `Result<T, E>` is `Ok(value)` or `Err(error)`. You cannot use the `T` inside without saying what happens in the other case: `let port: u16 = find_port(&config);` is error `E0308`, because the function returns `Option<u16>`. References are never null, so `Option<&T>` is the nullable pointer, with the same size as a plain reference.

Choose by what the caller needs. A lookup that may find nothing returns `Option`. Parsing external text, I/O and anything with several distinct causes of failure return `Result` with an error type that names them, often an `enum` such as `PortError`. The `?` operator replaces the `if (rc < 0) return rc;` ladder: it returns the error to the caller and unwraps the success value.

`unwrap()` and `expect(...)` turn `None` or `Err` into a panic. They belong in tests, examples and states that are truly impossible; for expected failures such as invalid input, return the `Result`. Unlike `errno`, an error value cannot be overwritten by a later call, and it travels with the result it describes.
writing.exampleCaption: `parse_count` returns its error as a value, `-1` parses as `Ok(-1)`, an unset variable is `None`, and `?` passes the first failure up.
writing.task: Port the commented C `parse_port`: return `Empty` for empty text, `NotANumber` if any character is not an ASCII digit (no sign and no spaces, stricter than `strtol`), `OutOfRange` for 0 or anything above 65535, and the port otherwise.
writing.success: `"8080"` parses, `"+80"` is `NotANumber`, and `"0"`, `"65536"` and a 20-digit number are `OutOfRange`.
writing.question: A C lookup returns `NULL` when a key is missing, and a config parser returns `-1` with `errno` set when a line is malformed. Which Rust return types fit those two cases?
answers: `Result<T, ()>` for both
`Option<T>` for both, with `None` for any problem
`*const V` for the lookup and `i32` plus a global error code for the parser
`Option<&V>` for the lookup and `Result<Config, ParseError>` for the parser
writing.feedback: A missing key is ordinary absence. A malformed line is a failure the caller should be able to explain or report, so it carries an error value.

recall.question: What does `?` do in this function, and what does it return for `"7"` and for `"x"`?
recall.answer: On `Err`, `?` returns that error from `double` immediately; on `Ok`, it unwraps the number. It prints `Ok(14) Err(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit })`.

recall.question: Is `Option<&T>` bigger than a nullable C pointer?
recall.code: println!("{} {}", size_of::<&u64>(), size_of::<Option<&u64>>());
recall.answer: No: on a 64-bit target this prints `8 8`. A reference is never null, so the compiler uses the null bit pattern for `None`. You get the representation of a nullable pointer with a check the compiler enforces.

bridge.fromCaption: `-1` is both the failure marker and a valid result, so the caller must clear and inspect `errno`; `getenv` returns `NULL` when the variable is absent.

contrasts.from: `NULL` means absent, and dereferencing it unchecked compiles.
contrasts.rust: `Option<T>` must be matched before the value can be used.

contrasts.from: `-1` plus `errno` signals failure out of band.
contrasts.rust: `Result<T, E>` carries the reason in the return value.

contrasts.from: `if (rc < 0) return rc;` after every call.
contrasts.rust: `?` returns the error early and unwraps the success value.

lessons.title: char Arrays to Strings

writing.summary: A Rust `String` is an owned, growable UTF-8 buffer with a stored length and no NUL, and text is never indexed by a single integer position.
writing.rule: `len()` counts UTF-8 bytes and `chars()` yields Unicode scalar values; indexing a string by an integer is forbidden because a byte offset may fall inside a character.
writing.explanation:
C strings are byte arrays ended by a NUL. Their length is a scan (`strlen`), their capacity is whatever the declaration said, and every copy (`strcpy`, `strcat`) trusts the destination to be big enough. In the example, `"Margaret"` needs 9 bytes in an 8-byte array: clang warns at compile time that the `strcpy` will always overflow, and AddressSanitizer reports the `stack-buffer-overflow` when it runs.

`String` owns a heap buffer and stores its length and capacity, so `len()` is O(1), there is no terminator, and `push_str` grows the buffer as needed. `&str` is a borrowed view of UTF-8 bytes, a pointer and a length like a slice; string literals are `&'static str`. Because a Rust string may contain interior NUL bytes and has no terminator, C APIs use `CString` and `CStr` from `std::ffi` instead.

Rust strings are always valid UTF-8, and that changes how you count. `"café".len()` is 5, the bytes, the same as `strlen`; `chars().count()` is 4 Unicode scalar values. A character a person sees can consist of several scalar values, so neither number is always what a reader would count. `toupper` works on bytes and leaves `é` alone; `to_uppercase()` maps Unicode and gives `CAFÉ`.

`word[0]` does not compile (`E0277`): indexing by an integer would have to pick a byte or a character, and a byte may be half of one. Byte ranges are allowed, as in `&word[0..3]`, but a range that ends inside a character panics. Code that cuts text to a byte budget therefore uses `is_char_boundary`, or `get(range)`, which returns `None` instead of panicking.
writing.exampleCaption: Byte length versus character count, a Unicode-aware uppercase, `get` refusing a cut inside `é`, and a `String` that grows instead of overflowing.
writing.task: Port the commented C helpers: `truncate_at_boundary` returns the longest prefix of at most `max_bytes` bytes that ends on a character boundary, and `initials` returns the uppercase first character of each whitespace-separated word.
writing.success: `truncate_at_boundary("café", 4)` is `"caf"` without a panic, and `initials("élodie durand")` is `"ÉD"`.
writing.question: `strlen("café")` is 5 in a UTF-8 C program. What do `"café".len()` and `"café".chars().count()` return in Rust?
answers: 4 and 4
5 and 4
6 and 5, counting a terminator
4 and 5
writing.feedback: `len()` counts UTF-8 bytes, so `é` contributes two, and there is no terminator. `chars()` yields four scalar values.

recall.question: What happens when this runs?
recall.answer: It prints `None`, because byte 4 is inside the two-byte `é`, and then the slice `&word[0..4]` panics with `byte index 4 is not a char boundary`. Use `get` or `is_char_boundary` when the offset comes from a byte budget.

recall.question: Why does Rust pass a `CString` rather than a `&str` to a C function that takes `const char *`?
recall.answer: A `&str` is not NUL-terminated and may contain interior NUL bytes. `CString::new` rejects interior NULs and appends the terminator, and `as_ptr()` then gives the `const char *` that C expects.

bridge.fromCaption: `strlen` counts bytes, `toupper` misses `é`, and copying a 9-byte string into `char[8]` overflows the buffer.

contrasts.from: Length is a scan to the NUL; capacity is fixed by the declaration.
contrasts.rust: `String` stores its length and capacity and grows as needed.

contrasts.from: Bytes and characters are both `char`.
contrasts.rust: `len()` counts UTF-8 bytes; `chars()` yields Unicode scalar values.

contrasts.from: `s[i]` reads byte `i`.
contrasts.rust: `s[i]` does not compile; `&s[a..b]` must fall on character boundaries.

lessons.title: Headers and make to Cargo

writing.summary: Cargo replaces headers and Makefiles: the crate is the unit of compilation, modules are found from `mod` declarations, and items are private until marked `pub`.
writing.rule: Items are private to their module unless marked `pub`; `src/main.rs` is the default binary target and `src/lib.rs` the library target.
writing.explanation:
A C project splits declarations into headers, definitions into `.c` files, and the build graph into a Makefile that must list which object depends on which header. Every function that is not `static` has external linkage and is visible to any translation unit that declares it, and a missing header dependency in the Makefile gives you a stale build that links old code.

In Rust the unit of compilation is the crate, a tree of modules compiled together, not a single file. There are no headers: `mod geometry;` in `src/main.rs` or `src/lib.rs` tells the compiler to load `src/geometry.rs` (or `src/geometry/mod.rs`), and the compiler reads the definitions directly. Because rustc sees the whole crate and Cargo records which files each build read, there is no dependency list to keep in sync.

Visibility is the reverse of C. Everything is private to its module by default, like `static` at file scope, and `pub` is the export. Calling a private function from another module is error `E0603`. `pub(crate)` exports an item to the whole crate but not to its users, which is what most internal C helpers wanted to be.

Cargo's conventions replace the Makefile. `Cargo.toml` names the package and its dependencies, `src/main.rs` is the default binary and `src/lib.rs` the library. A package may have both, in which case `main.rs` uses the library through the package name, like any outside user would. `cargo build` compiles, `cargo run` builds and runs, `cargo check` type-checks without generating code, and `cargo test` runs the tests.
writing.exampleCaption: One file stands in for `src/geometry.rs`: `clamp_positive` is private to the module, and only `pub fn area` is visible to `main`.
writing.task: Work out how `main.rs` reaches a function in `src/geometry.rs` when a package has both `src/lib.rs` and `src/main.rs`, then fix the practice program's call to a private function.
writing.success: You can name the two declarations that make `geometry::area` callable from `main.rs`, `pub mod geometry;` in `lib.rs` and `pub fn area`, and the path `main.rs` uses.
writing.question: A package named `shapes` has `src/lib.rs`, `src/main.rs` and `src/geometry.rs`. How does `main.rs` call `area` from `geometry.rs`?
answers: `#include "geometry.rs"` at the top of `main.rs`
Mark `area` as `extern` so that the linker finds it
`lib.rs` declares `pub mod geometry;`, `area` is `pub`, and `main.rs` calls `shapes::geometry::area`
`main.rs` calls `geometry::area` directly, because both files are in `src/`
writing.feedback: Files are not compilation units: `mod` puts `geometry.rs` into the library crate, `pub` exports it, and the binary crate uses the library through the package name.

recall.question: What does `pub(crate)` give you that C's `static` and default external linkage do not?
recall.answer: A middle level of visibility: the item is usable from every module in the crate but not by users of the crate. C has file-private (`static`) and global (everything else), with no boundary at the library.

recall.question: Which Cargo command replaces running `make` just to see whether the code compiles, and why is it faster?
recall.answer: `cargo check`. It runs the compiler's analysis, including type and borrow checking, without generating machine code, so it is the quickest way to see every compiler error.

contrasts.from: Functions are exported unless declared `static`.
contrasts.rust: Items are private unless marked `pub`; a call to a private item is `E0603`.

contrasts.from: Headers repeat declarations; the Makefile lists dependencies.
contrasts.rust: `mod name;` loads `name.rs`, and Cargo tracks what each build read.

contrasts.from: The translation unit is one `.c` file.
contrasts.rust: The crate is the unit: `src/main.rs` for a binary, `src/lib.rs` for a library.

lessons.title: unsafe, Raw Pointers and FFI

writing.summary: Raw pointers, `unsafe` and `extern "C"` let Rust do what C does, and `unsafe` marks exactly where you take over the proof that the compiler cannot do.
writing.rule: Creating a raw pointer is safe; dereferencing it needs `unsafe`, which is a claim that the pointer is valid, aligned, initialised and correctly aliased, not a switch that turns the checks off.
writing.explanation:
Everything in C is the programmer's proof: the pointer is valid, `n` is the real length, nothing else writes meanwhile. Rust keeps that model available. `*const T` and `*mut T` are raw pointers with no lifetime and no aliasing guarantees, and creating one with `as` or `as_ptr()` is safe, because nothing can go wrong until it is used.

Dereferencing a raw pointer, calling an `unsafe fn` (every foreign function is one), accessing a mutable `static` and reading a `union` field need an `unsafe` block; implementing an `unsafe trait` needs `unsafe impl`. Inside the block the compiler still applies every other rule, including type checks, borrow checks and slice bounds checks. What `unsafe` adds is your claim that the invariants it cannot check hold. Write that claim down: a `# Safety` section on an `unsafe fn` lists the caller's obligations, and a `// SAFETY:` comment on a block says why they are met.

The common pattern is a thin unsafe edge around safe code. `slice::from_raw_parts(ptr, len)` turns a C pointer and length into a `&[i32]`, and from then on indexing is checked again. The obligations of that one call are exactly what the C contract said in prose: non-null, aligned, `len` initialised elements, and no mutation while the slice is in use.

For FFI, `#[repr(C)]` gives a struct C's field order and padding for the target, so `Pair` is 8 bytes like `struct pair`; without it, Rust may reorder fields. It does not make the field types themselves C-compatible or make pointers valid. In edition 2024, foreign declarations go in an `unsafe extern "C" { ... }` block, and a Rust function exported to C is an `extern "C" fn` marked `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]`. Calling C needs `unsafe` because the compiler cannot check the declaration against the C side.
writing.exampleCaption: `#[repr(C)]` keeps C's layout, `sum_i32` turns a pointer and a length into a slice inside one documented `unsafe` block, and `abs` comes from the C library.
writing.task: Decide which line of the quiz needs `unsafe` and what that block asserts, then fix the practice program without changing what it prints.
writing.success: You can name the one operation that needs `unsafe` and the facts the block asserts about the pointer: non-null, aligned, pointing to a live, initialised value.
writing.question: In `let p = &x as *const i32; let q = p.wrapping_add(1); let v = *p; println!("{p:?} {q:?}");`, which operation needs `unsafe`, and what does the block claim?
answers: `*p`: the block claims `p` is non-null, aligned and points to a live, initialised `i32`
Creating `p`: a raw pointer turns off the borrow checker
`p.wrapping_add(1)` and `*p`: all raw pointer arithmetic is unsafe
Every line: inside `unsafe` the compiler skips its checks
writing.feedback: Creating a raw pointer, offsetting it with `wrapping_add` and printing it are safe. Only the dereference relies on facts the compiler cannot check.

recall.question: What must be true for `unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr, len) }` to be sound when `ptr` comes from C?
recall.answer: `ptr` is non-null and aligned, points to `len` consecutive initialised values of the element type within one allocation, the total size is at most `isize::MAX` bytes, and nothing mutates that memory while the slice is in use. These are the obligations in the function's `# Safety` documentation.

recall.question: Why is this `Header` not safe to pass to a C function that expects `struct header { uint16_t len; uint8_t kind; }`?
recall.answer: Without `#[repr(C)]`, Rust guarantees neither field order nor padding, so the layout may differ from the C struct. Add `#[repr(C)]` and compare `size_of::<Header>()` with `sizeof(struct header)`.

bridge.fromCaption: The pointer-and-length contract and the struct layout are stated only in comments.

contrasts.from: Every pointer dereference is trusted.
contrasts.rust: Only operations inside `unsafe` are trusted; everything else stays checked.

contrasts.from: The contract of `(ptr, n)` is prose.
contrasts.rust: `# Safety` docs and `// SAFETY:` comments mark the proof at each `unsafe`.

contrasts.from: Struct layout follows the C ABI.
contrasts.rust: Rust may reorder fields; `#[repr(C)]` requests C layout.

depth.correction: `Mutex<T>` wraps the data itself. Code that does not hold a guard has no path to the `T`, so forgetting to lock does not compile, and the guard makes forgetting to unlock impossible.

lessons.title: pthreads to std::thread

writing.summary: Rust threads are the same OS threads as pthreads, but a `Mutex` owns the data it protects and the compiler rejects data races.
writing.rule: `thread::spawn` needs a `Send + 'static` closure, so captures are moved in; shared state goes in `Arc<Mutex<T>>`, and the lock guard unlocks when it drops.
writing.explanation:
With pthreads, the relationship between a mutex and the data it protects is a convention: `lock` guards `safe_hits` because everyone agrees to lock first. Nothing stops the unprotected `hits++`, which ThreadSanitizer reports as a `data race`, and forgetting `pthread_mutex_unlock` on one early return deadlocks the next thread that locks.

`std::thread::spawn` starts an OS thread and returns a `JoinHandle`; `join()` waits for it and returns the thread's result. The closure must be `'static`, because the thread may outlive the function that spawned it, so borrowing a local is rejected with `E0373`, closure may outlive the current function. `move` makes the closure own its captures instead. When threads only need to borrow locals for a bounded time, `thread::scope` guarantees they are joined before the scope ends and lets them borrow.

`Mutex<T>` contains the `T`. The only way to reach the value is `lock()`, which returns a guard that dereferences to the data and unlocks when it is dropped, at the end of its statement or block, including on an early return or a panic. `Arc<T>` is an atomically reference-counted pointer, so each thread can own a handle to the same mutex; the non-atomic `Rc<T>` is not `Send`, and the compiler refuses to move it into a thread.

Those checks come from two marker traits. `Send` means a value can be moved to another thread, and `Sync` means `&T` can be shared between threads. Types implement them automatically when all their fields do, which is how the compiler proves a safe program free of data races. Deadlocks and lock ordering remain your design problem, as in C.
writing.exampleCaption: Each thread owns a clone of the `Arc`, the counter lives inside the `Mutex`, and each guard unlocks at the end of its statement.
writing.task: Explain where the quiz program unlocks its mutex and why the closure needs `move`, then fix the practice program with an `Arc<Mutex<u64>>`.
writing.success: You can point to the statement where each guard drops and explain why a spawned thread cannot borrow a local of `main`.
writing.question: In `let total = Arc::clone(&total); thread::spawn(move || { let mut n = total.lock().unwrap(); *n += 1; });`, where is the mutex unlocked, and why is `move` needed?
answers: At `join()`; `move` is optional because `Arc` is thread-safe
Only when `drop(total)` is called; `move` copies the counter into the thread
After the loop that spawns the threads; `move` makes the closure `Copy`
When the guard `n` drops at the end of the closure; `move` gives the thread its own `Arc`, because the thread may outlive the locals of the function that spawned it
writing.feedback: The guard is a local of the closure and unlocks when it goes out of scope. Without `move`, the closure would borrow `total`, and `spawn` requires `'static` captures.

recall.question: Why does rustc refuse to move an `Rc<RefCell<u64>>` into `thread::spawn`?
recall.answer: `Rc` updates its reference count without atomic operations, so two threads cloning or dropping it could corrupt the count. `Rc` is not `Send`, and `spawn` requires a `Send` closure. Use `Arc` for the shared ownership and a `Mutex` or an atomic for the value.

recall.question: When is `thread::scope` a better fit than `thread::spawn`?
recall.answer: When threads only need to borrow local data for a bounded time. Scoped threads are joined before `scope` returns, so they may borrow `left` and `right` without `move` or `Arc`; this prints `3 7`.

bridge.fromCaption: `hits` is shared without a lock, which ThreadSanitizer reports as a data race; `safe_hits` is protected only by convention.

contrasts.from: A mutex protects data by convention.
contrasts.rust: `Mutex<T>` owns the `T`; the data is reachable only through `lock()`.

contrasts.from: `pthread_mutex_unlock` must run on every path.
contrasts.rust: The guard unlocks when it drops, including on early returns.

contrasts.from: Passing `&local` to a thread compiles and may dangle.
contrasts.rust: `spawn` needs `'static`; borrowing a local is `E0373`, so use `move` or `thread::scope`.

lessons.title: Node.js runtime vs compiled Rust

writing.summary: Rust is compiled ahead of time to a native executable: rustc checks types, ownership and borrowing before anything runs, and there is no garbage collector or built-in event loop.
writing.rule: Rust is a compiled, statically typed language without a garbage collector: rustc checks types, ownership and borrowing before the program runs, then produces a native executable.
writing.explanation:
`node app.js` starts a runtime. V8 parses your JavaScript, interprets it and compiles hot functions to machine code while the program runs, and the Node.js process supplies the event loop, the garbage collector and APIs such as `fs`. Every machine that runs the program needs Node.js too. Rust works ahead of time: `rustc`, usually driven by `cargo build`, reads the whole crate, checks it and writes a native executable for one target, such as macOS on Apple silicon or Linux on x86-64, or a WebAssembly module as in the Crabrix app. The result runs without Rust or Node.js installed.

Checking happens before anything runs. rustc verifies types, ownership and borrowing in every function, including branches your tests never reach, and produces no executable while an error remains. The typo in the JavaScript `EUR` branch is a `TypeError` on the day that branch runs; the same typo in Rust is E0599 at build time. There is no separate `tsc` step to skip and no way to run the program anyway.

Two things you take for granted are not built in. There is no garbage collector: each value has an owner and is freed at a known point, which the next lesson shows. There is no event loop either: async code needs a runtime library such as Tokio, chosen by the program. In exchange, a Rust executable has no JIT warm-up, and its memory use follows from the code rather than from collector heuristics.

Static typing in Rust is mostly inferred. You annotate function signatures and struct fields; inside a function most `let` bindings need no annotation, and `let sum: u32 = prices.iter().sum();` needs one only because `sum` can produce several types. The types shape the compiled program: a `u32` occupies four bytes, and adding two of them compiles to an integer addition.
writing.exampleCaption: rustc checked both branches before this ran. The last line names the compile target: `macos aarch64` on an Apple silicon Mac, `wasi wasm32` for the app's WebAssembly target.
writing.task: Compile the practice code and read the error before running anything. Fix the typo, build again, and note that the program now runs although nothing ever calls the `EUR` branch.
writing.success: You can explain why an error appears in a branch that never runs, and what file `rustc` or `cargo build` produces.
writing.question: The `EUR` branch of the practice code has a typo, and your test only calls `total(&[3, 4], "USD")`. What happens?
answers: rustc refuses to build the program and reports E0599 for that branch, although it would never run
The program runs and fails only if the `EUR` branch executes, like the `TypeError` in Node.js
rustc prints a warning, and the executable skips the broken branch
writing.feedback: rustc checks every function and branch before it writes an executable. The typo is a compile error, E0599, whether or not a test reaches it.

recall.question: What does `cargo build` leave you with, and what must the machine that runs it have installed?
recall.answer: A native executable in `target/debug/`, or `target/release/` with `--release`, built for one target such as Linux on x86-64. The machine needs a compatible operating system and CPU, not Rust, Cargo or Node.js. For a browser or a WASI host you build a WebAssembly module instead.

recall.question: Why is this rejected, even though nothing ever passes `true`?
recall.answer: rustc type-checks every branch before it builds anything, whether or not the branch can run: E0308, expected `String`, found integer. There is no executable until the branch returns a `String`, for example `42.to_string()`.

depth.correction: There is no later point. A value is dropped exactly when its owner's scope ends, or when it is passed to `drop`, and the order follows the declarations.

lessons.title: Garbage collection vs deterministic drop

writing.summary: V8's garbage collector frees objects whenever it decides; Rust drops each value at the end of its owner's scope, in an order you can read from the code.
writing.rule: At scope end, remaining locals drop in reverse declaration order; struct fields drop in declaration order.
writing.explanation:
In Node.js, V8's garbage collector frees an object at some point after it becomes unreachable. The language leaves that point open: a `FinalizationRegistry` callback may run late, or not at all before the process exits, which is what the example shows. That is fine for memory, but it is why files, sockets and locks need an explicit `close()`, `try/finally` or `await handle.close()`; a forgotten handle stays open until the collector or the process exit gets to it.

Rust has no collector. Every value has one owner, and when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped right there: its `Drop` implementation runs, then its fields are dropped, then its memory is released. The order is defined. At the end of a scope the remaining locals drop in reverse declaration order, so the last one created is cleaned up first, and inside a struct the fields drop in declaration order. A value that was moved elsewhere is dropped by its new owner instead, exactly once.

Because cleanup is tied to scope, one mechanism manages every resource. A `File` closes its descriptor in `Drop`, a `MutexGuard` unlocks its mutex, a `TcpStream` closes its socket and a `Vec` frees its buffer. There are no collection pauses and no finalizer threads; the cost of freeing appears at the closing brace where it happens.

To release something earlier, end its scope or call `drop(value)`, the function `std::mem::drop`, which takes ownership and lets the value go. You never call the `drop` method yourself; rustc rejects that with E0040, because the destructor must run exactly once. Leaks are still possible, for example through `Rc` reference cycles or `std::mem::forget`, but they are explicit choices rather than an accident of the collector's timing.
writing.exampleCaption: The last local drops first, a struct's fields drop in declaration order, and `drop(early)` releases a value before its scope ends.
writing.task: Predict the order of all seven lines of the example before running it. Then move `let _second` into an inner block of its own and predict again.
writing.success: Your predicted order matches the output, including the two `pair` fields, and you can say where each value's memory is released.
writing.question: In the example, which message prints right after `leaving make_buffers`?
answers: `drop first`, because `_first` was declared first
Nothing yet: the memory is freed later, whenever the allocator decides
`drop pair.left`: the last local drops first, and its fields drop in declaration order
writing.feedback: At the closing brace, `_pair` is the last declared local, so it drops first, `left` before `right`; then `_second` and `_first` follow.

recall.question: What does this print, and in what order?
recall.answer: `body`, then `drop a`, then `drop b`. Moving `a` into `moved` hands the drop to `moved`, the last declared local, so it drops first, and `b` follows. The original binding `a` runs no destructor of its own.

recall.question: Why does rustc reject `conn.drop()`, and what do you write instead?
recall.answer: Calling the destructor method directly would let it run twice, once now and again at the end of the scope, so rustc rejects it with E0040. Write `drop(conn)`: the function takes ownership, the value is dropped inside it, and the binding cannot be used afterwards.

depth.correction: Rust's `as` performs a real conversion between compatible primitive types and is rejected for anything else, such as `&str` to `u32` (E0606). Converting outside data is a fallible operation such as `parse`.

lessons.title: TypeScript types vs Rust types

writing.summary: TypeScript types are erased and can be bypassed with `any` or `as`; Rust types are enforced by rustc, which builds nothing until its diagnostics are fixed.
writing.rule: rustc refuses to build a program with a type error: read each diagnostic's code, span and labels, and repair the first causal error before chasing its downstream messages.
writing.explanation:
TypeScript checks your code and then erases the types: the JavaScript that runs has no idea a `User` exists. `JSON.parse(raw) as User` is a promise to the compiler that nothing verifies, `any` switches checking off, and a wrong assertion raises no error. In the example, `user.id + 1` type-checks as numeric addition and produces the string `"421"` at runtime.

Rust has no `any` and no unchecked assertion between unrelated types. A value of type `u32` is a `u32` in the compiled program; text from outside becomes one only through a step that can fail and says so, such as `"42".parse::<u32>()`, which returns a `Result`. Serde's `serde_json::from_str::<User>` works the same way: a JSON string where the struct expects a number is an `Err`, not a quietly wrong object. The escape hatches that do exist, `as` between numeric types and `unsafe` code, are narrow and visible.

Because rustc refuses to build a program with a type error, reading its diagnostics is a daily skill. Each error has a code such as `E0308`, a primary span marked with `^^^` under the offending expression, labels such as `expected u32, found &str`, and often a `help:` line with a suggestion. `rustc --explain E0308` prints a longer explanation with examples. Treat a suggestion as a hint rather than an order: decide first what the program should mean.

Read the errors from the top and repair the first causal one. In the practice code, `id` is text, so both `id + 1` and `User { id }` fail; the root cause is the missing parse, and once `id` is a `u32` both messages disappear. Patching each later message with a cast or an annotation hides the real mistake and can create new errors further down.
writing.exampleCaption: Outside text becomes a `User` only through parsing, and each failure says what was wrong.
writing.task: Compile the practice code and read both errors: the code, the primary span and the labels. Fix only the root cause, compile again and confirm that both messages are gone. Then run `rustc --explain E0369`.
writing.success: You fixed both errors with one change, and you can point to the span and label that revealed the root cause.
writing.question: For the practice code, rustc reports E0369 at `id + 1` and E0308 at `User { id }`. What do you fix first?
answers: The `User` struct: change its `id` field to `&str`
The binding `id`: both errors start where text is used as a number, so parse it once with `"42".parse::<u32>()`
Add `as u32` at both error sites
writing.feedback: Both diagnostics trace back to `id` being a `&str`. Parsing it into a `u32` removes the root cause, and both messages go away; `as` cannot convert text at all (E0606).

recall.question: Why is this rejected, and what is the fix?
recall.answer: `as` converts only between compatible primitive types; it is not an unchecked assertion like TypeScript's `as`. Casting a `&str` to a `u32` is E0606. Parse instead, with `let id: u32 = raw.parse()?;` or a `match` on the `Result`.
recall.code:
let raw = "42";
let id = raw as u32;

recall.question: rustc prints `error[E0308]: mismatched types`, a `^^^` span and the label `expected u32, found &str`. What does each part tell you, and where do you find more?
recall.answer: `E0308` names the rule that was broken, the span marks the exact expression, and the label compares the type the context requires with the type the expression has. `rustc --explain E0308` prints a longer explanation with examples. Start with the first such error, because later ones are often consequences of it.

lessons.title: console.log vs println!

answers: When that line runs, like a `TypeError`
During compilation, while the macro expands
Never: the extra placeholder prints literally, as with `console.log`
writing.exampleCaption: `{rest:02}` does the work of `padStart(2, "0")`, and `{:?}` prints a value through `Debug`.
writing.explanation:
A Node.js module runs from top to bottom, so `console.log` can sit anywhere at the top level. A Rust binary has no top-level statements: execution starts in `fn main()`, and everything else is an item, such as a function, a struct or a `use` declaration, that runs only when `main` calls it.

`println!` is a macro, not a function; the `!` marks the call. It expands during compilation, so rustc checks the format string against the arguments before the program exists. A missing argument is a compile error, not a stray `%d` in the output as with `console.log("%s costs %d cents", "tea")`. `format!` builds the same text as a `String` instead of printing it, which is the job a template literal does in JavaScript.

Placeholders replace interpolation. `{}` formats with the `Display` trait, `{name}` captures a variable that is in scope, and `{:?}` formats with `Debug`. Format options cover what you used `padStart` and `toFixed` for: `{rest:02}` pads with zeros to width 2, `{:<8}` left-aligns in 8 columns and `{:.2}` prints two decimals. `console.log` inspects any object; a Rust type prints with `{:?}` only if it implements `Debug`, usually through `#[derive(Debug)]`.

`println!` writes to stdout and `eprintln!` to stderr, the counterparts of `console.log` and `console.error`. Neither is a way to hand data back from a function. Return a `String` and let the caller decide where it goes, which is also what makes the lab's `clock` function testable.
writing.feedback: The format string is checked while `println!` expands, so a program with the mismatch is never built.
writing.question: When does rustc report that `println!("{} costs {} cents", item)` is missing an argument?

recall.answer: The format string has two `{}` placeholders but only one argument, and `println!` checks that during compilation. Pass a second argument, as in `println!("{} costs {} cents", item, 705)`, or remove the second placeholder.
recall.code:
let item = "tea";
println!("{} costs {} cents", item);
recall.question: Why does this not compile, and what are two fixes?

recall.answer: `{}` requires `Display`, the user-facing format. `{name}` is the same `{}` placeholder, capturing the variable `name` from the surrounding scope. `{:?}` requires `Debug`, the developer format most types get from `#[derive(Debug)]`. Unlike `console.log`, nothing is inspected automatically.
recall.question: What do `{}`, `{name}` and `{:?}` each require from the value?

writing.rule: Execution starts in `fn main()`; `println!` and `format!` are macros whose placeholders are checked during compilation.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness passes every case, including `0` and single-digit seconds. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.summary: `println!` replaces `console.log`, and rustc checks every placeholder against its arguments before the program runs.

lessons.title: const and let vs let and let mut

answers: It compiles, but the push panics because the vector is frozen
It compiles, exactly like `const tags = []; tags.push("rust")`
rustc rejects the push: without `mut`, the binding cannot be used to change the vector
writing.exampleCaption: `mut` marks what changes, and the second `let input` shadows the text with an `i32`.
writing.explanation:
In JavaScript, `const` protects the binding, not the value: `const tags = []` can still `push`. Rust's `let` protects both. Without `mut` you cannot assign a new value, and you cannot call a method that needs `&mut self`, such as `Vec::push`. `let mut` is the explicit opt-in, so a reader finds every binding that changes by scanning for `mut`.

Rust also has `const`, but it means something else: a compile-time constant with a mandatory type, such as `const MAX_RETRIES: u32 = 3;`, which may live at module level. It is closer to a named literal that the compiler inlines than to a JavaScript `const` binding.

Shadowing replaces the common `let input = ...; input = Number(input)` pattern. A second `let input` declares a new binding that hides the first one for the rest of the scope, and it may have a different type, so `let input: i32 = input.trim().parse()?` turns text into a number without inventing `inputText` and `inputNumber`. The old value is not mutated; it is simply no longer reachable by that name. In JavaScript, declaring `let input` twice in one scope is a `SyntaxError`.

Mutability belongs to the binding, not to the type. Moving a value into a `let mut` binding makes it mutable there, and lending it out as `&mut` requires the owner to be `mut`. That is why the error for the practice code points at the declaration and suggests `let mut tags`.
writing.feedback: `push` takes `&mut self`, and a binding declared without `mut` cannot lend that out. rustc reports E0596 at compile time.
writing.question: Which statement about `let tags = Vec::new(); tags.push("rust");` is true?

recall.answer: `count` was declared without `mut`, so it cannot be assigned a second time: E0384. rustc suggests `let mut count = 1;`. Plain `let` behaves like a `const` binding whose value also cannot change.
recall.code:
let count = 1;
count += 1;
recall.question: Why is the second line rejected, and what does rustc suggest?

recall.answer: The first declares a new binding that shadows the old one; it may have a different type, and the original binding is left untouched. The second assigns into the same mutable binding, so the new value must have the same type as the old one.
recall.question: How is `let input = input.trim();` different from `input = input.trim();` on a `let mut input`?

writing.rule: `let` is immutable, `let mut` permits change, and a new `let` with the same name shadows the old binding.
writing.success: You can tell which bindings change by reading the `let` lines alone, and you predicted E0596 before compiling.
writing.summary: Rust's plain `let` is stricter than `const`: without `mut` you can neither reassign the binding nor change the value through it.

lessons.title: Number vs Rust integer types

answers: It panics with `attempt to subtract with overflow`
It returns `-2`, as in JavaScript
It returns `0`, because unsigned values saturate
writing.exampleCaption: Widen with `i32::from`, add with `checked_add`, narrow with `u16::try_from`: every boundary is visible.
writing.explanation:
JavaScript has one `Number`, an IEEE 754 double. Integers are exact only up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 − 1), `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` is `false`, and the bitwise operators quietly convert to 32-bit integers. `BigInt` exists but does not mix with `Number`. Rust has fixed-size integers from `i8` to `i128` and `u8` to `u128`, the pointer-sized `usize` and `isize`, and `f32` and `f64`. Floating point behaves as it does in JavaScript; integers are where your habits need to change.

Rust never converts between numeric types for you. `u16 + i32` does not compile, even when every value would fit. Lossless widening is `i32::from(stock)` or `.into()`. Narrowing that may fail is `u16::try_from(n)`, which returns a `Result`. `as` converts too, but it truncates or wraps silently, so keep it for casts you have proved safe.

Overflow is a decision, not an accident. In a debug build, `u32` arithmetic that leaves the range panics with `attempt to subtract with overflow`; in a release build it wraps unless `overflow-checks` is enabled. Neither gives JavaScript's `-2`. When the boundary is part of the contract, say so: `checked_sub` returns `None`, `saturating_sub` stops at `0` and `wrapping_sub` wraps on purpose.

Choose types from the domain. Counts and lengths are usually `usize` or `u32`, money is an integer number of cents rather than an `f64`, and a value that can be negative needs a signed type. The lab's `seats_left` shows why the choice matters: a `u32` has no negative answer, so the function returns `Option<u32>` and the caller handles the overbooked case.
writing.feedback: Debug builds check integer overflow and panic. A release build would wrap to `4294967294` unless overflow checks are enabled; use `checked_sub` when the boundary is expected.
writing.question: `fn left(capacity: u32, booked: u32) -> u32 { capacity - booked }` is called with `3` and `5` in a debug build. What happens?

recall.answer: `as` between integer types never fails: it keeps the low 8 bits, so `300` becomes `44`. `u8::try_from(300)` returns an `Err` instead of a silently different number, so the line prints `44 true`. Prefer `try_from` when a value might not fit.
recall.question: Why does this compile, and what does it print?

recall.answer: `u64` represents every integer from 0 to 2^64 − 1 exactly, so `2_u64.pow(53) + 1` is a different value from `2_u64.pow(53)`. Precision loss is a floating-point property. With integers the only boundary is overflow, which debug builds check.
recall.question: In JavaScript, `2 ** 53 + 1 === 2 ** 53` is `true`. What happens with `u64` in Rust?

writing.rule: Numeric types never mix implicitly: convert with `From` or `try_from`, and choose checked, wrapping or saturating arithmetic where overflow is possible.

writing.summary: Every JavaScript `Number` is an f64. Rust makes you pick a numeric type, convert between types explicitly and decide what happens on overflow.

lessons.title: JavaScript functions vs fn

answers: Rust needs `return` in every function
`x * 2` must be wrapped in parentheses
The semicolon makes the body evaluate to `()`, which is not `i32`
writing.exampleCaption: No `return` keywords: each body ends in an expression, and `if` replaces the ternary.
writing.explanation:
Arrow functions taught you expression bodies: `(x) => x * 2` returns without `return`. Rust applies that idea to every block. The last expression of a function body, without a trailing semicolon, is the return value. A semicolon turns it into a statement whose value is `()`, the unit type, so `fn double(x: i32) -> i32 { x * 2; }` is a type error. `return` still exists for early exits.

Because `if` and `match` are expressions, there is no need for the ternary operator: `let base = if weight_kg <= 1 { 5 } else { 5 + (weight_kg - 1) * 2 };`. A block `{ ... }` is an expression too, which is how a function body produces its value.

Parameters always have types, and the compiler never coerces arguments. JavaScript happily computed `shippingCost("3")` as `9` through `"3" - 1`; Rust rejects a `&str` where a `u32` is expected, at the call site. There are no default or optional parameters and no overloading. Pass an explicit value, add a second function such as `discounted_default`, take an `Option<T>`, or group options in a struct that implements `Default`.

The return type is part of the signature and is never inferred from the body. A function's contract stays readable without its body, and rustc can point at the exact semicolon that turned an `i32` into `()`.
writing.feedback: With the semicolon, `x * 2` is a statement and the block's value is `()`. rustc reports E0308 and suggests removing the semicolon.
writing.question: Why is `fn double(x: i32) -> i32 { x * 2; }` rejected?

recall.answer: `()`. The semicolon after `x + 1` makes it a statement, so the block has no tail expression and evaluates to the unit value, and `{:?}` prints `()`. Remove the semicolon and `value` is the integer `4`.
recall.question: What type does `value` have, and why?

recall.answer: Require the argument and let callers pass `5432`; provide a second function such as `connect_default(host)`; or take `port: Option<u16>` and use `port.unwrap_or(5432)`. For many options, a config struct that implements `Default`, filled in with `..Default::default()`, scales better.
recall.question: Rust has no default parameters. What are three idiomatic replacements for `function connect(host, port = 5432)`?

writing.rule: Every parameter has a type, arguments must match it exactly, and a block's final expression without a semicolon is its value.

writing.summary: A Rust function declares every parameter type and returns its final expression; there are no default parameters and no implicit coercions.

lessons.title: Truthiness vs bool, if and match

answers: `count > 0` is not a valid condition
The branches produce different types: an integer and a `&str`
`if` cannot appear on the right-hand side of `let`
writing.exampleCaption: `match` with a range covers every `u32`, and the `if` expression yields a `&str` from either branch.
writing.explanation:
`if (!count)` mixes several questions: is it `0`, `NaN`, `""`, `null` or `undefined`? Rust refuses to guess. `if count` with an integer is E0308, expected `bool`, found integer, so you write the question you mean: `count == 0`, `text.is_empty()`, `value.is_none()`. There is no `==` versus `===` either. `==` compares two values of compatible types through `PartialEq` and never converts, so `0 == ""` does not compile.

`if` is an expression, which replaces both the statement form and the ternary. `let urgent = if count > 0 && count < 5 { "yes" } else { "no" };` works because both branches are `&str`. If one branch yields a number and the other text, the expression has no single type and rustc rejects it. An `if` without `else` has type `()`, so it can only stand as a statement.

`match` is the tool for several cases of one value. Patterns can be literals, ranges such as `1..=4`, or `_` for everything else, and the compiler checks that the arms cover every possible value. For a `u32`, the arms `0`, `1..=4` and `_` are exhaustive, so no input can fall through, unlike a `switch` without `default`.

`&&` and `||` short-circuit as in JavaScript, but they accept and return only `bool`. There is no `a || b` default trick; that job belongs to `Option` methods such as `unwrap_or`, covered in the lesson on `null` and `undefined`.
writing.feedback: An `if` expression has one type. Return `count.to_string()` from the first branch and `String::from("none")` from the second, or a number from both.
writing.question: Why does `let label = if count > 0 { count } else { "none" };` not compile?

recall.answer: E0308: the condition must be a `bool`, and a `String` is not one. Ask the exact question, such as `if !name.is_empty()`. Rust never converts a string, a number or an `Option` to a boolean.
recall.question: What is the error, and what is the fix?

recall.answer: `100..=255`. rustc rejects the `match` with E0004 and names that range. Add an arm for it or a `_` arm: a `match` must cover every value of the type.
recall.question: Which values of `n: u8` are not covered by this `match`?

writing.rule: `if` requires a `bool`, and every branch of an `if` or `match` expression must produce the same type.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness passes every case, including `0` and exactly `100`. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.summary: Rust has no truthy or falsy values: a condition must be a `bool`, and `if` and `match` are expressions whose branches share one type.

lessons.title: Classes and objects vs structs

answers: The call consumes the value, so it cannot be used afterwards
The method is static and has no `this`
The method can be called only once per program
writing.exampleCaption: `increment` borrows mutably, `is_full` only reads, and `new` is a plain associated function.
writing.explanation:
A JavaScript class bundles fields, methods and a prototype chain, and every method receives the same mutable `this`. Rust splits the parts. A `struct` declares the fields and their types, and an `impl` block adds functions. There is no constructor keyword: `new` is an ordinary associated function returning `Self`, called as `Counter::new(2)`. There is no inheritance either; shared behaviour comes from traits.

The receiver is the part without a JavaScript equivalent. `fn is_full(&self)` only reads, so it works through a shared reference. `fn increment(&mut self)` changes fields, so the caller needs a `mut` binding and exclusive access for the duration of the call. `fn close(self)` takes ownership: after `wallet.close()` the caller can no longer use `wallet`, which is how Rust says "this object is finished" without a runtime flag.

Fields are private to their module by default. Outside it, `c.count = 99` does not compile unless the field is `pub`, so an invariant such as `count <= limit` is enforced by the methods rather than by convention. Inside the defining module, as in this single-file example, `main` can still read `c.count`.

A struct literal must set every field; there is no `undefined` property. Optional fields are `Option<T>`, and defaults come from `#[derive(Default)]` or an explicit constructor. Printing a struct with `{:?}` needs `#[derive(Debug)]`, and comparing two with `==` needs `PartialEq`.
writing.feedback: `self` by value moves the struct into the method. The second `c.finish()` is E0382, use of a moved value.
writing.question: What does `fn finish(self) -> u32` tell a caller that `fn count(&self) -> u32` does not?

recall.answer: `&self` is a shared reference, so the method may only read fields: E0594, cannot assign to `self.count`. Change the receiver to `&mut self`; callers then need a mutable binding.
recall.question: Why is the assignment rejected?

recall.answer: As an associated function without a receiver in the `impl` block, for example `fn from_text(text: &str) -> Option<Counter>`, called as `Counter::from_text("3")`. `new` is the same kind of function by convention, not a special constructor.
recall.question: How does Rust express a JavaScript `static` method such as `Counter.fromText(text)`?

writing.rule: `&self` reads, `&mut self` modifies and `self` consumes: the receiver tells the caller what a method does to the value.

lessons.title: TypeScript unions vs enums

answers: rustc reports E0004 for the new variant
The program panics when `Crypto` reaches the `match`
It compiles, and `Crypto` silently takes the wildcard arm
writing.exampleCaption: Each arm destructures its variant, and the guarded `Cash` arm is followed by an unguarded one.
writing.explanation:
A discriminated union is a set of object shapes sharing a tag such as `kind`, narrowed by a `switch`. Rust builds the same idea into the type system: `enum Payment { Card { last4: String }, Transfer { reference: String }, Cash }`. The variant is the tag. There is no string field to misspell, and data that belongs to one variant cannot be read through another.

`match` replaces the `switch` plus the `never` trick. TypeScript checks exhaustiveness only if you add a `default` with `const unhandled: never`, and only at compile time: at runtime a value from JSON can still carry an unknown `kind`. Rust's `match` must cover every variant or the program does not compile (E0004), and a value of type `Payment` cannot hold anything else, because outside data has to be parsed into a variant first.

Patterns destructure while they match. `Payment::Card { last4 } =>` binds the field, and a literal field such as `Shipped { days: 0, .. }` matches one specific value. A guard, `Payment::Cash if cents > 50_000 =>`, adds a condition; when it is false, matching continues with the next arm. Guards do not count toward exhaustiveness, so a plain `Payment::Cash =>` arm must still follow.

Be careful with `_`. A wildcard arm silences E0004 for every variant added later, which is exactly the check you came for. In code that should be revisited whenever the enum grows, list the variants explicitly.
writing.feedback: A wildcard covers every variant, including future ones, so the compiler has nothing to report. List the variants where a new one should force a review.
writing.question: A `match` on `Payment` ends with `_ => 0`. Later someone adds `Payment::Crypto`. What happens?

recall.answer: The compiler does not reason about guard conditions, so `Cash` still counts as uncovered, and `Transfer` is missing as well: E0004. Make the last `Cash` arm unguarded and add a `Transfer` arm.
recall.question: Why is this `match` rejected, even though both `Cash` amounts seem handled?

recall.answer: TypeScript types are erased, so the unknown `kind` reaches the `switch` at runtime and falls into the `never` branch. In Rust a `Payment` can only be built as one of its variants; parsing the JSON, for example with Serde, fails on the unknown tag before any `match` runs.
recall.question: In TypeScript, JSON with `kind: "crypto"` can reach a `switch` typed for three kinds. What happens instead in Rust?

writing.rule: An enum variant carries its own data, and `match` must cover every variant; a guard narrows an arm but never excuses a missing case.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness passes every variant, including 0 and 1 days. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.summary: A TypeScript discriminated union becomes a Rust `enum` whose variants carry their own data, and `match` must handle every variant.

lessons.title: null, undefined and ?? vs Option

answers: `Option<T>`
`Result<Option<T>, E>`
`T`, using `null` for both cases
writing.exampleCaption: `and_then` follows the optional chain and `unwrap_or` supplies the `??` default, so `Some(0)` stays `0`.
writing.explanation:
TypeScript with `strictNullChecks` already marks absence as `T | undefined`, but the value can still be `null`, `undefined` or a missing property, and the checks vanish at runtime. Rust has no null. A value that may be missing has type `Option<T>`, which is either `Some(value)` or `None`, and you cannot use it as a `T` until you decide what absence means. `network.retries + 1` with an `Option<u32>` is a compile error, not `NaN`.

The operators become methods. `a?.b` is `a.as_ref().and_then(|a| a.b)` when `b` is itself optional, and `.map(...)` when it is not. `x ?? 3` is `x.unwrap_or(3)`, or `unwrap_or_else(|| ...)` when the default is expensive to build. Inside a function that returns `Option`, `let n = config.network.as_ref()?;` returns `None` early, the closest thing to optional chaining across statements.

There is no `||` default. `retries || 3` turns a configured `0` into `3`, and `title || "Untitled"` discards an intentionally empty string. `unwrap_or` only replaces `None`, so `Some(0)` stays `0`. If zero really should count as missing, say so with `.filter(|&n| n != 0)` and a comment.

`Option` answers whether something is there; it does not say why not. When the caller needs a reason, such as "storage unreachable" rather than "no such user", return `Result<T, E>`, or `Result<Option<T>, E>` when missing is a normal outcome and failure is a separate one. That replaces returning `null` from one path and throwing from another.
writing.feedback: `Ok(Some(t))` means found, `Ok(None)` simply missing, and `Err(e)` carries the reason the lookup itself failed.
writing.question: A lookup finds nothing when the key is missing, and fails when the storage is unreachable. Which return type gives the caller both facts?

recall.answer: `0`, then `5`, then `Some(1)`. `unwrap_or` replaces only `None`, like `??`, so the present zero is kept. `map` transforms the value inside `Some` and would leave a `None` as `None`.
recall.question: What does each line print?

recall.answer: `and_then` takes the `Option` by value, which would move `network` out of a struct you only borrowed: E0507. Call `config.network.as_ref()` first to get an `Option<&Network>`; then `n.retries` copies the `Option<u32>` out through the reference.
recall.question: Why is this rejected when `config` is a `&Config`, and what fixes it?

writing.rule: Use `Option<T>` when a value may be absent and `Result<T, E>` when the caller needs the reason; `unwrap_or` replaces `??`, not `||`.

lessons.title: Array methods vs iterators

answers: Nothing: no consumer such as `sum`, `collect` or `for` asked for a value
It doubled all three prices into a new vector, like `Array.prototype.map`
It doubled the first price and then paused
writing.exampleCaption: The closure counter shows the difference: two calls for the total, and the search stops after one more.
writing.explanation:
`orders.filter(...).map(...).reduce(...)` runs each stage over the whole array and allocates an intermediate array between stages. Rust's `orders.iter().filter(...).map(...).sum()` first builds a description of the work. Nothing happens until `sum` asks for the first item; then each order flows through `filter` and `map` one at a time, with no intermediate `Vec`.

Laziness changes what runs. In the JavaScript example, `map(...).find(...)` calls the mapping function for all three orders before `find` looks at one. The Rust pipeline stops at the first match, so its closure runs once. A pipeline that is never consumed does nothing at all, which is why rustc warns that an unused `Map` must be used in the practice code.

The names mostly carry over: `map`, `filter` and `find` are the same, `some` is `any`, `every` is `all`, `reduce` with an initial value is `fold`, and `flatMap` is `flat_map`. The length of a filtered result is `count()`, and `collect::<Vec<_>>()` gives you a collection back. There is no index argument; add `.enumerate()` to get `(index, item)` pairs.

Watch what the iterator yields. `iter()` yields references (`&Order`), `iter_mut()` yields `&mut Order`, and `into_iter()` on a `Vec` yields owned values and consumes the vector. That is why the closures read `o.cents` through a reference, and why `find(|&c| c > 1000)` destructures the `&u64` it receives.
writing.feedback: An adapter only describes work. Without a consumer the closure never runs, and rustc warns that the `Map` must be used.
writing.question: In the practice code, what has `map` done by the time `done` prints?

recall.answer: `map 1`, `map 2`, then `Some(20)`. `find` pulls one item at a time and stops at the first match, so the closure never runs for `3`. An array's `map` would have logged all three before searching.
recall.question: What does this print, and why not three `map` lines?

recall.answer: `any`, `all`, `fold(initial, |acc, x| ...)` and `flat_map`. As in JavaScript, `any` and `all` short-circuit. Unlike the array methods, they work on any iterator, and the adapters before them run lazily.
recall.question: What are the Rust names for `some`, `every`, `reduce` with an initial value, and `flatMap`?

writing.rule: Iterator adapters are lazy: a consumer such as `sum`, `find`, `collect` or a `for` loop drives the work, one item at a time.

lessons.title: Objects and Map vs HashMap

answers: It keeps the keys sorted
It avoids allocating the key
It looks the key up once and returns a mutable reference whether or not the entry existed
writing.exampleCaption: `split_whitespace` drops empty words, `entry` updates in one lookup, and `constructor` is just another key.
writing.explanation:
Objects make convenient dictionaries until a key collides with the prototype. In the JavaScript example, `counts["constructor"]` finds `Object.prototype.constructor`, so `(counts[word] || 0) + 1` produces `"function Object() { [native code] }1"`. Keys are also converted to strings, so `1` and `"1"` are the same key. `Map` fixes both problems, and `HashMap<K, V>` is its Rust counterpart: keys and values have declared types, and only inserted keys exist.

The counting idiom becomes the `entry` API. `counts.entry(word)` looks the key up once and returns an `Entry`; `or_insert(0)` inserts the default if the slot was vacant and returns `&mut u32` in both cases, so `*... += 1` updates in place. `get` followed by `insert` does two lookups, and `insert` alone overwrites like `Map.set`, which is the classic bug when porting `totals.set(k, (totals.get(k) ?? 0) + v)`.

Reading is explicit about absence. `counts.get("be")` returns an `Option<&u32>`. `counts["be"]` also compiles, but it panics when the key is missing instead of returning `undefined`, so use indexing only for keys you know are present.

Iteration order is not insertion order. A `Map` preserves insertion order; a `HashMap` uses a randomly seeded hasher, so its order can differ between runs. Sort the keys, or use a `BTreeMap` for key order, when output must be stable. Splitting text differs too: `split(' ')` keeps the empty strings between double spaces in both languages, while `split_whitespace()` skips them.
writing.feedback: `or_insert` returns `&mut V` for both the vacant and the occupied case, so one lookup covers the update.
writing.question: Why is `*counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1` preferred over `get` followed by `insert`?

recall.answer: `Some(5) Some(2)`. `insert` replaces the value, like `Map.set`, and returns the previous one. To add instead, write `*m.entry("ana").or_insert(0) += 2`.
recall.question: What does this print?

recall.answer: `HashMap` uses a randomly seeded hasher to resist collision attacks, and its iteration order is unspecified. Collect the keys into a `Vec` and sort them, or use a `BTreeMap`, which iterates in key order. Insertion order, which a JavaScript `Map` keeps, is promised by neither type.
recall.question: Why might two runs of the same program print a `HashMap` in different orders, and what are two fixes?

writing.rule: `entry(key).or_insert(default)` looks the key up once and returns a mutable reference to the value, whether or not it was already there.
