writing.summary: Plain objects used as dictionaries become `HashMap<K, V>`: typed keys, no prototype keys, and `entry` for update-or-insert in one lookup.

lessons.title: UTF-16 strings vs UTF-8 String

answers: `4`, the number of characters
`5`, the number of UTF-8 bytes
`8`, the number of UTF-16 bytes
writing.exampleCaption: Byte length, scalar count and a checked slice: `get(0..4)` is `None` because byte 4 falls inside `é`.
writing.explanation:
A JavaScript string is a sequence of UTF-16 code units. `"café".length` is `4`, but `"👍".length` is `2`, because the emoji needs a surrogate pair, while `[..."👍"].length` is `1` because the string iterator walks code points. Indexing and `slice` work on code units, so `"👍👍👍".slice(0, 1)` returns half a character and the truncated output prints a replacement character.

A Rust `String`, like a borrowed `&str`, is UTF-8. `len()` is the byte length: `"café".len()` is `5` because `é` takes two bytes, and `"👍".len()` is `4`. `chars()` yields `char` values, which are Unicode scalar values, so `"👍".chars().count()` is `1`. Neither number counts characters as a reader sees them: `"👍🏽"` is one grapheme but two scalar values, and grapheme segmentation needs a crate such as `unicode-segmentation`.

Because a byte offset may fall inside a character, `text[0]` does not compile at all. Slicing by a byte range is allowed but panics if a bound is not on a character boundary, while `text.get(0..4)` returns `None` instead. For the first character use `text.chars().next()`, and for the first n characters `text.chars().take(n).collect::<String>()`.

Case conversion works on characters too. `char::to_uppercase` returns an iterator because one character can become several: `ß` becomes `SS`, the same answer JavaScript's `toUpperCase` gives. `flat_map(char::to_uppercase)` collects them all.
writing.feedback: `len()` is the byte length of the UTF-8 encoding. `é` (U+00E9) takes two bytes, so the total is 5.
writing.question: What does `"café".len()` return in Rust, where JavaScript's `"café".length` is `4`?

recall.answer: Byte 1 is inside `é`, which takes two bytes, so the slice would split a character and panics at runtime. Use `name.chars().next()` for the first `char`, or `name.get(..1)`, which returns `None` instead of panicking.
recall.question: Why does this panic, and what is a safe replacement?

recall.answer: `4` UTF-8 bytes, `1` Unicode scalar value and `2` UTF-16 code units. None of them counts graphemes: a skin-tone emoji such as `👍🏽` is one grapheme but two scalar values.
recall.question: For `s = "👍"`, what are `s.len()`, `s.chars().count()` and JavaScript's `s.length`?

writing.rule: `len()` counts UTF-8 bytes and `chars().count()` counts Unicode scalar values; neither counts graphemes, and a `String` cannot be indexed by position.

lessons.title: Shared references vs ownership

answers: Make the parameter `text: &str` and call `shout(&name)`
Declare `let mut name`
Wrap the call in a block: `{ shout(name) }`
writing.exampleCaption: `let b = a` moves the crab, `clone` makes an independent copy, and `rename` takes ownership and gives it back.
writing.explanation:
In JavaScript, `const b = a` copies a reference: both names reach the same object, and a change made through `b` is visible through `a`. The garbage collector frees the object once no reference remains. Rust has no garbage collector. Each value has exactly one owner, the owner frees it when it goes out of scope, and `let b = a;` for a `String`, a `Vec` or a struct containing them moves ownership to `b`. Using `a` after the move is E0382.

Function calls follow the same rule. A parameter of type `String` takes ownership, so `shout(name)` moves `name` into the function and the caller cannot print it afterwards. A parameter of type `&str`, or `&T` in general, borrows instead: the function reads the value while the caller keeps it. Returning a value moves ownership back out, which is why `let b = rename(b, "ferris");` works.

`clone()` is the explicit copy. For `Crab` it creates a new `String` and a new `Vec<String>` with new `String`s inside, which is closer to `structuredClone` than to `{ ...a }`: spread copies only the outer object and still shares `tags`. Each type decides what `Clone` means, and cloning an `Rc`, for instance, only increments a reference count. Small plain values such as integers, `bool` and `char` are `Copy`: assignment duplicates them and nothing moves.

Moves are checked at compile time and cost nothing at runtime. Moving a `String` copies its pointer, length and capacity, not the text. The point is that exactly one binding is responsible for freeing the buffer, which rules out double frees and use after free without a collector.
writing.feedback: A `&str` parameter only borrows, so ownership of `name` stays with the caller. `mut` does not prevent a move.
writing.question: In the practice code, what is the smallest change that keeps `name` usable after the call, without cloning?

recall.answer: `let all = tags;` moved the vector, so `tags` no longer owns anything: E0382, borrow of moved value. Use `all.len()`, borrow with `let all = &tags;`, or clone if two independent vectors are really needed.
recall.question: Why is the last line rejected?

recall.answer: `i32` is `Copy`: assignment duplicates the bits and there is nothing to free. A `String` owns a heap buffer, so assignment moves ownership to keep exactly one owner responsible for freeing it. `Copy` is only implemented for types where a bitwise copy is safe.
recall.question: Why does `let y = x;` leave `x` usable when `x` is an `i32`, but not when it is a `String`?

writing.rule: Each value has one owner: assignment or a by-value parameter moves it, `&T` lends it, and `clone()` makes an independent copy.
writing.success: You predicted E0382 for the original code, and you can explain why borrowing avoids both the move and the copy.
writing.summary: Assigning an object in JavaScript shares it; assigning a `String` or `Vec` in Rust moves it, and the old binding can no longer be used.

lessons.title: Mutating arguments vs borrowing

answers: `push` is not allowed inside any loop
`n` is a moved value
The loop holds a shared borrow of `queue`, and `push` needs exclusive `&mut` access while that borrow is alive
writing.exampleCaption: `add_unique` borrows mutably, `longest` borrows shared, and the index loop makes the growth explicit.
writing.explanation:
JavaScript passes objects by sharing, so `addUnique(tags, "cargo")` silently changes the caller's array. Rust makes the intent part of the signature. `fn add_unique(tags: &mut Vec<String>, tag: &str)` says the function will modify the vector and only read the tag, and the call site repeats it: `add_unique(&mut tags, "cargo")`. The caller still owns `tags` afterwards.

Borrows follow one rule: any number of shared references `&T`, or exactly one mutable reference `&mut T`, but not both at the same time. A mutable borrow is exclusive; while it exists, nothing else may read or write the value. That rule is what lets Rust rule out data races and iterator invalidation at compile time.

The JavaScript loop shows what the rule prevents. `for (const n of queue) queue.push(...)` keeps visiting the items it appends, so a slightly different condition never ends. In Rust, `for n in &queue` holds a shared borrow for the whole loop, and `queue.push` needs `&mut queue`, so rustc reports E0502; pushing could also reallocate the buffer the loop is reading. An index loop that rereads `queue.len()` on every pass makes the growing behaviour explicit.

Ask for the least access a function needs. Take `&[String]` rather than `&Vec<String>` to read, `&mut [String]` to change elements in place, and `&mut Vec<String>` only when the function must push or remove. Assigning through a shared reference is E0594; the fix belongs in the signature, not in the body.
writing.feedback: This is E0502. The shared borrow lasts for the whole loop, a mutable borrow cannot overlap it, and the push might reallocate the buffer being read.
writing.question: Why does rustc reject `queue.push(n + 1)` inside `for n in &queue`?

recall.answer: `first` is a shared borrow that is still used after `push`, which needs a mutable borrow: E0502. The push may reallocate and leave `first` dangling. Print `first` before the push, or copy the value with `let first = v[0];`.
recall.question: Why is this rejected, and what is the smallest fix?

recall.answer: `&[String]` accepts a borrowed `Vec`, an array or any slice of either, and promises only read access to the elements. `&Vec<String>` adds nothing a reader can use and rejects arrays and subslices. Use `&mut Vec<String>` only when the function must push or remove.
recall.question: Why should a read-only function take `&[String]` instead of `&Vec<String>`?

writing.rule: `&T` lends read-only access and `&mut T` lends exclusive write access; neither transfers ownership, and the two never overlap.

lessons.title: TypeScript interfaces vs traits

answers: `fn total<T: Priced>(items: &[T]) -> u64`
`fn total(items: &[Box<dyn Priced>]) -> u64`
`fn total(items: &[impl Priced]) -> u64`
writing.exampleCaption: Explicit `impl` blocks make both structs `Shape`s; `total_area` is generic, and `largest` takes trait objects.
writing.explanation:
TypeScript interfaces are structural. The object literals in the example have no `implements` clause, yet both are `Shape`s because they have `area` and `name`. Rust traits are nominal: `Square` satisfies `Shape` only after `impl Shape for Square { ... }`, and an inherent method with the same name does not count. That is the E0277 in the practice code, the trait bound `Square: Shape` is not satisfied.

A trait bound plays the role of `<T extends Shape>`. `fn total_area<T: Shape>(items: &[T])` is generic: the compiler generates a separate copy for each concrete `T` it is used with, and the calls are dispatched statically. Every item in that slice must be the same `T`, so it cannot hold a square and a rectangle together.

For a mixed collection, the counterpart of an array of interface values, use trait objects: `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>`. Each element is a pointer to some type that implements `Shape` plus a table of its methods, and calls are dispatched at runtime, which is how every JavaScript method call works anyway. Neither form is automatically faster: generics can grow code size, and trait objects add an indirection.

Traits cover other TypeScript patterns too. Default methods replace a shared base class, `impl Display for T` replaces `toString`, and implementing a standard trait such as `PartialOrd` plugs your type into existing generic code. You may implement your own trait for a foreign type such as `u32`, but not a foreign trait for a foreign type.
writing.feedback: A generic type parameter, written either way, is one concrete type per call. A slice of `Box<dyn Priced>` holds different types behind one trait.
writing.question: Which signature lets one call handle a list that mixes `Book` and `Coffee` values?

recall.answer: `User` has an inherent `name` method but no `impl Named for User`, so the bound is not satisfied: E0277. Traits are nominal. Move the method into `impl Named for User { fn name(&self) -> String { ... } }`.
recall.question: Why is the call rejected, and what fixes it?

recall.answer: When one collection must hold different concrete types, or when the type is only known at runtime. Generics fix one `T` per instantiation and are compiled into a separate copy for each; trait objects store a pointer plus a method table and dispatch at runtime. Measure before assuming either is faster.
recall.question: When is `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>` the right choice over a generic `Vec<T>` with `T: Shape`?

writing.rule: A type implements a trait only through an explicit `impl`; use a generic bound for static dispatch over one type and `dyn Trait` for a collection of mixed types.

lessons.title: try/catch vs Result

answers: It panics: the thread unwinds, or the process aborts if panics are configured to abort
It returns the `Err` to the caller automatically, like an uncaught `throw` bubbling up
It returns `0`, as `Number` does for bad input
writing.exampleCaption: `?` returns the wrapped parse error early, the range check produces its own variant, and `main` matches both.
writing.explanation:
In JavaScript any function may throw anything, and nothing in its signature says so. A caller learns that `parsePort` throws by reading its code or by watching it crash. Rust puts failure in the type: `fn parse_port(text: &str) -> Result<u16, PortError>` returns either `Ok(port)` or `Err(reason)`, and the caller cannot reach the `u16` without deciding what to do about the error.

The error type is yours to design. An enum such as `PortError { NotANumber(ParseIntError), OutOfRange(u32) }` lets a caller tell the cases apart with `match` instead of comparing message strings, and it can wrap the lower-level error as its cause. `map_err` converts one error type into another, and the `?` operator returns the `Err` early, like an exception propagating, but visibly at every call site and only from a function that itself returns a compatible `Result`.

Panics are not exceptions. `unwrap()`, `expect()`, indexing out of bounds and integer overflow in a debug build panic: the thread unwinds, or the process aborts if the build sets `panic = "abort"`. Use them for bugs, where continuing would be wrong, not for invalid user input. A `Result` is for situations the caller can reasonably handle: bad text, a missing file, a refused connection.

Parsing stops being lenient as well. `Number("")` is `0` and `Number("0x50")` is `80`, while `"".parse::<u32>()` is an `Err` of kind `Empty` and `"0x50"` one of kind `InvalidDigit`. One surprise runs the other way: integer `parse` accepts a leading `+`, so validate the exact format first when your contract forbids a sign.
writing.feedback: `unwrap` is a deliberate crash on `Err`. Handing the error back to the caller is what `?` does.
writing.question: In the practice code, what does `unwrap()` do when `parse` returns `Err`?

recall.answer: `?` hands the error back to the caller, so the function itself must return a compatible `Result` or `Option`: E0277. Change the signature to `fn port() -> Result<u16, std::num::ParseIntError>` and return `Ok(n)`.
recall.question: Why does `?` not compile here, and how do you fix it?

recall.answer: When an `Err` would mean a bug in your own program, such as parsing a constant literal or a value an earlier check guaranteed. The message documents the broken invariant. For anything that depends on input, files or the network, return a `Result` so that the caller can respond.
recall.question: When is `expect("...")` acceptable instead of returning a `Result`?

writing.rule: Return `Result` for a failure the caller can act on, propagate it with `?`, and keep panics such as `unwrap` for bugs and broken invariants.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness passes every case, including `24h`, `+5s` and a number too large for `u32`. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.summary: `throw` and `try/catch` become `Result<T, E>`: failure is part of the return type, `?` propagates it, and panics are reserved for bugs.

Return `DurationError::BadFormat` for anything else, including a missing number or a sign, and `DurationError::TooLong` above 86,400 seconds, even when the number does not fit an integer type. lessons.title: npm and package.json vs Cargo

answers: Exactly 1.3.0, as in npm
Any version at all; only the lockfile decides
Any SemVer-compatible version: at least 1.3.0 and below 2.0.0
writing.exampleCaption: The manifest lives in `Cargo.toml`, `src/main.rs` is the binary target, and Cargo sets `CARGO_PKG_VERSION` when it builds.
writing.explanation:
The files map closely. `Cargo.toml` is the manifest: `[package]` holds the name, version and edition, `[dependencies]` and `[dev-dependencies]` match their npm counterparts, and `[build-dependencies]` serve a `build.rs` script. `Cargo.lock` records the exact resolved versions, like `package-lock.json`; commit it for applications. Downloaded crate sources are cached once per user under `~/.cargo/registry`, and build output goes to `target/`, so there is no `node_modules` directory.

The version trap: in `package.json`, `"left-pad": "1.3.0"` pins exactly that version, and only `"^1.3.0"` allows updates. In `Cargo.toml`, `left-pad = "1.3.0"` already means `^1.3.0`, at least 1.3.0 and below 2.0.0. For `0.x` versions the caret is narrower in both tools, so `"0.4.1"` allows `>=0.4.1, <0.5.0`. To pin exactly, write `"=1.3.0"`; most projects rely on the lockfile instead.

There is no `scripts` section and no `main` or `bin` field. Cargo finds targets by path: `src/main.rs` is the default binary, `src/lib.rs` the library, and each file in `src/bin/` an extra binary. `cargo build`, `cargo run`, `cargo test`, `cargo check` and `cargo fmt` are built in; project-specific tasks usually become a small binary or an `xtask` crate.

Dependencies must be declared to be visible. Node resolves `require("serde")` by walking up the directory tree to any `node_modules`, so an undeclared package can work by accident. Cargo passes only the declared crates to rustc, which is why the practice code fails with E0432 instead of finding a crate that happens to be on disk. Optional functionality is chosen with features, as in `serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }`.
writing.feedback: Cargo's default requirement is the caret, so `"1.3.0"` means `^1.3.0`. Write `"=1.3.0"` for an exact pin.
writing.question: In `package.json`, a bare `"1.3.0"` pins exactly that version. What does `left-pad = "1.3.0"` mean in `Cargo.toml`?

recall.answer: `a`: `>=0.4.1, <0.5.0`, because the caret treats the first non-zero component as the breaking one. `b`: `>=1.2.0, <2.0.0`. `c`: exactly 2.0.3. npm's `^0.4.1` and `^1.2` allow the same ranges as the first two.
recall.question: Which versions can each requirement select: `a = "0.4.1"`, `b = "1.2"` and `c = "=2.0.3"`?

recall.answer: `src/main.rs` is the default binary and `src/lib.rs` the library; extra binaries go in `src/bin/`. `cargo test` builds the test targets and runs unit tests, integration tests in `tests/` and documentation examples, with no script entry needed.
recall.question: Which files define the default binary and the library target, and what replaces `npm test`?

writing.rule: In `Cargo.toml` a bare version such as `"1.3.0"` is a caret requirement, `>=1.3.0, <2.0.0`; pin exactly with `"=1.3.0"`, and let `Cargo.lock` record what was resolved.
writing.success: Your manifest uses `=` only where an exact pin is intended, and you can name the default binary and library paths without looking them up.
writing.summary: `package.json` becomes `Cargo.toml`, `package-lock.json` becomes `Cargo.lock`, and npm scripts become built-in Cargo commands, but a bare version number means something different.

lessons.title: Promises vs futures

answers: `saved invoice-7` then `done`, like calling an async function in Node.js
Only `done`: the future returned by `save` is never polled
Nothing: rustc rejects calling an `async fn` without `.await`
writing.exampleCaption: `created` prints before `fetching`: the future runs only when `block_on` polls it, and the unused one never runs.
writing.explanation:
Calling an async function in JavaScript runs its body synchronously up to the first `await`, and the event loop keeps the rest going. That is why the example prints `fetching` before `created`, and why the unused second call still logs. Calling a Rust `async fn` runs nothing: it returns a value that implements `Future`, a state machine waiting to be polled. Only polling, normally through `.await`, executes the body.

Rust has no built-in event loop. Something must poll the top-level future: an executor such as the Tokio runtime behind `#[tokio::main]`, or, in this example, a ten-line `block_on` that polls in a loop. That `block_on` only suits futures that never wait on I/O; a real runtime parks the thread and uses the `Waker` to resume work when a socket or timer is ready. `.await` itself is only allowed inside `async` functions and blocks (E0728).

Laziness has consequences you can use. A future that is dropped before it completes simply stops, which is how timeouts and `select!` cancel work, whereas a JavaScript promise cannot be cancelled from outside; there is only an `AbortSignal` the callee may honour. Writing `let pending = fetch_price();` and awaiting it later starts nothing early. To run several futures concurrently, combine them with `join!` or spawn them as tasks, the counterparts of `Promise.all` and of starting promises without awaiting them.

rustc helps with the most common mistake. A future that is created and never used triggers the `unused_must_use` warning, unused implementer of `Future` that must be used. Treat that warning as an error in async code; it almost always means a missing `.await`.
writing.feedback: The call creates a future and drops it at the end of the statement. rustc warns that it must be used, but the program builds and prints only `done`.
writing.question: What does the practice program print?

recall.answer: Only `end`. Each call creates a future without running it, `drop(a)` destroys one that was never polled, and `let _ = b;` does not poll the other. In JavaScript both calls would have logged immediately.
recall.question: What does this print, and why?

recall.answer: Node.js ships an event loop that runs promise callbacks and I/O. Rust's standard library defines the `Future` trait but no executor, so a library provides one: it polls futures, parks the thread while they are pending, and uses `Waker`s from timers and sockets to resume them. Choosing the runtime is part of the program's design.
recall.question: Why does Rust need a runtime such as Tokio when Node.js does not?

writing.rule: Futures are lazy: calling an `async fn` only creates a future, and no code inside it runs until something polls it.
writing.success: Your predictions match the program: `created` before `fetching`, and the unused future never prints.
writing.summary: A Promise starts running when it is created; a Rust future does nothing until it is polled, usually by `.await` inside a runtime such as Tokio.
